teachingStrategy:
══ Pattern A – newest FBISE model paper (“50% MCQs & 50% Descriptive”)
The most likely pattern for 2027–28, but confirm with FBISE.
- Theory paper: 60 marks.
- Section A (1 h 20 min): 60 MCQs × 0.5 = 30 marks: 40 straight MCQs + 20 scenario/stimulus MCQs (5 scenarios × 4).
- Section B: 6 short questions × 3 = 18 marks, each with an internal choice (OR).
- Section C: 2 long questions × 6 = 12 marks, each with an internal choice.
- Sections B and C together: 1 h 40 min.
- Only summative SLOs are examined; practical (PBA) SLOs are tested in the practical exam.
══ Pattern B – used in the Annual 2026 exam (Inclusive Scheme of Studies 2024)
- Section A: 12 MCQs × 1 = 12 marks (15 min).
- Section B: 10 short questions × 3 = 30 marks, each with an OR choice.
- Section C: 3 long questions × 6 = 18 marks, each with an OR choice (2 h 45 min for B + C).
- A list of useful formulas is printed at the bottom of the paper.
══ Older papers in your files
- Annual 2025, 2nd Annual 2025 and the Annual 2026 “Curriculum 2022-23 (Old)” Physics papers used 12 MCQs + 11 short (33) + 4 long (20). Their content is the same 2022-23 curriculum, so they are included as past-paper practice.
- The “Curriculum 2006 (OLD)” Physics papers and the 2023–2024 paper books follow the old syllabus and are not used.

chapters.title: Physical Quantities and Measurement
chapters.introduction:
Physics is built on measurement. This unit explains what physics is and its branches, the difference between physical and non-physical quantities, base and derived quantities, the seven SI base units, scientific notation and prefixes, scalars and vectors (including adding two vectors at right angles), measuring instruments – metre rule, vernier callipers, screw gauge, balances, measuring cylinder and stopwatch – and their least count, errors (systematic and random), precision and accuracy, significant figures and rounding off.

19 SLOs, all summative (8 are practical/PBA). Asked in every paper: prefix conversions (0.002 m → mm, 2000 ng → µg), scientific notation, base vs derived quantities with units, scalar vs vector, precision vs accuracy, digital balance giving different readings (random error), branches of physics, least count, significant figures.

19 SLOs, all summative (8 are practical/PBA). Asked in every paper: prefix conversions (0.002 m → mm, 2000 ng → µg), scientific notation, base vs derived quantities with units, scalar vs vector, precision vs accuracy, digital balance giving different readings (random error), branches of physics, least count, significant figures.
Note: Two exponents in the textbook numericals (Q IV 2a and 2b) are faint in the scan; they are read as 10⁻¹⁰ and 10⁻². The vernier and screw-gauge figures in Q IV 6–7 are too small in the scan to read the coinciding division with certainty, so the method is shown with the values that can be read.

══ 1.1 Physics, its branches and its role in technology (pp. 6–7) ══
Physics is the branch of science that studies matter, energy, space and time and their interactions. It is the most fundamental natural science: chemistry, biology, astronomy, geology and meteorology all use its principles (e.g. biology uses fluid physics to explain blood flow).
Physics and technology: computers, smartphones, the internet, rockets, space shuttles, magnetically levitating trains, PET scans, nuclear power and medical robots are all based on physics.
Main branches:
- Mechanics – motion of objects and the forces that cause it.
- Thermodynamics – heat, temperature and energy transfer (e.g. how an air-conditioner or freezer works).
- Optics – nature and behaviour of light (lenses, spectacles, microscopes).
- Oscillations and waves / acoustics – vibrations, sound and its transmission.
- Electromagnetism – electricity and magnetism together.
- Atomic physics – structure and properties of atoms.
- Nuclear physics – the nucleus and nuclear reactions (fission, fusion, radioactivity).
- Quantum physics/mechanics – behaviour of microscopic particles (electrons, photons).
- Relativity – motion at very high speeds and gravity.
- Astrophysics/astronomy – stars, planets and galaxies; cosmology – origin and evolution of the universe.
- Biophysics – physics of living things; geophysics – physics of the Earth; particle physics – fundamental particles.
Physics and mathematics: physics uses mathematics as its language and tool.
فزکس مادے، توانائی، خلا اور وقت اور ان کے باہمی تعامل کا علم ہے۔ یہ سب سے بنیادی قدرتی سائنس ہے۔ کمپیوٹر، موبائل، راکٹ اور طبی آلات سب فزکس پر مبنی ہیں۔ اہم شاخیں: میکینکس (حرکت اور قوت)، تھرموڈائنامکس (حرارت)، آپٹکس (روشنی)، الیکٹرو میگنیٹزم (بجلی اور مقناطیس)، نیوکلیئر فزکس (مرکزہ)، کوانٹم فزکس (خوردبینی ذرات)، فلکیاتی طبیعیات، بایو فزکس اور جیو فزکس۔

══ 1.2 Physical and non-physical quantities; base and derived quantities (pp. 8–10) ══
- Physical quantities can be measured: length, mass, time, density, temperature, force.
- Non-physical quantities cannot be measured: taste, feeling, love, beauty, colour preference.
A physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit: e.g. height = 1.65 m (1.65 = magnitude, metre = unit).
Measurement is the comparison of an unknown quantity with a standard; the standard is the unit. (The ancient Egyptians used the cubit – elbow to the tip of the middle finger – to build the pyramids.)
Base (fundamental) quantities are the simplest quantities from which all others are derived: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.
Derived quantities are obtained by multiplying or dividing base quantities: area, volume, speed, velocity, acceleration, force, pressure, energy, power, density, charge.
System of units: a complete set of units for all physical quantities. The International System of Units (SI, Système International d'Unités) has 7 base units.
[Table: Table 1.1 – SI base quantities and units]
Base quantity | Symbol | SI unit | Unit symbol
• Length | l | metre | m
• Mass | m | kilogram | kg
• Time | t | second | s
• Electric current | I | ampere | A
• Temperature | T | kelvin | K
• Amount of substance | n | mole | mol
• Luminous (light) intensity | Iᵥ | candela | cd
[Table: Table 1.2 – Some derived quantities]
Derived quantity | Symbol | SI unit | In base units
• Area | A | square metre | m²
• Volume | V | cubic metre | m³
• Speed, velocity | v | metre per second | m s⁻¹
• Acceleration | a | metre per second squared | m s⁻²
• Density | ρ | kilogram per cubic metre | kg m⁻³
• Force | F | newton (N) | kg m s⁻²
• Pressure | P | pascal (Pa) | N m⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²
• Energy, work | E, W | joule (J) | N m = kg m² s⁻²
• Power | P | watt (W) | J s⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻³
• Charge | Q | coulomb (C) | A s
Exam Tip: Base quantities involved: force (kg, m, s), pressure (kg, m, s), power (kg, m, s), charge (A, s).
طبعی مقداریں ناپی جا سکتی ہیں (لمبائی، کمیت، وقت)؛ غیر طبعی نہیں (ذائقہ، احساس)۔ ہر طبعی مقدار میں عدد اور اکائی ہوتی ہے۔ بنیادی مقداریں سات ہیں (لمبائی، کمیت، وقت، برقی رو، درجہ حرارت، مادے کی مقدار، روشنی کی شدت)؛ ان کو ضرب یا تقسیم کر کے ماخوذ مقداریں بنتی ہیں (رفتار، قوت، دباؤ، توانائی)۔

══ 1.3 Scientific notation and prefixes (pp. 10–13) ══
Scientific notation (standard form): a number is written as M × 10^n, where the mantissa M is ≥ 1 and < 10 and n is an integer (the exponent).
- Decimal moved left → n positive: 149 530 000 000 m = 1.4953 × 10¹¹ m (Earth–Sun distance).
- Decimal moved right → n negative: 0.0003 g = 3 × 10⁻⁴ g.
- Seconds in a day: 24 × 60 × 60 = 86 400 s = 8.64 × 10⁴ s.
- Width of observable universe ≈ 8.8 × 10²⁶ m; mass of Earth ≈ 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg.
Prefixes are words placed before a unit to show multiples or sub-multiples in powers of ten. Converting: write the number in powers of ten, then replace the power with its prefix.
- 1 ton = 1000 kg = 10⁶ g = 1 Mg; diameter of proton 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m = 1.7 fm.
- Larger unit → smaller unit: multiply; smaller → larger: divide.
- micro (10⁻⁶) is 1000 times smaller than milli (10⁻³), because 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³.
[Table: Table 1.3 – SI prefixes]
Prefix | Symbol | Multiplier | Prefix | Symbol | Multiplier
• exa | E | 10¹⁸ | deci | d | 10⁻¹
• peta | P | 10¹⁵ | centi | c | 10⁻²
• tera | T | 10¹² | milli | m | 10⁻³
• giga | G | 10⁹ | micro | µ | 10⁻⁶
• mega | M | 10⁶ | nano | n | 10⁻⁹
• kilo | k | 10³ | pico | p | 10⁻¹²
• hecto | h | 10² | femto | f | 10⁻¹⁵
• deca | da | 10¹ | atto | a | 10⁻¹⁸
Exam Tip: Exam favourites: 0.002 m = 2 mm; 5 × 10⁻⁶ s = 5000 ns = 5 µs; 3000 g = 3 kg; 2000 ng = 2 µg; 2 GB = 2000 MB; 1 pg = 10⁻¹² g.
سائنسی ترقیم میں عدد کو M × 10^n لکھتے ہیں جہاں M ایک اور دس کے درمیان ہو۔ اعشاریہ بائیں طرف ہٹے تو طاقت مثبت، دائیں طرف ہٹے تو منفی۔ سابقے (کلو، میگا، ملی، مائیکرو، نینو) دس کی طاقتوں کو آسان نام دیتے ہیں۔ بڑی اکائی سے چھوٹی میں ضرب اور چھوٹی سے بڑی میں تقسیم۔

══ 1.4 Scalars and vectors; resultant of two vectors at right angles (pp. 14–17) ══
- Scalar quantity: has magnitude only (number + unit). Examples: distance, speed, time, mass, energy, temperature, volume, density, work, power.
- Vector quantity: has magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, electric field strength, gravitational field strength.
Why? Speed of 20 m/s says nothing about direction, so it is a scalar; velocity of 20 m/s north needs a direction, so it is a vector. Energy has no direction (scalar); displacement is the straight-line distance in a given direction from start to finish (vector).
Representing a vector:
- Symbolically: a bold letter (F) or a letter with an arrow over it (F⃗); its magnitude is written |F| or F.
- Graphically: by an arrow – the length (to a chosen scale) shows magnitude, the arrowhead shows direction.
Steps to represent a vector in a coordinate system: (1) draw coordinate axes (N, E, S, W or x, y); (2) choose a suitable scale, e.g. 5 km = 1 cm; (3) draw a line from the origin in the given direction, cut to the scaled length; (4) put an arrowhead at the end. Example: helicopter displacement 20 km at 60° north of west → 4 cm line at 60° from the west axis toward north.
Vector addition (head-to-tail rule): draw the vectors to scale, placing the tail of each at the head of the previous one; the resultant joins the tail of the first to the head of the last. Order does not matter (A + B = B + A).
Two vectors at right angles: the resultant is the hypotenuse:
R = √(A² + B²), direction θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) from A.
اسکیلر میں صرف مقدار ہوتی ہے (فاصلہ، رفتار، وقت، کمیت، توانائی، درجہ حرارت)۔ ویکٹر میں مقدار اور سمت دونوں ہوتی ہیں (ڈسپلیسمنٹ، ولاسٹی، اسراع، قوت، وزن، مومینٹم)۔ ویکٹر کو تیر سے ظاہر کرتے ہیں: لمبائی مقدار اور تیر کی نوک سمت بتاتی ہے۔ دو عمودی ویکٹرز کا حاصل R = √(A² + B²)۔

══ 1.5 Measuring length: metre rule, vernier callipers and screw gauge (pp. 17–23) ══
Least count: the smallest value that can be measured on an instrument's scale. Every measurement is limited by it.
Metre rule and measuring tape: 1 m long with 1000 mm divisions → least count 1 mm (0.1 cm). Read with the eye directly above the mark (avoid parallax). Measuring tapes measure larger distances.
Vernier callipers: measures a fraction of the smallest main-scale division by sliding a vernier scale over the main scale. Parts: main scale with fixed jaw, sliding vernier scale with moving jaw, outside jaws (external diameter, thickness), inside jaws (internal diameter of a pipe/beaker), depth probe (depth of a hole), retainer screw.
Least count = smallest main-scale division ÷ number of vernier divisions = 1 mm ÷ 10 = 0.1 mm (0.01 cm). Digital vernier: 0.01 mm.
Reading: total = main-scale reading (before vernier zero) + (coinciding vernier division × least count) ± zero correction.
Zero error: when the jaws are closed, the vernier zero should coincide with the main zero. If the vernier zero is to the right → positive zero error (subtract it); to the left → negative zero error (add it).
Micrometer screw gauge: measures even smaller lengths (thickness of paper, diameter of a thin wire) by rotating a circular (thimble) scale. Parts: U-shaped frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve with linear (main) scale and datum line, thimble with circular scale, ratchet.
- Pitch = distance moved by the spindle in one complete rotation (e.g. 0.5 mm).
- Least count = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions = 0.5 mm ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.
Reading: total = main-scale reading + (circular division on datum line × least count) ± zero correction. Turn the ratchet until it clicks so that the object is not squeezed.
Precision order: metre rule (1 mm) < vernier (0.1 mm) < screw gauge (0.01 mm). A screw gauge is more precise because its least count is 10 times smaller.
[Table: Choosing a length instrument]
Instrument | Least count | Best for
• Metre rule | 1 mm | Lengths of books, tables
• Measuring tape | 1 mm | Long distances (room, field)
• Vernier callipers | 0.1 mm (digital 0.01 mm) | External/internal diameter (pipe, beaker), depth
• Screw gauge | 0.01 mm | Thickness of paper, diameter of a thin wire or small ball
Exam Tip: Internal diameter of a pipe or beaker → vernier callipers (inside jaws). Thickness of a page or a thin wire → screw gauge.
لیسٹ کاؤنٹ کسی آلے سے ناپی جانے والی سب سے چھوٹی قدر ہے۔ میٹر رول کا لیسٹ کاؤنٹ 1 mm، ورنیئر کیلیپر کا 0.1 mm (مین اسکیل کی چھوٹی تقسیم ÷ ورنیئر کی تقسیموں کی تعداد) اور اسکرو گیج کا 0.01 mm (پچ ÷ دائری اسکیل کی تقسیمیں) ہے۔ اسکرو گیج سب سے زیادہ یکساں پیمائش دیتا ہے۔ صفر کی غلطی کو درست کرنا ضروری ہے۔

══ 1.6 Measuring mass, volume and time (pp. 23–25) ══
Mass:
- Physical (beam) balance: a beam on a knife-edge with two pans, a pointer and levelling screws, kept in a glass case (so dust and air do not affect it); compares the object with standard masses from a weight box; measures to milligrams.
- Electronic (digital) balance: quick and precise (e.g. 0.01 g); tare/zero it before use; keep it on a level surface away from draughts.
- A force meter (spring balance) measures weight in newtons.
Volume with a measuring cylinder:
- Liquid: pour into the cylinder, place it on a level surface and read the bottom of the meniscus (top for mercury) with the eye level with it.
- Irregular solid (stone): put some water in the cylinder, note V₁; lower the stone gently on a thread until fully immersed, note V₂; volume of stone = V₂ − V₁ (displacement method). A displacement (overflow) can may be used for larger objects.
- Precautions: cylinder vertical on a flat surface, eye level, no air bubbles, object fully immersed, no splashing.
Time: stopwatch – mechanical/analogue (least count about 0.1 s, wound by a knob; a second hand on a dial) and digital (least count 0.01 s, start/stop and reset buttons, lap/split times). Human reaction time (≈ 0.2 s) limits hand timing, so time many oscillations (e.g. 10) and divide to find the period of a pendulum.
[Table: Mechanical vs digital stopwatch]
Mechanical stopwatch | Digital stopwatch
• Dial with second hand | Digital display
• Least count about 0.1 s | Least count 0.01 s
• Needs winding; no battery | Needs a battery
• Lower precision | Higher precision; can record lap times
کمیت کے لیے فزیکل بیلنس اور الیکٹرانک بیلنس؛ وزن کے لیے اسپرنگ بیلنس۔ پیمائشی سلنڈر میں مائع کا حجم مینسکس کے نچلے حصے کو آنکھ کی سطح پر رکھ کر پڑھیں۔ بے قاعدہ پتھر کا حجم = پتھر ڈالنے کے بعد کا حجم − پہلے کا حجم۔ مکینیکل اسٹاپ واچ کا لیسٹ کاؤنٹ تقریباً 0.1 s اور ڈیجیٹل کا 0.01 s ہے۔

══ 1.7 Errors, averages, precision and accuracy (pp. 25–27) ══
Error is the uncertainty in a measurement; no measurement is perfectly exact.
Systematic errors – occur consistently in one direction (always too high or too low):
- instrumental errors (poor calibration, zero error),
- faulty technique or changing conditions (temperature, wind),
- personal bias or wrong set-up (always reading from one angle – parallax).
Reduced by calibrating, correcting zero error, better instruments and technique. Repeating does not remove them.
Random errors – unpredictable, scattered on both sides (reaction time, fluctuations, a digital balance giving slightly different readings each time). Reduced by taking repeated readings and finding the average (mean).
Average value: time 10 (or 20) oscillations of a pendulum and divide by 10 to get one period; measure the thickness of 100 pages and divide by 100.
Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other (consistency/reproducibility) – depends on the instrument's least count and the care of the user.
Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true (accepted) value – depends on absence of systematic error.
Dartboard: darts close together and at the bullseye = accurate and precise; close together but off-centre = precise, not accurate; scattered round the centre = accurate on average, not precise.
Example: a scale always reading 0.5 kg too high but within 0.1 kg each time is precise but not accurate.
[Table: Precision vs accuracy]
Precision | Accuracy
• Closeness of repeated readings to each other | Closeness of a reading to the true value
• Shows random error | Shows systematic error
• Improved by a smaller least count and care | Improved by calibration and removing zero error
• Example: 5.01, 5.02, 5.01 g | Example: average 6.00 g for a 6.00 g mass
[Table: Systematic vs random error]
Systematic error | Random error
• Same direction every time | Unpredictable, either direction
• Zero error, poor calibration, parallax, bias | Reaction time, fluctuations, noise
• Removed by calibration / correction | Reduced by averaging repeated readings
منظم غلطی ہر بار ایک ہی سمت میں ہوتی ہے (صفر کی غلطی، غلط کیلیبریشن)؛ آلے کو درست کر کے دور ہوتی ہے۔ بے ترتیب غلطی غیر متوقع ہوتی ہے (ردعمل کا وقت)؛ بار بار پیمائش کر کے اوسط لینے سے کم ہوتی ہے۔ یکسانیت (precision) بار بار کی پیمائشوں کا آپس میں قریب ہونا، اور درستگی (accuracy) حقیقی قدر کے قریب ہونا ہے۔

══ 1.8 Significant figures, rounding off and estimates (pp. 28–31) ══
Significant figures are all the accurately known digits plus the first doubtful digit of a measurement. A pencil between 17.0 and 17.1 cm is reported as 17.05 cm (17.0 certain, the last 5 estimated).
Rules:
1. All non-zero digits are significant: 23.457 → 5.
2. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant: 100.8 → 4.
3. Leading zeros (before the first non-zero digit) are not significant: 0.0029 → 2.
4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 0.00290 → 3; 210.0 → 4.
5. Trailing zeros in a whole number (29 000) are ambiguous – write in scientific notation: 2.90 × 10⁴ (3 s.f.).
6. Exact counted values (57 000 books counted one by one) have unlimited significant figures.
Rounding off: look at the digit to the right of the last digit kept: less than 5 → leave it (round down); 5 or more → add 1 (round up); replace dropped whole-number digits by zeros.
- 3.876 → 3.88; 657.873 → 657.87; 0.0857 → 0.09 (2 d.p.)
- 24.68 → 24.7; 0.07683 → 0.0768; 7847 → 7850 (3 s.f.)
Answer in correct significant figures: a calculated result should not have more significant figures than the least precise data (e.g. 500 N ÷ 8000 N/m = 0.0625 → 0.063 m to 2 s.f.).
Reasonable estimates: mass of an apple ≈ 200 g; physics textbook ≈ 1 kg; height of a door ≈ 2 m; your age ≈ 15 years ≈ 4.7 × 10⁸ s.
اہم ہندسے وہ تمام یقینی ہندسے اور پہلا مشکوک ہندسہ ہیں۔ غیر صفر ہندسے ہمیشہ اہم؛ دو ہندسوں کے درمیان صفر اہم؛ شروع کے صفر غیر اہم؛ اعشاریہ کے بعد آخری صفر اہم۔ گول کرنے میں اگلا ہندسہ 5 سے کم ہو تو ویسا ہی چھوڑیں، 5 یا زیادہ ہو تو ایک بڑھا دیں۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Adding two vectors at right angles (head to tail): A = 3 units east, B = 4 units north → R = 5 units at 53° north of east.
2. Reading a vernier callipers: Main-scale reading is taken just before the vernier zero; add (coinciding vernier line × 0.1 mm).
chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 1 in one page
- Physics: matter, energy, space, time. Branches: mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, acoustics, electromagnetism, atomic, nuclear, quantum, relativity, astrophysics, cosmology, biophysics, geophysics, particle physics.
- Physical (measurable: number + unit) vs non-physical (taste, feeling). Base quantities (7): length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, luminous intensity cd. Derived: speed m s⁻¹, force N = kg m s⁻², pressure Pa, energy J, power W, charge C = A s.
- Scientific notation: M × 10^n, 1 ≤ M < 10. Prefixes: T 10¹², G 10⁹, M 10⁶, k 10³, c 10⁻², m 10⁻³, µ 10⁻⁶, n 10⁻⁹, p 10⁻¹². micro is 1000× smaller than milli.
- Scalar (distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature) vs vector (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, field strength). Arrow to scale; head-to-tail; R = √(A² + B²), θ = tan⁻¹(B/A).
- Least count: metre rule 1 mm; vernier 1 mm/10 = 0.1 mm (inside jaws for internal diameter, depth probe); screw gauge pitch/50 = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm (ratchet). Zero error: positive → subtract, negative → add.
- Mass: physical balance, electronic balance (tare). Volume: measuring cylinder, read bottom of meniscus at eye level; stone = V₂ − V₁. Time: mechanical 0.1 s, digital 0.01 s; time 10 oscillations.
- Errors: systematic (one direction; calibrate) vs random (scatter; average). Precision = repeat readings agree; accuracy = close to true value.
- Significant figures: non-zero, sandwiched zeros, trailing zeros after decimal count; leading zeros don’t. Rounding: < 5 down, ≥ 5 up.

فزکس مادے اور توانائی کا علم ہے۔ سات بنیادی مقداریں اور SI اکائیاں یاد کریں۔ سائنسی ترقیم M × 10^n اور سابقے (کلو، ملی، مائیکرو، نینو)۔ اسکیلر صرف مقدار، ویکٹر مقدار اور سمت۔ میٹر رول 1 mm، ورنیئر 0.1 mm، اسکرو گیج 0.01 mm۔ منظم غلطی کیلیبریشن سے، بے ترتیب غلطی اوسط سے کم ہوتی ہے۔ یکسانیت اور درستگی میں فرق یاد رکھیں۔

Exam Focus: 19 SLOs, all summative (8 are practical/PBA). chapters.definitions:
• Physics (طبیعیات) [p. 6]: The branch of science that studies matter, energy, space and time and their interactions.
• Physical quantity (طبعی مقدار) [p. 8]: A quantity that can be measured; it has a numerical magnitude and a unit.
• Non-physical quantity (غیر طبعی مقدار) [p. 8]: A quantity that cannot be measured, e.g. taste, feeling.
• Measurement (پیمائش) [p. 8]: Comparison of an unknown physical quantity with a standard to see how large or small it is.
• Unit (اکائی) [p. 8]: The standard with which a physical quantity is compared.
• Base quantities (بنیادی مقداریں) [p. 8]: The seven simplest quantities from which all others are derived (length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity).
• Derived quantities (ماخوذ مقداریں) [p. 8]: Quantities obtained by multiplying or dividing base quantities, e.g. speed, force, pressure.
• System International (SI) (بین الاقوامی نظامِ اکائیات) [p. 8]: The internationally agreed system of units with seven base units.
• Scientific notation (سائنسی ترقیم) [p. 10]: Writing a number as M × 10^n where 1 ≤ M < 10 and n is an integer.
• Prefix (سابقہ) [p. 11]: A word or symbol placed before a unit to show a multiple or sub-multiple in powers of ten.
• Scalar (اسکیلر) [p. 14]: A quantity described by magnitude only.
• Vector (ویکٹر) [p. 14]: A quantity described by magnitude and direction.
• Resultant vector (حاصل ویکٹر) [p. 16]: A single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors combined.
• Least count (لیسٹ کاؤنٹ) [p. 17]: The minimum value that can be measured on the scale of an instrument.
• Vernier callipers (ورنیئر کیلیپر) [p. 18]: A device that measures a fraction of the smallest main-scale division by sliding a vernier scale over it.
• Zero error (صفر کی غلطی) [p. 19]: A reading shown by an instrument when the true value is zero.
• Screw gauge (اسکرو گیج) [p. 21]: A device that measures a fraction of the smallest scale division by rotating a circular scale over it.
• Pitch (پچ) [p. 21]: The distance moved by the spindle of a screw gauge in one complete rotation of the thimble.
• Error (غلطی / عدم یقینیت) [p. 25]: The uncertainty that arises in a measurement.
• Systematic error (منظم غلطی) [p. 25]: An error that occurs consistently in one direction.
• Random error (بے ترتیب غلطی) [p. 26]: An unpredictable error that varies from reading to reading.
• Precision (یکسانیت) [p. 26]: The degree of agreement between repeated measurements of the same quantity.
• Accuracy (درستگی) [p. 27]: How close a measured value is to the true or accepted value.
• Significant figures (اہم ہندسے) [p. 28]: All the accurately known digits and the first doubtful digit in a measurement.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Measurement (پیمائش): Comparing with a standard
• Unit (اکائی): Standard of measurement
• Base quantity (بنیادی مقدار): Independent quantity
• Derived quantity (ماخوذ مقدار): Formed from base quantities
• Prefix (سابقہ): Power-of-ten word
• Scalar (اسکیلر): Magnitude only
• Vector (ویکٹر): Magnitude + direction
• Resultant (حاصل): Combined vector
• Least count (لیسٹ کاؤنٹ): Smallest readable value
• Zero error (صفر کی غلطی): Reading when true value is zero
• Precision (یکسانیت): Agreement of repeats
• Accuracy (درستگی): Closeness to true value
• Significant figures (اہم ہندسے): Reliable digits
• Meniscus (ہلالی سطح): Curved liquid surface
• Estimate (اندازہ): Approximate value
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Scientific notation: number = M × 10^n, 1 ≤ M < 10
• Resultant of perpendicular vectors: R = √(A² + B²); θ = tan⁻¹(B/A)
• Least count of vernier callipers: LC = smallest main-scale division ÷ number of vernier divisions (1 mm/10 = 0.1 mm)
• Vernier reading: main-scale reading + (coinciding division × LC) − zero error
• Least count of screw gauge: LC = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions (0.5 mm/50 = 0.01 mm)
• Screw-gauge reading: main-scale reading + (circular division × LC) − zero error
• Volume of irregular solid: V = V₂ − V₁ (Displacement method)
• Period of pendulum (average): T = total time for n oscillations ÷ n
• Unit conversions: 1 km = 10³ m; 1 mm = 10⁻³ m; 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m; 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• R = √(A² + B²) — Magnitude of the resultant of two perpendicular vectors (Pythagoras).
• θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) — Direction of the resultant measured from vector A.
• LC = 1 mm ÷ 10 = 0.1 mm — Vernier callipers.
• LC = 0.5 mm ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm — Screw gauge.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Can a vector have zero magnitude?
   Answer: Yes – a null (zero) vector, e.g. displacement after returning to the starting point.
2. Why is it better to measure the thickness of 100 pages and divide by 100?
   Answer: The total is large compared with the least count, so the percentage error is much smaller (averaging also reduces random error).
3. Is “taste” a physical quantity?
   Answer: No – it cannot be measured with an instrument and a unit; it is non-physical.
4. Two students measure the same rod as 15.2 cm and 15.20 cm. Which is more precise?
   Answer: 15.20 cm – it shows one more significant figure, i.e. a smaller least count.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Estimate the mass of an apple and the height of a classroom door.
   Answer: About 200 g (0.2 kg); about 2 m.
2. A tailor and a carpenter both measure length. Why does the tailor use a measuring tape and the carpenter a steel rule?
   Answer: The tape is flexible for curved body measurements; the steel rule is rigid for straight, precise wood measurements.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Convert to standard form: (a) 149 530 000 000 m (b) 0.0003 g (c) seconds in a day. (Example 1.1)
   Solution: (a) Move the decimal 11 places left: 1.4953 × 10¹¹ m. (b) Move 4 places right: 3 × 10⁻⁴ g. (c) 24 × 60 × 60 = 86 400 s = 8.64 × 10⁴ s.

2. Write in standard form and with a prefix: (a) one ton of rice in grams (b) diameter of a proton 0.0000000000000017 m. (Example 1.2)
   Solution: (a) 1 ton = 1000 kg = 1 000 000 g = 1.0 × 10⁶ g = 1 Mg. (b) 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m = 1.7 fm (femto = 10⁻¹⁵).

3. Two vectors A = 6 N (east) and B = 8 N (north) act at right angles. Find the resultant.
   Given: A = 6 N east, B = 8 N north (perpendicular)
   Required: Resultant R and its direction θ
   Formula: R = √(A² + B²), θ = tan⁻¹(B/A)
   Substitution: R = √(6² + 8²); θ = tan⁻¹(8/6)
   Calculation: R = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10; θ = tan⁻¹(1.33) ≈ 53°
   Final Answer: R = 10 N at 53° north of east

4. Find the number of significant figures and write in scientific notation: (a) 100.8 s (b) 0.00580 km (c) 210.0 g. (Example 1.3)
   Solution: (a) 4 s.f. → 1.008 × 10² s. (b) 3 s.f. (leading zeros not significant, final zero is) → 5.80 × 10⁻³ km. (c) 4 s.f. → 2.100 × 10² g.

5. Round off: (a) to two decimal places 3.876, 657.873, 0.0857 (b) to three significant figures 24.68, 0.07683, 7847. (Example 1.4)
   Solution: (a) 3.88, 657.87, 0.09 (b) 24.7, 0.0768, 7850.

6. A vernier callipers has 1 mm main-scale divisions and 10 vernier divisions. The main-scale reading is 2.4 cm and the 7th vernier line coincides. Zero error is +0.02 cm. Find the corrected length.
   Given: MSR = 2.4 cm, coinciding division = 7, LC = 0.01 cm, zero error = +0.02 cm
   Required: Corrected reading
   Formula: Reading = MSR + (n × LC) − zero error
   Substitution: = 2.4 + (7 × 0.01) − 0.02
   Calculation: = 2.4 + 0.07 − 0.02 = 2.45
   Final Answer: 2.45 cm


══ ADDITIONAL SLO NUMERICAL PRACTICE ══

1. Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
   Given: 72 km/h; 1 km = 1000 m; 1 h = 3600 s
   Required: speed in m/s
   Formula: m/s = km/h × 1000/3600
   Substitution: 72 × 1000/3600
   Calculation: 72 000/3600 = 20
   Final Answer: 20 m/s

2. Find the average period if 20 oscillations of a pendulum take 40.6 s.
   Given: n = 20, total time = 40.6 s
   Required: Period T
   Formula: T = total time ÷ n
   Substitution: T = 40.6 ÷ 20
   Calculation: = 2.03
   Final Answer: 2.03 s
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 1 Exercises (32–34):

— Exercise MCQs —
1. Which one of the following units is not a derived unit? → B (kilogram) | Kilogram is a base unit.
2. Amount of a substance in terms of numbers is measured in: → D (mole) | Mole is the SI unit of amount of substance.
3. The number of significant figures in 0.00650 s is: → B (3) | 6, 5 and the trailing 0 are significant.
4. Which of the following numbers shows 4 significant digits? → D (0.001248) | 1, 2, 4, 8. (9000.8 has 5; 5174.00 has 6.)
5. Which of the following prefixes represents the largest value? → C (peta) | peta = 10¹⁵.
6. Micrometer can be used to measure: → C (length) | A micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths.
7. The instrument that best measures the internal diameter of a pipe is: → B (vernier callipers) | Inside jaws of vernier callipers.
8. Least count of screw gauge is 0.01 mm. If the main-scale reading is zero and the third line of its circular scale coincides with the datum line, the measurement is: → C (0.03 mm) | 0 + 3 × 0.01 = 0.03 mm.
9. 9.483 × 10³ m is the standard form of: → D (9483 m) | Move decimal 3 places right.
10. Which of the following is a base unit? → D (mole) | Mole is one of the seven base units.
11. The number having one significant digit is: → D (6 × 10²) | Only the 6 is significant.
12. Ratio of millimetre to micrometre is: → C (1000) | 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 1000 (no unit).
13. 0.2 mm in units of metres is: → C (both A and B) | 0.2 × 10⁻³ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.0002 m.

— Q II. Short-answer questions —
1 How does physics play an important role in our life?
   Answer: Physics explains everyday phenomena and gives us technology: electricity and appliances, mobile phones and internet, transport (cars, aeroplanes), medical imaging (X-rays, PET, MRI), weather forecasting and energy generation. It also underlies chemistry, biology and engineering.
2 Estimate your age in minutes and seconds.
   Answer: For a 15-year-old: 15 × 365 × 24 × 60 ≈ 7.9 × 10⁶ minutes; × 60 ≈ 4.7 × 10⁸ seconds. (Use your own age; ignoring leap days is fine for an estimate.)
3 What base quantities are involved in these derived quantities: force, pressure, power and charge?
   Answer: Force (kg m s⁻²): mass, length, time. Pressure (kg m⁻¹ s⁻²): mass, length, time. Power (kg m² s⁻³): mass, length, time. Charge (A s): electric current and time.
4 Show that prefix micro is a thousand times smaller than prefix milli.
   Answer: milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶. 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³ = 1000, so 1 µ is 1000 times smaller than 1 m (e.g. 1 mm = 1000 µm).
5 Justify that displacement is a vector quantity while energy is a scalar quantity.
   Answer: Displacement is the shortest distance from start to end in a particular direction; 5 m east and 5 m west are different displacements, so it needs direction → vector. Energy (e.g. 100 J) is completely described by its magnitude; it has no direction → scalar.
6 A screw gauge can give more precise length than vernier callipers. Briefly explain why.
   Answer: Its least count (0.01 mm) is ten times smaller than that of vernier callipers (0.1 mm), so it can read a smaller fraction of a millimetre and repeated readings agree more closely.
7 Differentiate between a mechanical stopwatch and a digital stopwatch.
   Answer: Mechanical: dial and second hand, wound by a knob, least count about 0.1 s. Digital: electronic display, battery-operated, least count 0.01 s, can record lap/split times; more precise.
8 How is a measuring cylinder used to measure the volume of an irregular-shaped stone?
   Answer: Pour water into the cylinder and note V₁. Tie the stone to a thread and lower it gently until fully immersed; note the new level V₂ (bottom of meniscus, eye level). Volume of stone = V₂ − V₁.
9 What precautions should be kept in mind while taking a measurement using a measuring cylinder?
   Answer: Place it vertically on a level surface; read the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it (avoid parallax); avoid air bubbles and splashing; make sure the object is fully immersed; use a cylinder of suitable size.
10 Why do we need to consider significant digits in measurements?
   Answer: They show how precise a measurement is (which digits are reliable and which one is estimated). Reporting more digits than the instrument can give would be misleading; results of calculations must keep a sensible number of significant figures.
11 How can random error be reduced?
   Answer: By taking many repeated readings and finding their average, timing many oscillations instead of one, using instruments with a smaller least count, and controlling conditions (draughts, vibrations).
12 Differentiate between precision and accuracy.
   Answer: Precision: closeness of repeated readings to each other (consistency). Accuracy: closeness of a reading to the true value. A balance that always reads 0.5 kg too high but gives the same value each time is precise but not accurate.

— Q III. Long-answer questions —
1 Define physics. Describe its revolutionary role in technology.
   Answer: Physics is the study of matter, energy, space and time and their interactions. Its laws led to: electricity generation and appliances; electronics and computers (semiconductors, transistors); communication (radio, mobile phones, internet, satellites); transport (engines, aeroplanes, maglev trains, rockets); medicine (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI, PET, radiotherapy, laser surgery); energy (nuclear power, solar cells); and space exploration. Technology in turn gives physicists better instruments.
2 List with a brief description the different branches of physics.
   Answer: Mechanics (motion and forces); thermodynamics (heat and energy); optics (light); oscillations, waves and acoustics (vibrations and sound); electromagnetism (electricity and magnetism); atomic physics (atoms); nuclear physics (nucleus, fission, fusion); quantum physics (microscopic particles); relativity (very high speeds, gravity); astrophysics and cosmology (stars, universe); biophysics, geophysics and particle physics.
3 What are physical quantities? Distinguish between base and derived physical quantities. Give at least three examples showing that derived quantities are derived from base quantities.
   Answer: Physical quantities are measurable quantities with a magnitude and unit. Base quantities are the seven independent quantities (length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity); derived quantities are formed from them. Examples: speed = length/time (m s⁻¹); density = mass/volume = mass/length³ (kg m⁻³); force = mass × acceleration = mass × length/time² (kg m s⁻² = N); pressure = force/area (kg m⁻¹ s⁻² = Pa).
4 What do you mean by the unit of a physical quantity? Define base units and derived units.
   Answer: A unit is the standard with which a quantity is compared, e.g. metre for length. Base units are the units of the seven base quantities (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd), defined independently. Derived units are combinations of base units, e.g. m s⁻¹, N = kg m s⁻², J = kg m² s⁻², Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
5 What are prefixes? What is their use in measurements?
   Answer: Prefixes are words/symbols placed before units to represent powers of ten (kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, tera 10¹², deci 10⁻¹, centi 10⁻², milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, pico 10⁻¹²). They let very large and small measurements be written compactly and conveniently, e.g. 0.000 000 5 m = 500 nm; 5 000 000 W = 5 MW.
6 What is scientific notation (standard form)? Give at least five examples.
   Answer: Writing a number as M × 10^n with one non-zero digit before the decimal point (1 ≤ M < 10). Examples: 1234 m = 1.234 × 10³ m; 0.000023 s = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ s; 86 400 s = 8.64 × 10⁴ s; mass of Earth 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg; Earth–Sun distance 1.5 × 10¹¹ m; diameter of proton 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
7 Describe the construction and working of vernier callipers in detail.
   Answer: Construction: a steel main scale (mm) with a fixed jaw; a sliding vernier scale with a moving jaw; outside jaws (external diameter), inside jaws (internal diameter), depth probe, retainer screw. Least count = 1 mm ÷ 10 = 0.1 mm. Working: check zero error by closing the jaws; place the object between the outside jaws; note the main-scale reading just before the vernier zero; find the vernier line that coincides with a main-scale line; reading = MSR + (coinciding division × LC); subtract a positive or add a negative zero error.
8 What is a screw gauge? What are its pitch and least count? How is it used to measure the thickness of a thin copper wire?
   Answer: A micrometer screw gauge measures very small lengths by rotating a thimble (circular scale) over a linear scale. Pitch = distance moved by the spindle in one rotation (e.g. 0.5 mm); least count = pitch ÷ circular divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. Use: find zero error with anvil and spindle closed; place the wire between anvil and spindle; turn the ratchet until it clicks; read the linear scale (MSR) and the circular division on the datum line; diameter = MSR + (division × 0.01 mm) − zero error; repeat at different places and average.
9 Define error. Differentiate between random and systematic error. How can these errors be reduced?
   Answer: Error is the uncertainty in a measurement. Systematic: same direction each time (zero error, poor calibration, parallax, bias) – reduced by calibrating, correcting zero error, better technique and instruments. Random: unpredictable variation (reaction time, fluctuations) – reduced by repeated readings and averaging, timing many oscillations.
10 Differentiate between scalars and vectors. Justify that distance, speed, mass and energy are scalars while displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors.
   Answer: Scalars need only magnitude; vectors need magnitude and direction. Distance (total path length), speed (distance per time), mass (quantity of matter) and energy are fully described by a number and unit. Displacement (straight-line change of position in a direction), velocity (rate of displacement), acceleration (rate of change of velocity) and force (push/pull acting in a direction) change their effect when their direction changes, so they are vectors and add by the head-to-tail rule.
11 Justify and illustrate the use of a measuring cylinder to measure the volume of a liquid.
   Answer: A measuring cylinder is graduated in cm³ (mL) and gives a quick, reasonably accurate volume. Place it on a level surface, pour in the liquid, wait for it to settle, and read the bottom of the meniscus (top for mercury) with the eye level with the surface. Choose a cylinder whose capacity is close to the volume to be measured for better precision.
12 Differentiate between precision and accuracy.
   Answer: See short question 12 and topic 1.7: precision = agreement among repeated readings (random error, least count); accuracy = closeness to true value (systematic error, calibration). Dartboard illustration: tight cluster at centre = both; tight cluster off-centre = precise only; scattered round centre = accurate on average but not precise.

— Exercise Numerical Problems —
1. Write in scientific notation: (a) 1234 m (b) 0.000023 s (c) 469.3 × 10⁵ m (d) 0.00985 × 10⁷ s
   Solution: (a) 1.234 × 10³ m (b) 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ s (c) 4.693 × 10² × 10⁵ = 4.693 × 10⁷ m (d) 9.85 × 10⁻³ × 10⁷ = 9.85 × 10⁴ s
2. Express using prefixes: (a) 27.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (b) 0.00023 × 10⁻² s
   Solution: (a) 27.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 2.75 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.75 nm. (b) 0.00023 × 10⁻² s = 2.3 × 10⁻⁶ s = 2.3 µs.
3. A boy is 15 years 2 months and 10 days old. Convert his age into (a) seconds (b) milliseconds (c) megaseconds.
   Solution: 
4. How many kilometres are there in 25 micrometres?
   Solution: 
5. Find the pitch/least count of (a) vernier callipers: smallest main-scale division 1 mm, 20 vernier divisions (b) screw gauge: smallest main-scale division 0.5 mm, 50 circular divisions.
   Solution: (a) LC = 1 mm ÷ 20 = 0.05 mm. (b) Pitch = 0.5 mm (one rotation moves one smallest division); LC = 0.5 ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.
6. Look at the vernier-callipers figure: (a) main-scale reading (b) coinciding vernier division (c) total reading.
   Solution: Method: main-scale reading is the mark just before the vernier zero – in the figure the vernier zero lies just past 2.5 cm. Find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main-scale line (n). Total = 2.5 cm + n × 0.01 cm. For example, if the 4th line coincides, the reading is 2.54 cm.
7. Look at the screw-gauge figure (steel ball between anvil and thimble): (a) main-scale reading (b) coinciding circular division (c) diameter of the ball.
   Solution: Method: main-scale reading = last visible mark on the sleeve (about 6 mm in the figure); circular-scale reading = division on the datum line × 0.01 mm; diameter = MSR + circular reading (− zero error). E.g. 6 mm + 15 × 0.01 mm = 6.15 mm if the 15th division is on the datum line.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] Convert using prefixes: (a) 0.002 m into mm (b) 5 × 10⁻⁶ s into ns (c) 3000 g into kg.
   Answer: (a) 0.002 m × 1000 = 2 mm (b) 5 × 10⁻⁶ s ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 5000 ns (c) 3000 ÷ 1000 = 3 kg.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B)] Briefly describe scalar and vector quantities with one example each.
   Answer: Scalar: magnitude only, e.g. mass 5 kg. Vector: magnitude and direction, e.g. velocity 20 m/s north. Vectors are drawn as arrows and added head-to-tail.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B)] Briefly describe the branches: (a) optics (b) cosmology (c) biophysics.
   Answer: (a) Optics: study of light and its behaviour (lenses, mirrors, spectacles). (b) Cosmology: origin, structure and evolution of the universe. (c) Biophysics: physics applied to living things (nerve signals, blood flow, medical imaging).

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] Briefly describe: (a) astronomy (b) particle physics (c) geophysics.
   Answer: (a) Astronomy: study of stars, planets and other celestial bodies. (b) Particle physics: fundamental particles (quarks, electrons) and forces. (c) Geophysics: physics of the Earth – earthquakes, magnetic field, interior.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B, D)] A digital balance gives slightly different readings each time a stone is placed on it: (a) identify the error (b) how can this error be fixed?
   Answer: (a) Random error (readings scatter unpredictably; draughts, vibration, placing). (b) Take several readings and find the average; place the balance on a firm level surface away from draughts; tare it before each reading. (If all readings were shifted the same way, it would be a systematic/zero error fixed by taring/calibration.)

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B, D); AF Model Paper] Compare precision and accuracy in measurements.
   Answer: Precision = how close repeated readings are to each other; accuracy = how close a reading is to the true value. Precise but inaccurate: consistent readings with a zero error. Improve precision with smaller least count and averaging; improve accuracy by calibration.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] What is meant by precision? How can a measurement be precise but not accurate? (example)
   Answer: Precision is the closeness of repeated readings. A thermometer that always reads 2 °C too high gives the same value each time (precise) but is not close to the true temperature (not accurate).

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D); Model Paper (50%)] What is meant by base and derived quantities? Give one example of each.
   Answer: Base: independent quantities, e.g. mass (kg). Derived: formed from base quantities, e.g. speed (m s⁻¹) = length/time.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Curriculum 2022-23, old scheme)] Convert 0.00045 m into (a) millimetres (b) micrometres.
   Answer: (a) 0.00045 × 10³ = 0.45 mm (b) 0.00045 × 10⁶ = 450 µm.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] Enlist any three base physical quantities with their names, symbols and units.
   Answer: Length (l) – metre (m); mass (m) – kilogram (kg); time (t) – second (s). (Also current – ampere A; temperature – kelvin K; amount – mole mol; luminous intensity – candela cd.)

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Differentiate between scalar and vector quantities. Give two examples of each.
   Answer: Scalar: magnitude only – mass, speed (also time, energy). Vector: magnitude and direction – force, velocity (also displacement, acceleration).

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Show 2000 nanograms in micrograms.
   Answer: 2000 ng = 2000 × 10⁻⁹ g = 2 × 10⁻⁶ g = 2 µg.

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] Enlist the steps to represent a vector in a coordinate system.
   Answer: (1) Draw a coordinate system (x–y or N–E–S–W). (2) Choose a suitable scale. (3) Draw a line from the origin in the given direction, of length = magnitude ÷ scale. (4) Put an arrowhead at the end to show direction.

14. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] Show 4000 nanograms in milligrams.
   Answer: 4000 ng = 4 × 10⁻⁶ g = 4 × 10⁻³ mg = 0.004 mg.

15. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] How many kilometres are there in 25 micrometres?
   Answer: 25 × 10⁻⁶ m = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ km.

16. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Compare scalar and vector quantities (any three points).
   Answer: (1) Scalar has magnitude only; vector has magnitude and direction. (2) Scalars add by simple arithmetic; vectors by the head-to-tail (geometric) rule. (3) Scalar shown by a number and unit; vector by an arrow (or bold/arrowed letter).

17. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Justify that displacement is a vector quantity. Also draw a diagram.
   Answer: Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish in a specified direction. Walking 3 m east and 4 m north gives a displacement of 5 m at 53° north of east, drawn as an arrow from start to finish; reversing the direction gives a different displacement. Hence it is a vector.

18. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Show that prefix micro is a thousand times smaller than prefix milli.
   Answer: 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 10³, so micro is 1000 times smaller.

19. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Express using prefixes: (a) 29.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (b) 0.00034 × 10⁻³ s.
   Answer: (a) 2.93 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.93 nm (b) 3.4 × 10⁻⁷ s = 0.34 µs = 340 ns.

20. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Briefly describe any three sub-fields of physics.
   Answer: Mechanics – motion and forces; thermodynamics – heat and energy transfer; electromagnetism – electricity and magnetism (or optics, nuclear physics, quantum physics).

21. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M); 2nd Annual 2025] Compare classical mechanics and quantum mechanics (any three points).
   Answer: Classical mechanics (Newton) deals with large, everyday objects at ordinary speeds, gives exact predictable motion, energy can take any value. Quantum mechanics deals with atoms, electrons and photons, gives probabilities, and energy comes in discrete amounts (quanta).

22. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] How is a vector represented graphically and symbolically?
   Answer: Graphically: an arrow drawn to scale – length gives magnitude, arrowhead gives direction. Symbolically: a bold letter (F) or a letter with an arrow over it; its magnitude is |F|.

23. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Define astrophysics, biophysics and optics.
   Answer: Astrophysics: physics of stars, galaxies and the universe. Biophysics: physics of biological systems. Optics: study of light and its interaction with matter.

24. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] What steps would you take to minimize random error in a measurement?
   Answer: Take many repeated readings and average them; time many oscillations; use an instrument with a smaller least count; control conditions (draughts, vibrations); read at eye level.

25. Determine the least count of a vernier callipers whose main scale is in mm and vernier has 20 divisions.
   Answer: 1 mm ÷ 20 = 0.05 mm.

26. Find the resultant of displacements 12 m east and 5 m north.
   Answer: R = √(144 + 25) = 13 m at tan⁻¹(5/12) ≈ 22.6° north of east.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme) Q3] Use scientific notation to convert these readings using suitable prefixes: (i) 0.00000067 m (ii) 230000000 kg (iii) 0.00045 N (iv) 700000000 W (v) 0.000000835 s.
   Answer: (i) 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ m = 670 nm (ii) 2.3 × 10⁸ kg = 230 Gg (2.3 × 10¹¹ g) (iii) 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ N = 450 µN (iv) 7 × 10⁸ W = 700 MW (v) 8.35 × 10⁻⁷ s = 835 ns.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B) Q3; (D) Q5] What is meant by base and derived quantities? Give three examples of each with symbol and SI units.
   Answer: Base: length (l, m), mass (m, kg), time (t, s) [also current A, temperature K]. Derived: velocity (v, m s⁻¹), force (F, N = kg m s⁻²), pressure (P, Pa = N m⁻²) [also density kg m⁻³, energy J].

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B) Q4; (D) Q4] Briefly discuss any ten fields of physics.
   Answer: Mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, acoustics, electromagnetism, atomic physics, nuclear physics, quantum physics, relativity, astrophysics/cosmology, biophysics, geophysics, particle physics, plasma physics – one line each as in topic 1.1.

4. Describe the construction and use of a screw gauge, and explain why it is more precise than vernier callipers.
   Answer: See textbook long question 8: frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve with linear scale and datum line, thimble with 50 divisions, ratchet; pitch 0.5 mm, LC 0.01 mm; zero error, reading = MSR + n × LC. More precise because its least count is 10× smaller than the vernier’s 0.1 mm.

══ Chapter 1 in one page
- Physics: matter, energy, space, time. Branches: mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, acoustics, electromagnetism, atomic, nuclear, quantum, relativity, astrophysics, cosmology, biophysics, geophysics, particle physics.
- Physical (measurable: number + unit) vs non-physical (taste, feeling). Base quantities (7): length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, luminous intensity cd. Derived: speed m s⁻¹, force N = kg m s⁻², pressure Pa, energy J, power W, charge C = A s.
- Scientific notation: M × 10^n, 1 ≤ M < 10. Prefixes: T 10¹², G 10⁹, M 10⁶, k 10³, c 10⁻², m 10⁻³, µ 10⁻⁶, n 10⁻⁹, p 10⁻¹². micro is 1000× smaller than milli.
- Scalar (distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature) vs vector (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, field strength). Arrow to scale; head-to-tail; R = √(A² + B²), θ = tan⁻¹(B/A).
- Least count: metre rule 1 mm; vernier 1 mm/10 = 0.1 mm (inside jaws for internal diameter, depth probe); screw gauge pitch/50 = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm (ratchet). Zero error: positive → subtract, negative → add.
- Mass: physical balance, electronic balance (tare). Volume: measuring cylinder, read bottom of meniscus at eye level; stone = V₂ − V₁. Time: mechanical 0.1 s, digital 0.01 s; time 10 oscillations.
- Errors: systematic (one direction; calibrate) vs random (scatter; average). Precision = repeat readings agree; accuracy = close to true value.
- Significant figures: non-zero, sandwiched zeros, trailing zeros after decimal count; leading zeros don’t. Rounding: < 5 down, ≥ 5 up.

فزکس مادے اور توانائی کا علم ہے۔ سات بنیادی مقداریں اور SI اکائیاں یاد کریں۔ سائنسی ترقیم M × 10^n اور سابقے (کلو، ملی، مائیکرو، نینو)۔ اسکیلر صرف مقدار، ویکٹر مقدار اور سمت۔ میٹر رول 1 mm، ورنیئر 0.1 mm، اسکرو گیج 0.01 mm۔ منظم غلطی کیلیبریشن سے، بے ترتیب غلطی اوسط سے کم ہوتی ہے۔ یکسانیت اور درستگی میں فرق یاد رکھیں۔

chapters.title: Kinematics
chapters.introduction:
Kinematics (Greek kinema = motion) describes motion without asking what causes it. This unit covers rest and motion (both relative to an observer), types of motion (translatory – rectilinear, curvilinear, circular, random; rotatory; vibratory), distance vs displacement, speed vs velocity (average, instantaneous, uniform, variable), the universal speed limit, acceleration (uniform and non-uniform), free fall with g ≈ 9.8 m/s², and distance–time and speed–time graphs – gradients and the area under a graph.

16 summative SLOs – the most-asked chapter for numericals. Expect: types of motion with examples, distance vs displacement, speed/velocity calculations (km/h ↔ m/s), acceleration from Δv/t, free-fall (v = gt with 9.8 or 10), reading distance–time and speed–time graphs (gradient = speed/acceleration, area = distance), sketching graphs for rest, constant speed, acceleration and deceleration.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
16 summative SLOs – the most-asked chapter for numericals. Expect: types of motion with examples, distance vs displacement, speed/velocity calculations (km/h ↔ m/s), acceleration from Δv/t, free-fall (v = gt with 9.8 or 10), reading distance–time and speed–time graphs (gradient = speed/acceleration, area = distance), sketching graphs for rest, constant speed, acceleration and deceleration.
Note: Textbook numerical Q IV 4 prints the answer as “1 km”; the correct distance is 700 m (400 m at constant speed + 300 m while braking). The app gives the corrected answer.

══ 2.1 Rest and motion (pp. 36) ══
A body is at rest if it does not change its position with respect to an observer (surroundings) with time; it is in motion if it changes its position with respect to the observer.
Rest and motion are relative: a passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but in motion relative to a person on the road. Even a "stationary" parked car moves with the Earth (spinning and orbiting the Sun), the Sun moves in the Milky Way, and the galaxy moves through space. So we must always state the reference (observer).
Position is the distance and direction of a body from a fixed reference point.
اگر کوئی جسم مشاہدہ کرنے والے کے لحاظ سے اپنی جگہ نہ بدلے تو ساکن اور جگہ بدلے تو حرکت میں ہے۔ سکون اور حرکت نسبتی ہیں: چلتی بس میں بیٹھا مسافر بس کے لحاظ سے ساکن مگر سڑک پر کھڑے شخص کے لحاظ سے حرکت میں ہے۔

══ 2.2 Types of motion (pp. 37–39) ══
1. Translatory (linear) motion: the body moves as a whole so that all its points move in the same direction without change in orientation.
- Rectilinear motion: in a straight line – a train on a straight track, a falling apple, a bullet.
- Curvilinear motion: along a curved path – a kicked football, a roller coaster, a car turning a corner.
- Circular motion: a special curvilinear motion with constant radius around a fixed point – a stone whirled on a string, a satellite in orbit.
- Random motion: irregular, no fixed path – a butterfly, a mosquito, kites in the sky, dust/gas molecules (Brownian motion).
2. Rotatory (rotational) motion: the body spins about its own axis (an axis passing through the body); its particles move in circles – blades of a fan, a spinning top, wheel, helicopter rotor, Earth spinning.
3. Vibratory (oscillatory) motion: to-and-fro motion about a mean position – a simple pendulum, swing, guitar string, mass on a spring.
An object can have a combination: a rolling wheel rotates and translates; a Ferris wheel rotates, while its riders move in a circle (circular translatory motion).
[Table: Types of motion with examples]
Type | Description | Examples
• Rectilinear | Straight-line path | Falling apple, train on straight track
• Curvilinear | Curved path | Kicked football, car at a turn
• Circular | Path of fixed radius | Stone on a string, satellite
• Random | Irregular, no fixed path | Butterfly, mosquito, gas molecules
• Rotatory | Spinning about own axis | Fan blades, top, wheel
• Vibratory | To and fro about mean position | Pendulum, swing, guitar string
انتقالی حرکت: پورا جسم ایک ہی سمت میں حرکت کرے – سیدھی (گرتا سیب)، خمیدہ (فٹ بال)، دائری (ڈوری سے بندھا پتھر) اور بے ترتیب (تتلی، مچھر)۔ گردشی حرکت: جسم اپنے محور کے گرد گھومے (پنکھا)۔ ارتعاشی حرکت: وسطی مقام کے گرد آگے پیچھے حرکت (پینڈولم، جھولا)۔

══ 2.3 Distance and displacement (pp. 40–41) ══
- Distance (s): the total length of the path travelled, whatever the direction. Scalar, SI unit metre (m).
- Displacement (d): the shortest (straight-line) distance from the initial to the final position, in a specified direction: Δd = df − dᵢ. Vector, unit m.
Example: driving from Faisal Masjid to Blue Area by a twisting road is a longer distance than the straight-line displacement.
- One full lap of a 400 m track: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 (start = finish).
- Displacement can never be greater than distance; they are equal only for motion in a straight line in one direction.
- Displacement is zero but distance is not: walking round a park back to the gate; a pendulum completing a full oscillation.
Δ (delta) means "change in": Δt = tf − tᵢ.
فاصلہ طے کیے گئے راستے کی کل لمبائی ہے (اسکیلر)۔ ڈسپلیسمنٹ ابتدائی اور آخری مقام کے درمیان سیدھا کم سے کم فاصلہ ہے، سمت کے ساتھ (ویکٹر)۔ 400 m ٹریک کا ایک چکر: فاصلہ 400 m، ڈسپلیسمنٹ صفر۔ ڈسپلیسمنٹ کبھی فاصلے سے زیادہ نہیں ہوتا؛ سیدھی لکیر میں ایک ہی سمت میں حرکت پر دونوں برابر ہوتے ہیں۔

══ 2.4 Speed, average speed and instantaneous speed (pp. 41–44) ══
Speed is the distance covered per unit time (rate of change of distance). Scalar, SI unit m/s (m s⁻¹).
v = s/t  (or v = Δs/Δt)
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time: v_av = s_total/t_total. Example: Tarnol to Swabi interchange (≈ 70 km) in 1 h → 70 km/h.
Instantaneous speed: the speed at a particular instant, shown by a car's speedometer; speed-limit signs (70 km/h) refer to instantaneous speed.
Uniform speed: equal distances in equal intervals of time (however small). Variable (non-uniform) speed: unequal distances in equal times.
Unit conversion: km/h → m/s: multiply by 1000/3600 (= ÷ 3.6); m/s → km/h: × 3.6. E.g. 72 km/h = 20 m/s; 36 m/s = 129.6 km/h.
Speed facts: Usain Bolt 100 m in 9.58 s (≈ 10.4 m/s); peregrine falcon up to ≈ 108.9 m/s (≈ 390 km/h); cheetah ≈ 120 km/h on land; three-toed sloth ≈ 0.0013 m/s.
Universal speed limit: nothing with mass can reach the speed of light in vacuum, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (299 792 458 m/s); light always moves at this speed whatever the motion of the observer (Einstein). Light could go round the Earth about 7.5 times in one second; sound in air is only ≈ 343 m/s.
رفتار فی اکائی وقت طے شدہ فاصلہ ہے (v = s/t، اکائی m/s، اسکیلر)۔ اوسط رفتار = کل فاصلہ ÷ کل وقت۔ لمحاتی رفتار کسی خاص لمحے کی رفتار ہے جو اسپیڈومیٹر دکھاتا ہے۔ کائنات میں حد رفتار روشنی کی رفتار (3 × 10⁸ m/s) ہے؛ کمیت والی کوئی شے اس تک نہیں پہنچ سکتی۔

══ 2.5 Velocity: average, instantaneous, uniform and variable (pp. 44–45) ══
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement – speed in a given direction. Vector, unit m/s.
v = d/t  (v = Δd/Δt)
Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. Instantaneous velocity: velocity at an instant (very small time interval), with its direction.
Uniform velocity: equal displacements in equal intervals of time – constant speed in a straight line in one direction. Variable velocity: the velocity changes because the speed changes, or the direction changes, or both.
A satellite moving at constant speed in a circular orbit does not have constant velocity – its direction keeps changing.
For straight-line motion in one direction, speed = magnitude of velocity.
Speed vs velocity: speed is a scalar (distance/time); velocity is a vector (displacement/time); average velocity can be zero for a round trip while average speed is not.
[Table: Speed vs velocity]
Speed | Velocity
• Distance covered per unit time | Displacement per unit time
• Scalar | Vector (has direction)
• Never negative | Can be positive, negative or zero
• Round trip: not zero | Round trip: zero (zero displacement)
• Measured by speedometer | Needs speed + direction
ولاسٹی فی اکائی وقت ڈسپلیسمنٹ ہے یعنی سمت کے ساتھ رفتار (ویکٹر)۔ یکساں ولاسٹی: برابر وقفوں میں برابر ڈسپلیسمنٹ، یعنی سیدھی لکیر میں مستقل رفتار۔ رفتار یا سمت بدلے تو ولاسٹی متغیر ہوتی ہے؛ دائرے میں یکساں رفتار سے گھومتے سیٹلائٹ کی ولاسٹی بدلتی رہتی ہے۔

══ 2.6 Acceleration: uniform and non-uniform (pp. 46–48) ══
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Vector in the direction of the change in velocity; SI unit m/s² (m s⁻²) – derived from (m/s) ÷ s.
a = Δv/Δt = (vf − vᵢ)/t
- Positive acceleration: velocity increases with time (speeding up; acceleration in the direction of motion).
- Negative acceleration (deceleration/retardation): velocity decreases (slowing down; acceleration opposite to the motion). A car moving right while braking has acceleration to the left.
- Zero acceleration: constant velocity (e.g. car cruising at steady speed on a straight motorway).
- A change in direction alone produces acceleration (circular motion, a drone turning) – so an object can accelerate without speeding up or slowing down.
- Uniform acceleration: equal changes in velocity in equal intervals of time (free fall). Non-uniform acceleration: unequal changes (car in city traffic).
- Can a body have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration? Yes – a ball thrown up is momentarily at rest at the top, but its acceleration is still g downward.
Controls that accelerate a car: accelerator pedal (speed up), brakes (slow down), steering wheel (change direction).
Example: cheetah 0 → 26.8 m/s in 3 s: a = 26.8/3 ≈ 8.9 m/s² (cars ≈ 3–4 m/s²).
اسراع ولاسٹی میں تبدیلی کی شرح ہے: a = (vf − vᵢ)/t، اکائی m/s²، ویکٹر۔ رفتار بڑھے تو مثبت، کم ہو تو منفی اسراع (ڈی سیلریشن)۔ صرف سمت بدلنے سے بھی اسراع پیدا ہوتا ہے، جیسے دائری حرکت۔ برابر وقفوں میں ولاسٹی میں برابر تبدیلی یکساں اسراع ہے۔

══ 2.7 Free fall and acceleration due to gravity (pp. 49–50) ══
Galileo dropped objects of different masses from the Leaning Tower of Pisa and found that (without air resistance) they reach the ground at the same time.
Free fall: motion of a body under gravity alone. All freely falling bodies have the same gravitational acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (≈ 10 m/s² for quick calculations) near the Earth's surface, directed downward, independent of mass.
- Air resistance makes a sheet of paper fall slower than a coin; crumple the paper (or remove the air) and both fall together. In a vacuum, a feather and a coin fall together.
Sign convention: moving with gravity (falling) → +g; moving against gravity (thrown up) → −g.
Equations of motion for free fall (from vf = vᵢ + at and the area under the v–t graph, with a = ±g, s = h):
- vf = vᵢ + gt
- h = vᵢ t + ½ g t²
- 2gh = vf² − vᵢ^2
For a body dropped from rest (vᵢ = 0): v = gt, h = ½gt². For a ball thrown up: at the highest point v = 0, but the acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downward; time to top t = vᵢ/g; maximum height h = vᵢ²/2g.
Example: dropped from a tower, reaches ground in 4 s → v = 9.8 × 4 = 39.2 m/s; h = ½ × 9.8 × 16 = 78.4 m.
Exam Tip: Heavy and light stones dropped from the same height (no air resistance) hit the ground at the same time with the same velocity, because g does not depend on mass.
گیلیلیو نے دکھایا کہ ہوا کی مزاحمت نہ ہو تو بھاری اور ہلکے اجسام ایک ساتھ زمین پر گرتے ہیں۔ آزادانہ گرنے والے ہر جسم کا اسراع g ≈ 9.8 m/s² نیچے کی طرف ہوتا ہے جو کمیت پر منحصر نہیں۔ نیچے گرتے وقت +g اور اوپر پھینکنے پر −g لیتے ہیں۔ اوپر پھینکی گیند کی سب سے اونچی جگہ پر ولاسٹی صفر مگر اسراع پھر بھی g ہوتا ہے۔

══ 2.8 Distance–time graphs (pp. 51–53) ══
A distance–time graph has time on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis; it always lies in the positive quadrant (distance never decreases).
Gradient (slope) = speed: choose two points P₁(t₁, s₁) and P₂(t₂, s₂):
gradient = Δs/Δt = (s₂ − s₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = speed.
Shapes:
- (a) Horizontal line → distance not changing → at rest (speed = 0).
- (b) Straight sloping line → constant slope → uniform speed; steeper line = faster.
- (c) Curve bending upward (slope increasing) → speeding up (accelerating).
- (d) Curve bending downward / flattening (slope decreasing) → slowing down (decelerating).
Example (Peshawar → rest area → Islamabad on M1): 100 km in 1 h → 100 km/h (27.8 m/s); 30 min stop (horizontal part, speed 0); 75 km in 1 h → 75 km/h (20.8 m/s); whole trip 175 km in 2.5 h → 70 km/h (19.4 m/s).
فاصلہ–وقت گراف کی ڈھلوان رفتار دیتی ہے۔ افقی لکیر = ساکن؛ سیدھی ترچھی لکیر = یکساں رفتار؛ اوپر کو مڑتی لکیر = رفتار بڑھ رہی ہے؛ ہموار ہوتی لکیر = رفتار کم ہو رہی ہے۔

══ 2.9 Speed–time graphs: gradient and area (pp. 53–56) ══
A speed–time graph has time on the x-axis and speed on the y-axis.
1. Gradient = acceleration: gradient = Δv/Δt = (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = a.
- Horizontal line → constant speed → zero acceleration.
- Straight line rising (from origin: starting from rest) → uniform acceleration; steeper = greater acceleration.
- Straight line falling → uniform deceleration (negative gradient).
- Curve → non-uniform (variable) acceleration.
2. Area under the graph = distance travelled (justification without calculus):
- Rectangle (constant speed v for time t): area = v × t = distance (since s = vt).
- Triangle (uniform acceleration from rest to v in time t): area = ½ × v × t; average speed = (0 + v)/2, so distance = average speed × t = ½vt — the same.
- Trapezium: area = ½ (vᵢ + vf) × t.
Worked example (textbook): car 0 → 30 m/s in 20 s, constant 30 s, then stops in 10 s.
Accelerations: 30/20 = 1.5 m/s²; 0; −30/10 = −3 m/s² (deceleration).
Distance = ½ × 20 × 30 + 30 × 30 + ½ × 10 × 30 = 300 + 900 + 150 = 1350 m; average speed = 1350/60 = 22.5 m/s.
رفتار–وقت گراف کی ڈھلوان اسراع اور گراف کے نیچے کا رقبہ طے شدہ فاصلہ دیتا ہے۔ افقی لکیر = صفر اسراع؛ اوپر جاتی سیدھی لکیر = یکساں اسراع؛ نیچے آتی سیدھی لکیر = یکساں ڈی سیلریشن۔ مستطیل کا رقبہ vt اور مثلث کا ½vt۔

══ CHAPTER SUMMARY TABLES ══
[Table: Reading motion graphs]
Motion | Distance–time graph | Speed–time graph
• At rest | Horizontal line | Line on the time axis (v = 0)
• Uniform speed | Straight sloping line | Horizontal line
• Uniform acceleration | Curve bending upward | Straight rising line
• Uniform deceleration | Curve flattening | Straight falling line

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Distance–time graphs: (a) rest (b) uniform speed (c) speeding up (d) slowing down.
2. Speed–time graph of the textbook example: 0 → 30 m/s in 20 s, steady for 30 s, stops in 10 s. Area = 300 + 900 + 150 = 1350 m.
chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 2 in one page
- Rest/motion are relative to an observer. Types: translatory (rectilinear – falling apple; curvilinear – kicked ball; circular – stone on string; random – butterfly, mosquito), rotatory (fan, wheel), vibratory (pendulum, swing).
- Distance (path length, scalar) vs displacement (straight line start→end, vector); displacement ≤ distance; round trip → displacement 0.
- Speed v = s/t (scalar); average = total distance/total time; instantaneous (speedometer); uniform vs variable. km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s. Speed limit: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
- Velocity = displacement/time (vector); uniform = same speed, same direction; circular motion = changing velocity.
- Acceleration a = (vf − vᵢ)/t, m/s²; deceleration opposite to motion; direction change alone = acceleration; zero velocity with non-zero acceleration at top of a throw.
- Free fall: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² down, same for all masses (Galileo). vf = vᵢ + gt; h = vᵢ t + ½gt²; 2gh = vf² − vᵢ². Up → −g; at top v = 0.
- s–t graph: gradient = speed; horizontal = rest; straight = uniform speed; curving up = speeding up; flattening = slowing down.
- v–t graph: gradient = acceleration; area = distance (rectangle vt, triangle ½vt, trapezium ½(vᵢ+vf)t).

سکون اور حرکت نسبتی ہیں۔ حرکت کی اقسام: انتقالی، گردشی، ارتعاشی۔ فاصلہ اسکیلر، ڈسپلیسمنٹ ویکٹر۔ رفتار = فاصلہ/وقت، ولاسٹی = ڈسپلیسمنٹ/وقت، اسراع = ولاسٹی میں تبدیلی/وقت۔ آزادانہ گرنے میں g = 9.8 m/s²۔ فاصلہ–وقت گراف کی ڈھلوان رفتار، رفتار–وقت گراف کی ڈھلوان اسراع اور اس کے نیچے کا رقبہ فاصلہ ہے۔

Exam Focus: 16 summative SLOs – the most-asked chapter for numericals. Expect: types of motion with examples, distance vs displacement, speed/velocity calculations (km/h ↔ m/s), acceleration from Δv/t, free-fall (v = gt with 9.8 or 10), reading distance–time and speed–time graphs (gradient = speed/acceleration, area = distance), sketching graphs for rest, constant speed, acceleration and deceleration.
chapters.definitions:
• Kinematics (کائنیمیٹکس / حرکیات) [p. 36]: The study of motion without considering its causes.
• Rest (سکون) [p. 36]: A body is at rest if it does not change its position with respect to an observer.
• Motion (حرکت) [p. 36]: A body is in motion if it changes its position with respect to an observer.
• Translatory motion (انتقالی حرکت) [p. 37]: Motion in which all points of a body move in the same direction without change in orientation.
• Rotatory motion (گردشی حرکت) [p. 37]: Spinning of a body about an axis passing through it.
• Vibratory motion (ارتعاشی حرکت) [p. 38]: To-and-fro motion of a body about its mean position.
• Random motion (بے ترتیب حرکت) [p. 39]: Irregular translatory motion with no fixed path.
• Circular motion (دائری حرکت) [p. 39]: Motion along a circular path of constant radius.
• Position (مقام) [p. 40]: The distance and direction of a body from a fixed reference point.
• Distance (فاصلہ) [p. 40]: The total length of the path travelled by an object (scalar).
• Displacement (ڈسپلیسمنٹ / ہٹاؤ) [p. 40]: The shortest distance between the initial and final positions in a specified direction (vector).
• Speed (رفتار) [p. 41]: The time rate of change of distance (scalar).
• Average speed (اوسط رفتار) [p. 42]: Total distance covered divided by total time taken.
• Instantaneous speed (لمحاتی رفتار) [p. 43]: The speed at a particular instant of time.
• Uniform speed (یکساں رفتار) [p. 43]: Equal distances covered in equal intervals of time.
• Velocity (ولاسٹی / سمتی رفتار) [p. 44]: The time rate of change of displacement (vector).
• Uniform velocity (یکساں ولاسٹی) [p. 45]: Equal displacements in equal intervals of time.
• Acceleration (اسراع) [p. 46]: The time rate of change of velocity (vector).
• Deceleration (تقلیلِ رفتار) [p. 46]: Negative acceleration: velocity decreasing with time.
• Uniform acceleration (یکساں اسراع) [p. 47]: Equal changes in velocity in equal intervals of time.
• Free fall (آزادانہ گرنا) [p. 49]: Motion of a body under the action of gravity alone.
• Acceleration due to gravity (g) (ثقلی اسراع) [p. 49]: The uniform acceleration of freely falling bodies, about 9.8 m/s² downward near Earth.
• Gradient (slope) (ڈھلوان) [p. 51]: Difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates between two points of a graph.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Kinematics (حرکیات): Description of motion
• Rest (سکون): No change of position
• Motion (حرکت): Change of position
• Translatory (انتقالی): Moving as a whole
• Rotatory (گردشی): Spinning
• Vibratory (ارتعاشی): To and fro
• Displacement (ہٹاؤ): Straight-line change in position
• Speed (رفتار): Distance per time
• Velocity (سمتی رفتار): Displacement per time
• Acceleration (اسراع): Change of velocity per time
• Deceleration (تقلیلِ رفتار): Slowing down
• Free fall (آزادانہ گراؤ): Falling under gravity
• Gradient (ڈھلوان): Slope of a graph
• Instantaneous (لمحاتی): At an instant
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Speed: v = s/t (m/s)
• Average speed: v_av = total distance/total time
• Velocity: v = d/t (displacement/time)
• Acceleration: a = (vf − vᵢ)/t (m/s²)
• First equation of motion: vf = vᵢ + at
• Second equation of motion: s = vᵢ t + ½ a t²
• Third equation of motion: 2as = vf² − vᵢ^2
• Average speed (uniform acceleration): v_av = (vᵢ + vf)/2
• Free fall from rest: v = gt; h = ½gt² (g = 9.8 m/s²)
• Unit conversion: km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s; m/s × 3.6 = km/h
• Speed of light: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (Universal speed limit)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• Gradient of s–t graph = Δs/Δt = speed — Justification: speed is distance per time.
• Gradient of v–t graph = Δv/Δt = acceleration — Justification: acceleration is change of velocity per time.
• Area of rectangle under v–t graph = v × t = s — Constant speed.
• Area of triangle under v–t graph = ½ v t = (v/2) × t = s — Uniform acceleration from rest; v/2 is the average speed.
• vf = vᵢ + at  →  a = (vf − vᵢ)/t — Rearranged definition of acceleration.
• s = ½(vᵢ + vf)t  and with vf = vᵢ + at  →  s = vᵢ t + ½at² — Area of trapezium under v–t graph.
• From s = ½(vᵢ + vf)t and t = (vf − vᵢ)/a  →  2as = vf² − vᵢ^2 — Third equation.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Can the speedometer of a car show average speed?
   Answer: No – it shows instantaneous speed.
2. Why is it impossible for a rocket to reach the speed of light?
   Answer: Anything with mass would need infinite energy to reach c; c is the universal speed limit.
3. A body moves in a circle at constant speed. Is its velocity constant?
   Answer: No – its direction keeps changing, so velocity changes and it accelerates.
4. What is the acceleration of a car moving at a steady 90 km/h on a straight road?
   Answer: Zero.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why do cricket umpires use a speed gun rather than a stopwatch to measure a fast bowler’s speed?
   Answer: The ball takes only about 0.4 s to reach the batsman; human reaction time (~0.2 s) makes stopwatch timing very inaccurate.
2. Why do motorway signs specify maximum speed and not average speed?
   Answer: Safety depends on the speed at every instant (instantaneous speed), not the average.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Shoaib Akhtar bowled at 161.3 km/h. If the batsman is 17.5 m from the bowler, how much time does the batsman have to react? (Example 2.1)
   Given: v = 161.3 km/h = 161.3 × 1000/3600 = 44.8 m/s; s = 17.5 m
   Required: Time t
   Formula: v = s/t → t = s/v
   Substitution: t = 17.5/44.8
   Calculation: t ≈ 0.39
   Final Answer: t ≈ 0.39 s

2. Shanghai Maglev travelled 30 km in 7 min 30 s. Find its speed in m/s and km/h. (Example 2.2)
   Given: s = 30 km = 30 000 m; t = 7 × 60 + 30 = 450 s
   Required: Speed v
   Formula: v = s/t
   Substitution: v = 30 000/450
   Calculation: v = 66.7 m/s; × 3.6 = 240 km/h
   Final Answer: 66.7 m/s = 240 km/h

3. A car travels a curvy track of 800 m in 40 s; the straight-line distance between start and end is 600 m. Find (a) average speed (b) average velocity. (Example 2.3)
   Given: distance = 800 m, displacement = 600 m, t = 40 s
   Required: v_av (speed) and v_av (velocity)
   Formula: speed = distance/time; velocity = displacement/time
   Substitution: 800/40; 600/40
   Calculation: 20; 15
   Final Answer: (a) 20 m/s (b) 15 m/s in the direction start → end

4. A cheetah accelerates from 0 to 26.8 m/s east in 3 s. Find its acceleration. (Example 2.4)
   Given: vᵢ = 0, vf = 26.8 m/s, t = 3 s
   Required: a
   Formula: a = (vf − vᵢ)/t
   Substitution: a = (26.8 − 0)/3
   Calculation: a = 8.93
   Final Answer: 8.9 m/s² east

5. A 2 kg block is dropped from a building and strikes the ground at 78.5 m/s. How long does it take? (Example 2.5)
   Given: vᵢ = 0, vf = 78.5 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s² (mass not needed)
   Required: t
   Formula: g = (vf − vᵢ)/t → t = (vf − vᵢ)/g
   Substitution: t = 78.5/9.8
   Calculation: t ≈ 8.0
   Final Answer: ≈ 8 s

6. Peshawar → rest area 100 km in 1 h, stop 30 min, then 75 km to Islamabad in 1 h. Find speeds. (Example 2.6)
   Solution: (a) 100 km/1 h = 100 km/h = 27.8 m/s. (b) 75 km/1 h = 75 km/h = 20.8 m/s. (c) 175 km/2.5 h = 70 km/h = 19.4 m/s (average, including the stop).

7. A car goes 0 → 30 m/s in 20 s, stays at 30 m/s for 30 s, then stops uniformly in 10 s. Find accelerations, total distance and average speed. (Example 2.7)
   Solution: Accelerations: OA 30/20 = 1.5 m/s²; AB 0; BC −30/10 = −3 m/s². Distance = area = 300 + 900 + 150 = 1350 m. Average speed = 1350/60 = 22.5 m/s.


══ ADDITIONAL SLO NUMERICAL PRACTICE ══

1. A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 8 s. Find the distance covered.
   Given: vᵢ = 10, vf = 30 m/s, t = 8 s
   Required: s
   Formula: s = ½(vᵢ + vf)t
   Substitution: ½ × (10 + 30) × 8
   Calculation: 20 × 8 = 160
   Final Answer: 160 m

2. A stone is dropped from a cliff and hits the water after 3 s. How high is the cliff? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
   Given: vᵢ = 0, t = 3 s, g = 9.8 m/s²
   Required: h
   Formula: h = ½gt²
   Substitution: ½ × 9.8 × 3²
   Calculation: 4.9 × 9 = 44.1
   Final Answer: 44.1 m

3. A bus slows from 72 km/h to rest in 10 s. Find its deceleration and stopping distance.
   Given: vᵢ = 72 km/h = 20 m/s, vf = 0, t = 10 s
   Required: a, s
   Formula: a = (vf − vᵢ)/t; s = ½(vᵢ + vf)t
   Substitution: (0 − 20)/10; ½ × 20 × 10
   Calculation: −2 m/s²; 100 m
   Final Answer: Deceleration 2 m/s²; 100 m
