NBF Chapter 2 Exercises (57–60):

— Exercise MCQs —
1. Change in position of a body from initial to final point is called: → B (Displacement) | Definition.
2. Motion of a screw of a rotating fan is: → D (Rotatory motion) | Spins about its own axis.
3. A cyclist travelling westward produces a deceleration of 8 m/s² to stop. The direction of its acceleration is towards: → B (East) | Deceleration is opposite to motion.
4. A girl walks 3 km west and 4 km south. Her total distance and displacement respectively are: → D (7 km, 5 km) | 3 + 4 = 7; √(9 + 16) = 5.
5. A horse moves 60 m right in 3 s, then turns back 30 m in 2 s. Its average velocity is: → A (6 m/s) | Displacement 30 m in 5 s.
6. A cyclist has acceleration 2 m/s² for 5 s. The change in velocity is: → B (10 m/s) | Δv = at.
7. A car moving at 10 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 10 s. Final velocity: → A (30 m/s) | 10 + 20.
8. When the slope of a body’s displacement–time graph increases, the body is moving with: → A (increasing velocity) | Slope = velocity.
9. A ball is thrown straight up. The magnitude of acceleration at the top of its path is: → B (9.8 m/s²) | g acts throughout.
10. Slope of a distance–time graph is: → C (speed) | Δs/Δt.
11. Area under a speed–time graph is equal to ______ of the moving body: → A (distance) | v × t.
12. In 5 s a car accelerates so that its velocity increases by 20 m/s. The acceleration is: → B (4 m/s²) | 20/5.
13. A ball dropped freely from a tower reaches the ground in 4 s. The speed of impact is: → D (39.2 m/s) | 9.8 × 4.
14. Which distance–time graph represents increasing speed of a car? (A horizontal line, B straight sloping line, C curve bending upward, D curve flattening) → C (C) | Slope increasing.

— Q II. Short-response questions —
1 Children ride a Ferris wheel. What kind of motion does the big wheel have, and what kind do the riders have?
   Answer: The wheel has rotatory motion (spins about its axle). The riders have circular (translatory) motion – their seats stay upright while moving round a circular path.
2 Give two situations in which a boy’s displacement is zero but distance covered is not zero.
   Answer: (1) He runs one full lap of a 400 m track (distance 400 m). (2) He walks from home to the shop and back home (or swings on a swing back to the start).
3 A stone tied to a string is whirled in a circle. What is the direction of its velocity at any instant?
   Answer: Along the tangent to the circle at that point (perpendicular to the string); if the string breaks the stone flies off along this tangent.
4 Is it possible to accelerate an object without speeding it up or slowing it down?
   Answer: Yes – by changing its direction. In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but velocity changes direction, so there is (centripetal) acceleration.
5 Can a car moving towards the right have its acceleration towards the left?
   Answer: Yes – when it is slowing down (braking), the acceleration is opposite to the velocity, i.e. towards the left.
6 With daily-life examples, describe situations where: (a) acceleration is in the direction of motion (b) acceleration is against the direction of motion (c) acceleration is zero and the body is moving.
   Answer: (a) A bus pulling away from a stop / a stone falling. (b) A car braking at a signal / a ball thrown upward. (c) A car cruising at a steady 100 km/h on a straight motorway.
7 Examine the distance–time graph of a motorcyclist (straight line through the origin). What does it tell about his speed? Also plot the velocity–time graph.
   Answer: A straight line through the origin means a constant (uniform) speed equal to the gradient (distance ÷ time read from the graph, roughly 8–10 m/s). The velocity–time graph is therefore a horizontal straight line at that speed.
8 Which controls in a car can produce acceleration or deceleration?
   Answer: Accelerator pedal (increase speed), brake pedal (decrease speed), steering wheel (change direction – also an acceleration); gears also change acceleration.
9 Stones of 10 kg and 1 kg are dropped from a 1 km high tower. Which hits the ground with greater velocity? Which first? (no air resistance)
   Answer: Both fall with the same acceleration g, so they hit the ground at the same time with the same velocity.
10 A 100 g ball is released from rest and another is thrown downward at 10 m/s. Which has greater acceleration? (no air resistance)
   Answer: Both have the same acceleration, g = 9.8 m/s² downward; acceleration does not depend on initial velocity (only the thrown ball is faster).

— Q III. Long-response questions —
1 Differentiate between rest and motion. With examples, show that rest and motion are relative to the observer.
   Answer: Rest: no change of position w.r.t. surroundings; motion: change of position w.r.t. surroundings. A passenger in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus and other passengers but moving relative to people on the road; a parked car is at rest relative to the road but moves with the Earth around the Sun. Hence rest and motion depend on the observer (frame of reference).
2 What are the different types of motion? Define each with examples from daily life.
   Answer: Translatory (rectilinear – falling apple; curvilinear – kicked ball; circular – stone on string; random – butterfly), rotatory (fan blades, spinning top, wheel), vibratory (pendulum, swing, guitar string). See topic 2.2.
3 What are scalars and vectors? Give examples. How are vectors represented symbolically and graphically?
   Answer: Scalars: magnitude only (distance, speed, mass, time, energy). Vectors: magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force). Symbolically: bold letter or letter with arrow over it; graphically: arrow drawn to scale – length = magnitude, arrowhead = direction.
4 Define the term position. Differentiate between distance and displacement.
   Answer: Position: distance and direction of a body from a fixed reference point. Distance: total path length, scalar, never less than displacement; displacement: straight line from initial to final position with direction, vector, can be zero for a round trip.
5 Differentiate between speed and velocity. Also define average speed, uniform and variable speeds, average velocity, uniform and variable velocities.
   Answer: Speed = distance/time (scalar); velocity = displacement/time (vector). Average speed = total distance/total time. Uniform speed: equal distances in equal times; variable speed: unequal. Average velocity = total displacement/total time. Uniform velocity: equal displacements in equal times (same speed, same direction); variable velocity: speed and/or direction changes.
6 What are freely falling bodies? What is gravitational acceleration? Write the sign conventions and three equations of motion for a freely falling body.
   Answer: Bodies falling under gravity alone (no air resistance). Gravitational acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward, same for all masses. Sign: falling → +g, moving up → −g. Equations: vf = vᵢ + gt; h = vᵢ t + ½gt²; 2gh = vf² − vᵢ².
7 Draw distance–time graphs for rest, uniform speed, increasing speed and decreasing speed.
   Answer: Rest: horizontal line. Uniform speed: straight line with constant positive slope. Increasing speed: curve bending upward (slope increasing). Decreasing speed: curve bending towards horizontal (slope decreasing). See the diagram in Tables & Diagrams.
8 Draw speed–time graphs for zero acceleration, uniform acceleration and uniform deceleration. Also show that the area under a speed–time graph represents the distance covered.
   Answer: Zero acceleration: horizontal line; uniform acceleration: straight line with positive slope; uniform deceleration: straight line with negative slope. Area: for constant speed the rectangle v × t = s; for uniform acceleration from rest the triangle ½ × v × t = (average speed v/2) × t = s. Therefore area = distance.

   Solution: (a) 160 × 1000/3600 = 44.44 m/s (b) 36 × 3.6 = 129.6 km/h (c) 15 × 1000/(3600)² = 0.00116 m/s² ≈ 0.001 m/s² (d) 1 × 3600²/1000 = 12 960 km/h²

   Solution: (a) OB (OA) – acceleration (5 m/s²); CD (BC in the book’s labels) – deceleration (5 m/s²); BC (AB) – zero acceleration. (b) Area of rectangle = 50 × 10 = 500 m.

══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B); 2nd Annual 2025] Sketch distance–time graphs of an object (a) at rest (b) moving with constant speed (c) accelerating.
   Answer: (a) Horizontal line. (b) Straight sloping line. (c) Curve bending upward. (Decelerating: curve flattening.)

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B)] A cyclist applies brakes and slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 3 s. Calculate the acceleration.
   Answer: a = (4 − 12)/3 = −2.67 m/s² (deceleration).

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] A car travels A→B: 6 m in t₁ = 2 s, 8 m more in t₂ = 4 s, 10 m more in t₃ = 2 s (marks 0, 6, 14, 24 m). Find total distance, total time and average speed.
   Answer: Total distance 24 m; total time 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 s; average speed 24/8 = 3 m/s.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] What is meant by velocity? Justify that speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector.
   Answer: Velocity = rate of change of displacement. Speed only says how fast (e.g. 20 m/s); velocity also says which way (20 m/s north), and changes if direction changes even at constant speed.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] How do different slopes represent three types of motion in a speed–time graph? Make sketches.
   Answer: Zero slope (horizontal) – constant speed; positive slope – uniform acceleration; negative slope – uniform deceleration.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] A ball is thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s (g = 9.8 m/s²): (a) time to reach the highest point (b) velocity at the highest point.
   Answer: (a) t = vᵢ/g = 19.6/9.8 = 2 s (b) 0 m/s.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] Velocity–time graph: v = 2, 4, 6 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3 s (straight line from origin). Determine (a) type of motion (b) acceleration.
   Answer: (a) Uniformly accelerated motion (b) a = 6/3 = 2 m/s².

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] Differentiate between distance and displacement.
   Answer: Distance: total path length, scalar; displacement: straight-line change of position with direction, vector; displacement ≤ distance.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] A train travels 30 km in 7 min 30 s. What is its speed? Convert to km/h.
   Answer: 30 000 m/450 s = 66.7 m/s = 240 km/h.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] What kind of motion does a butterfly have? Briefly describe this kind.
   Answer: Random motion – irregular translatory motion with no fixed path; direction and speed change unpredictably.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B, D)] Can the directions of velocity and acceleration be opposite? Explain briefly.
   Answer: Yes – when a body slows down, e.g. a braking car or a ball moving upward (velocity up, g down).

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] Is it possible to accelerate an object without speeding up or slowing down? Justify.
   Answer: Yes – by changing direction at constant speed, e.g. uniform circular motion.

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] Differentiate between uniform acceleration and non-uniform acceleration.
   Answer: Uniform: equal changes in velocity in equal time intervals (free fall; straight v–t line). Non-uniform: unequal changes (car in traffic; curved v–t graph).

14. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] Compare rotatory motion and vibratory motion.
   Answer: Rotatory: body spins about an axis through itself (fan, wheel), particles move in circles. Vibratory: body moves to and fro about a mean position (pendulum, swing), repeating its path.

15. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] The velocity of a car increases uniformly from 15 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 s. Find v_avg and acceleration.
   Answer: v_avg = (15 + 25)/2 = 20 m/s; a = (25 − 15)/5 = 2 m/s².

16. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Draw distance–time graphs for a body (a) decelerating (b) at rest (c) moving with constant speed.
   Answer: (a) Curve whose slope decreases (flattens). (b) Horizontal line. (c) Straight sloping line.

17. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Draw the speed–time graph for uniform acceleration and use it to show that the gradient gives acceleration.
   Answer: Straight line from (0, vᵢ) to (t, vf). Gradient = (vf − vᵢ)/t, which is the definition of acceleration.

18. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] What is the average speed of a car that completes a circle of radius 200 m in 5 minutes?
   Answer: Distance = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 200 = 1256.6 m; t = 300 s; speed = 4.19 m/s.

19. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] A car starts from rest and reaches 20 m/s in 5 s. Calculate its average velocity and the distance covered.
   Answer: v_av = (0 + 20)/2 = 10 m/s; distance = 10 × 5 = 50 m.

20. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Can a body have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration? Explain with a physical example.
   Answer: Yes – a ball thrown up is momentarily at rest at its highest point, yet its acceleration is g = 9.8 m/s² downward.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D) Q3] A car starts from rest, moves with constant speed, then accelerates and finally comes to rest. (a) Draw the distance–time graph showing all four stages. (b) How does the gradient of each section represent the car’s speed?
   Answer: Graph: horizontal line (rest) → straight sloping line (constant speed) → curve bending upward (accelerating) → curve flattening to horizontal (slowing to rest). Gradient = speed: zero, constant, increasing, decreasing to zero respectively.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M) Q5] A speed–time graph shows a car speeding up from 0 to 15 m/s in 5 s, staying constant for 5 s, then decreasing to 0 in 3 s. (a) Type of motion in each interval (b) acceleration in the first 5 s (c) deceleration in the last 3 s.
   Answer: (a) 0–5 s uniform acceleration; 5–10 s uniform speed (zero acceleration); 10–13 s uniform deceleration. (b) a = 15/5 = 3 m/s². (c) a = −15/3 = −5 m/s² (deceleration 5 m/s²). (Distance = 37.5 + 75 + 22.5 = 135 m.)

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme) Q3] Speed–time graph: constant 8 m/s for 4 s, then uniform deceleration to rest in 3 s. (a) Sketch and label (b) explain how it shows deceleration.
   Answer: Horizontal line at 8 m/s from 0 to 4 s, then a straight line sloping down to 0 at 7 s. The negative gradient (−8/3 = −2.67 m/s²) shows uniform deceleration. Distance = 32 + 12 = 44 m.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025 Q4] A 3 kg block is dropped from the top of a building and strikes the ground at 80 m/s (no air resistance). Find the time to reach the ground and the height (g = 10 m/s²).
   Answer: t = v/g = 80/10 = 8 s; h = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 64 = 320 m (or v²/2g = 6400/20 = 320 m). Mass is not needed.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF) Q3] What are the different types of motion? Give two examples of each.
   Answer: Translatory – rectilinear (falling stone, train on straight track), curvilinear (thrown ball, car turning), circular (stone on string, satellite), random (butterfly, gas molecules); rotatory (fan, wheel); vibratory (pendulum, guitar string).

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%) Q8] Define acceleration. What does it tell us about motion? If the slope of a speed–time graph is steeper, what can you say about the motion?
   Answer: Acceleration = rate of change of velocity (m/s²). It tells how quickly velocity changes (speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction). A steeper slope means a larger acceleration – the velocity changes faster.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 2 in one page
- Rest/motion are relative to an observer. Types: translatory (rectilinear – falling apple; curvilinear – kicked ball; circular – stone on string; random – butterfly, mosquito), rotatory (fan, wheel), vibratory (pendulum, swing).
- Distance (path length, scalar) vs displacement (straight line start→end, vector); displacement ≤ distance; round trip → displacement 0.
- Speed v = s/t (scalar); average = total distance/total time; instantaneous (speedometer); uniform vs variable. km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s. Speed limit: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
- Velocity = displacement/time (vector); uniform = same speed, same direction; circular motion = changing velocity.
- Acceleration a = (vf − vᵢ)/t, m/s²; deceleration opposite to motion; direction change alone = acceleration; zero velocity with non-zero acceleration at top of a throw.
- Free fall: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² down, same for all masses (Galileo). vf = vᵢ + gt; h = vᵢ t + ½gt²; 2gh = vf² − vᵢ². Up → −g; at top v = 0.
- s–t graph: gradient = speed; horizontal = rest; straight = uniform speed; curving up = speeding up; flattening = slowing down.
- v–t graph: gradient = acceleration; area = distance (rectangle vt, triangle ½vt, trapezium ½(vᵢ+vf)t).

chapters.title: Dynamics – I
chapters.introduction:
Dynamics studies motion together with its cause – force. This unit covers force and its types (contact: normal, friction, tension, air resistance; non-contact: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic), the four fundamental forces (and Dr Abdus Salam’s electroweak unification), free-body diagrams, net/resultant force, Newton’s three laws of motion with inertia, their limitations, mass and weight, the force meter and electronic balance, gravitational field strength, momentum, force as rate of change of momentum, impulse and the law of conservation of momentum (gun and bullet, rockets).

21 summative SLOs – the heaviest chapter. Every paper asks: Newton’s laws (statements, examples, F = ma numericals, limitations), inertia examples (bus, carpet, coin on card), mass vs weight, g on other planets (200 N → 50 N), momentum p = mv, impulse FΔt = Δp, conservation of momentum (gun–bullet recoil, rocket), fundamental forces in order of strength, contact vs non-contact forces.

══ 3.1 Force; contact and non-contact forces (pp. 62–64) ══
Force is a push or a pull that moves or tends to move a body, stops or tends to stop it, or changes its speed or direction (it can also change shape). It is a vector; SI unit newton (N).
Effects of force on velocity: it can change the speed (speed up/slow down), the direction, or both.
Contact forces act when objects touch:
- Normal force (F_N): perpendicular to the contact surface; stops objects passing through each other (a book on a table).
- Friction (f): opposes motion or attempted motion between surfaces in contact.
- Tension (T): pull in a stretched string, rope or cable.
- Air resistance (drag): friction from air on a moving object.
- Applied/elastic forces: pushes, pulls; restoring force of a stretched spring.
Non-contact forces (action at a distance):
- Gravitational force: attraction between masses (Earth on the Moon, weight).
- Electrostatic force: attraction/repulsion between charges (nucleus and electron).
- Magnetic force: attraction/repulsion between magnetic poles (two north poles repel).
[Table: Contact vs non-contact forces]
Contact forces | Non-contact forces
• Act only when bodies touch | Act at a distance, no touching needed
• Normal force, friction, tension, air resistance, applied push | Gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic force
• Bat hitting a ball | Earth pulling the Moon; magnet attracting a pin
قوت وہ دھکا یا کھنچاؤ ہے جو جسم کو حرکت دے یا روکے، یا اس کی رفتار یا سمت بدلے (اکائی نیوٹن، ویکٹر)۔ رابطے کی قوتیں چھونے پر عمل کرتی ہیں: نارمل قوت، رگڑ، تناؤ، ہوا کی مزاحمت۔ غیر رابطے کی قوتیں فاصلے سے عمل کرتی ہیں: ثقلی، برقی سکونی اور مقناطیسی قوت۔

══ 3.2 The fundamental forces of nature (pp. 64–66) ══
All forces belong to four fundamental forces, each carried by exchange particles:
1. Strong nuclear force – strongest; holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus against proton repulsion; very short range (≈ size of a nucleus, 10⁻¹⁵ m); carried by pions/gluons.
2. Electromagnetic force – between electric charges (electric + magnetic); attractive or repulsive; infinite range; carried by photons. Normal force, friction and tension are electromagnetic in origin.
3. Weak nuclear force – responsible for radioactive (beta) decay; changes the type of quark (neutron → proton); shortest range; carried by W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰ bosons.
4. Gravitational force – attraction between all masses; weakest; infinite range; noticeable only when a mass is large (planets, stars); carrier graviton (not yet detected).
Order of strength: strong > electromagnetic > weak > gravitational. (The textbook SLO mentions “three fundamental forces” because electromagnetic and weak forces are unified.)
Electroweak theory: in the late 1960s Dr Abdus Salam (Pakistan), Steven Weinberg and Sheldon Glashow showed that the electromagnetic and weak forces are two aspects of one electroweak force (Nobel Prize in Physics, 1979). Carriers: photon, W⁺, W⁻, Z⁰.
[Table: Fundamental forces]
Force | Relative strength | Range | Carrier | Acts on / role
• Strong nuclear | 1 (strongest) | ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m | Pions / gluons | Holds the nucleus together
• Electromagnetic | ≈ 10⁻² | Infinite | Photon | Charges; friction, normal force, chemistry
• Weak nuclear | ≈ 10⁻⁶ (10 000× weaker than strong) | ≈ 10⁻¹⁸ m (shortest) | W^±, Z⁰ bosons | Radioactive decay
• Gravitational | ≈ 10⁻³⁸ (weakest) | Infinite | Graviton (not detected) | All masses; planets, stars
چار بنیادی قوتیں: مضبوط نیوکلیائی (سب سے طاقتور، مرکزے کو جوڑے رکھتی ہے، بہت کم فاصلہ)، برقی مقناطیسی (چارجز کے درمیان، لامحدود فاصلہ، فوٹون)، کمزور نیوکلیائی (تابکاری، W اور Z بوسون) اور ثقلی (سب سے کمزور، تمام اجسام کے درمیان)۔ پاکستانی سائنسدان ڈاکٹر عبدالسلام نے برقی مقناطیسی اور کمزور قوت کو یکجا کرنے والی الیکٹرو ویک تھیوری پیش کی اور 1979 میں نوبل انعام حاصل کیا۔

══ 3.3 Free-body diagrams and resultant (net) force (pp. 66–68) ══
- A system diagram (SD) shows all the objects involved.
- A free-body diagram (FBD) shows only the object being studied (as a box/dot) with arrows for every force acting on it, lengths proportional to magnitude, labelled: Fg (weight), F_N (normal), f (friction), T (tension), F_app (applied).
Examples: book on a table – Fg down, F_N up; hanging lamp – Fg down, T up; box pushed on a floor – F_app forward, f backward, Fg down, F_N up.
Net (resultant) force: the single force with the same effect as all the forces together (vector sum).
- Balanced forces: net force = 0 → no change in motion (equal tug-of-war).
- Unbalanced forces: net force ≠ 0 → change in motion (acceleration).
Forces along one line: like parallel (same direction) → add; unlike parallel (opposite) → subtract; the resultant points in the direction of the larger force. E.g. 30 N right and 20 N left → 10 N right. Forces at an angle are added by the head-to-tail rule.
فری باڈی ڈایاگرام میں صرف زیرِ مطالعہ جسم اور اس پر لگنے والی تمام قوتیں تیروں سے دکھائی جاتی ہیں (وزن نیچے، نارمل قوت اوپر، رگڑ حرکت کے خلاف)۔ حاصل قوت تمام قوتوں کا مجموعی اثر ہے؛ ایک ہی سمت کی قوتیں جمع اور مخالف سمت کی قوتیں تفریق ہوتی ہیں۔ متوازن قوتوں میں حاصل قوت صفر ہوتی ہے۔

══ 3.4 Newton’s first law and inertia (pp. 68–71) ══
Newton’s first law: an object continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless an external net (unbalanced) force acts on it. If F_net = 0, then v = constant (a = 0).
On Earth friction and gravity keep stopping moving things, so we rarely see this; in space a moving probe keeps moving at constant velocity.
Inertia: the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia – more mass, more inertia (a heavy man on a swing is harder to start and stop than a child). Hence the first law is called the law of inertia.
Examples of inertia:
- A standing passenger falls backward when a bus starts suddenly (lower body moves with the bus, upper body stays at rest) and forward when it stops suddenly; sideways when it turns.
- Dust flies off a carpet beaten with a stick (carpet moves, dust stays).
- Coin on a card over a glass: flick the card – the coin drops into the glass.
- Pulling a paper quickly from under a stack of coins; leaves fall when a branch is shaken; seat belts and air bags protect passengers.
- A motorcyclist hitting a stationary car flies forward (body keeps moving); the car driver’s head jerks back (body pushed forward, head stays) – neck injury.
Deducing the first law from the second: F = ma; if F = 0 then a = 0, so velocity stays constant (rest stays rest).
نیوٹن کا پہلا قانون: کوئی جسم اپنی حالتِ سکون یا یکساں سیدھی حرکت پر قائم رہتا ہے جب تک اس پر کوئی بیرونی غیر متوازن قوت عمل نہ کرے۔ جمود جسم کا اپنی حالت میں تبدیلی کی مزاحمت کرنا ہے؛ کمیت جمود کی پیمائش ہے۔ مثالیں: بس اچانک چلے تو مسافر پیچھے گرتا ہے، رکے تو آگے؛ قالین جھاڑنے سے گرد اڑتی ہے۔

══ 3.5 Newton’s second law of motion (pp. 71–72) ══
The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force (a ∝ F) and in its direction, and inversely proportional to its mass (a ∝ 1/m):
a = F_net/m   or   F = ma
- Double the force (same mass) → acceleration doubles; double the mass (same force) → acceleration halves.
Newton (N): the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
Example: an engine of 3000 N in a 12 000 kg bus gives 0.25 m/s², in a 1200 kg car 2.5 m/s².
Proving F = ma from momentum (second law in terms of momentum): F = Δp/Δt = (mvf − mvᵢ)/t = m(vf − vᵢ)/t = ma.
Units of momentum: N s = (kg m s⁻²) × s = kg m s⁻¹.
Moving vertically: a 2 kg book held at rest needs 19.6 N; to lift it with a = 3 m/s² up: F = m(g + a) = 2 × 12.8 = 25.6 N.
نیوٹن کا دوسرا قانون: اسراع حاصل قوت کے راست متناسب اور کمیت کے معکوس متناسب ہوتا ہے: F = ma۔ ایک نیوٹن وہ قوت ہے جو 1 kg کمیت میں 1 m/s² اسراع پیدا کرے۔ قوت دگنی تو اسراع دگنا؛ کمیت دگنی تو اسراع آدھا۔

══ 3.6 Newton’s third law; limitations of Newton’s laws (pp. 72–74) ══
Newton’s third law: whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first: F_AB = −F_BA (to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction).
- Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other; they are of the same type (both contact, or both gravitational, etc.) and act at the same time.
- A body can move under an action–reaction pair, because only the force on that body matters for its motion.
Examples: kicking a football (foot pushes ball, ball pushes foot – it hurts); jumping (legs push ground down, ground pushes you up); walking; swimming (push water back, water pushes you forward); punching a wall hurts; rocket (pushes exhaust gases down, gases push rocket up – works in space too); gun recoil; the Earth pulls a falling ball and the ball pulls the Earth with the same force – the ball moves visibly because its mass is tiny (a = F/m).
A man stranded on frictionless ice can throw his bag in one direction to move in the other (third law/conservation of momentum).
Limitations of Newton’s laws:
- Not valid for very small particles (atoms, electrons) – use quantum mechanics.
- Not valid for very high speeds close to the speed of light – use relativity.
- (Also need an inertial, non-accelerating frame of reference.) They are excellent approximations for everyday (macroscopic) objects.
تیسرا قانون: ہر عمل کا برابر اور مخالف ردعمل ہوتا ہے، F_AB = −F_BA۔ عمل اور ردعمل مختلف اجسام پر لگتے ہیں اس لیے ایک دوسرے کو ختم نہیں کرتے۔ مثالیں: راکٹ، بندوق کا پیچھے ہٹنا، چلنا، تیرنا۔ حدود: نیوٹن کے قوانین بہت چھوٹے ذرات (کوانٹم میکینکس) اور روشنی کے قریب رفتار (اضافیت) پر لاگو نہیں ہوتے۔

══ 3.7 Mass, weight, force meter and electronic balance (pp. 74–77) ══
- Mass (m): the quantity of matter in a body and a measure of its inertia; scalar; unit kg; same everywhere; measured with a beam/electronic balance.
- Weight (W): the force with which a planet’s gravity pulls a body towards its centre; vector (downward); unit N; changes from place to place; measured with a spring balance/force meter.
W = mg (a special case of F = ma). On the Moon (g ≈ 1.6 m/s²) weight is about 1/6 of that on Earth but mass is unchanged.
Force meter (spring balance/newton meter): a spring stretches in proportion to the force; a pointer moves over a scale in newtons. Force sensor: an electronic gauge with digital readout/graph via computer, very accurate.
Electronic balance: a load cell/strain gauge senses the force of the object pressing down and the electronics display mass (weighing scales are calibrated in kg by dividing W by g) – so a “weight machine” really shows mass in kg. Tare/zero before use.
Example: an 8 kg school bag weighs 8 × 9.8 = 78.4 N on Earth and 8 × 1.625 = 13 N on the Moon.
[Table: Mass vs weight]
Mass | Weight
• Quantity of matter; measure of inertia | Gravitational force on the body
• Scalar | Vector (towards centre of planet)
• Unit kg | Unit N
• Same everywhere | Changes with g (≈ 1/6 on the Moon)
• Beam or electronic balance | Spring balance / force meter
• m = W/g | W = mg
کمیت جسم میں مادے کی مقدار اور جمود کی پیمائش ہے (kg، اسکیلر، ہر جگہ یکساں)۔ وزن وہ قوت ہے جس سے سیارہ جسم کو اپنی طرف کھینچتا ہے (N، ویکٹر، جگہ کے ساتھ بدلتا ہے)۔ W = mg۔ چاند پر وزن تقریباً چھٹا حصہ رہ جاتا ہے مگر کمیت وہی رہتی ہے۔ اسپرنگ بیلنس وزن اور الیکٹرانک بیلنس کمیت دکھاتا ہے۔

══ 3.8 Gravitational field and gravitational field strength (pp. 77–78) ══
A force field is the region where a non-contact force acts. The gravitational field is the region around a massive object (Earth, Sun) where its gravitational force acts.
Gravitational field strength (g): the gravitational force per unit mass at a point:
g = F/m = W/m; unit N/kg (= m/s²); vector, directed towards the centre of the planet. On Earth’s surface g = 9.8 N/kg, numerically equal to the acceleration due to gravity.
- g decreases with height above the Earth’s surface and is different on each planet.
Finding g on another planet: mass is the same, so gₚ = Wₚ/m = Wₚ × g_E/W_E.
Example: a box weighs 400 N on Earth and 150 N on a planet: m = 400/9.8 = 40.8 kg; g = 150/40.8 = 3.68 N/kg – this matches Mars.
[Table: Table 3.2 – Approximate g on different bodies]
Body | g (N/kg)
• Sun | 274
• Mercury | 3.7
• Venus | 8.9
• Earth | 9.8
• Moon | 1.6
• Mars | 3.7
• Jupiter | 24.8
• Saturn | 10.4
ثقلی میدان کسی بڑے جسم کے گرد وہ علاقہ ہے جہاں اس کی کشش ثقل عمل کرتی ہے۔ ثقلی میدان کی شدت فی اکائی کمیت ثقلی قوت ہے: g = W/m، اکائی N/kg، ویکٹر۔ زمین پر g = 9.8 N/kg؛ اونچائی پر کم ہو جاتی ہے اور ہر سیارے پر مختلف ہے۔

══ 3.9 Momentum, force and impulse (pp. 78–81) ══
Linear momentum (p): the product of mass and velocity: p = mv. Vector (direction of velocity); SI unit kg m/s = N s.
A truck and a car at the same speed: the truck has more momentum (harder to stop).
Resultant force in terms of momentum (Newton’s second law): the net force equals the rate of change of momentum:
F = Δp/Δt = (mvf − mvᵢ)/t
A sudden change in momentum (small Δt) needs a large force; spreading the change over a longer time reduces the force.
Impulse (J): the product of force and the time for which it acts: J = FΔt = Δp = mvf − mvᵢ. Vector (direction of force); unit N s. For a varying force, impulse = area under the force–time graph (e.g. bat hitting a ball).
Applications (increase Δt → reduce force): catching a ball by moving hands back; padded cricket gloves and helmets; crumple zones, air bags and seat belts in cars; landing with bent knees; packing materials; sand pits for long jump.
Example: car 1200 kg and truck 10 000 kg each moving at 8 m/s, stopped in 5 s: F_car = −1920 N, F_truck = −16 000 N – the truck is much harder to stop.
مومینٹم کمیت اور ولاسٹی کا حاصل ضرب ہے: p = mv (ویکٹر، اکائی kg m/s = N s)۔ حاصل قوت مومینٹم میں تبدیلی کی شرح ہے: F = Δp/Δt۔ امپلس = قوت × وقت = مومینٹم میں تبدیلی۔ وقت بڑھانے سے قوت کم ہوتی ہے، اس لیے کرکٹ کے دستانوں میں فوم اور گاڑیوں میں ایئر بیگ ہوتے ہیں۔

══ 3.10 Conservation of momentum (pp. 81–82) ══
A system is a group of bodies under study, separated from the surroundings by a boundary. An isolated system is one on which the net external force is zero.
Law of conservation of momentum: if no net external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant (total momentum before = total momentum after):
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Gun and bullet (recoil): before firing, total momentum = 0. After firing: mb vb + mg vg = 0 → vg = −mb vb/mg. The gun moves backward with a much smaller speed because its mass is much larger.
Example: 20 g bullet at 300 m/s from a 5 kg rifle → v = −(0.02 × 300)/5 = −1.2 m/s.
Rocket: hot gases are pushed out backward with large momentum; the rocket gains equal momentum forward (works in space – needs no air to push on).
Other examples: a boat moves back when you jump ashore; balloon released with its mouth open; a man on frictionless ice throwing his bag; jet engines.
مومینٹم کی بقا کا قانون: اگر کسی نظام پر بیرونی حاصل قوت صفر ہو تو اس کا کل مومینٹم مستقل رہتا ہے۔ گولی چلنے سے پہلے بندوق اور گولی کا کل مومینٹم صفر ہوتا ہے، اس لیے گولی آگے اور بندوق پیچھے (کم رفتار سے) جاتی ہے۔ راکٹ گیسیں پیچھے پھینک کر آگے بڑھتا ہے۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Free-body diagrams: (a) book on a table (b) box pushed along a rough floor (c) lamp hanging from a string.
chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 3 in one page
- Force: push/pull changing state of motion, speed, direction or shape; vector; N. Contact: normal, friction, tension, air resistance. Non-contact: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic.
- Fundamental forces: strong (strongest, nucleus, 10⁻¹⁵ m) > electromagnetic (photon, infinite) > weak (radioactive decay, W/Z) > gravitational (weakest, infinite). Abdus Salam: electroweak theory, Nobel 1979.
- FBD: object + all force arrows. Like forces add, unlike subtract; balanced → no acceleration.
- 1st law (inertia): rest/uniform motion continues unless net force acts. Mass measures inertia. Bus start/stop, carpet dust, coin on card, seat belts.
- 2nd law: F = ma; 1 N = 1 kg m/s². Also F = Δp/Δt. Lifting with acceleration: F = m(g + a).
- 3rd law: F_AB = −F_BA; act on different bodies, never cancel. Rocket, recoil, walking, swimming.
- Limitations: atomic scale (quantum), speeds near c (relativity).
- Mass vs weight: kg vs N; W = mg; Moon ≈ 1/6. Spring balance → weight; electronic balance → mass.
- Field strength: g = F/m, N/kg, 9.8 on Earth, decreases with height.
- Momentum p = mv (kg m/s = N s). Impulse J = FΔt = Δp; padding/air bags increase Δt to cut force.
- Conservation: isolated system → total momentum constant; recoil V = −mv/M.

قوت دھکا یا کھنچاؤ ہے۔ چار بنیادی قوتیں (مضبوط، برقی مقناطیسی، کمزور، ثقلی)۔ نیوٹن کا پہلا قانون جمود، دوسرا F = ma، تیسرا عمل اور ردعمل۔ وزن W = mg، کمیت ہر جگہ یکساں۔ مومینٹم p = mv، امپلس FΔt = Δp، اور بیرونی قوت نہ ہو تو مومینٹم محفوظ رہتا ہے (بندوق کا پیچھے ہٹنا، راکٹ)۔

Exam Focus: 21 summative SLOs – the heaviest chapter. Every paper asks: Newton’s laws (statements, examples, F = ma numericals, limitations), inertia examples (bus, carpet, coin on card), mass vs weight, g on other planets (200 N → 50 N), momentum p = mv, impulse FΔt = Δp, conservation of momentum (gun–bullet recoil, rocket), fundamental forces in order of strength, contact vs non-contact forces.
chapters.definitions:
• Dynamics (ڈائنامکس / حرکیات بمع اسباب) [p. 62]: The branch of mechanics that studies motion together with its causes (forces).
• Force (قوت) [p. 62]: A push or pull that moves or tends to move a body, stops or tends to stop it, or changes its speed or direction.
• Contact force (رابطے کی قوت) [p. 62]: A force between objects that are in physical contact.
• Non-contact force (غیر رابطے کی قوت) [p. 63]: A force that acts at a distance without contact.
• Normal force (عمودی قوت) [p. 62]: Force perpendicular to a contact surface that keeps objects from passing through each other.
• Tension (تناؤ) [p. 63]: The pulling force in a stretched string, rope or cable.
• Free-body diagram (فری باڈی ڈایاگرام) [p. 66]: A diagram showing only the object with arrows for all the forces acting on it.
• Net (resultant) force (حاصل قوت) [p. 67]: A single force having the same effect as all the forces acting on a body.
• Newton’s first law (نیوٹن کا پہلا قانون) [p. 68]: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an external net force.
• Inertia (جمود) [p. 70]: The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion; measured by mass.
• Newton’s second law (نیوٹن کا دوسرا قانون) [p. 71]: Acceleration is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to mass: F = ma.
• Newton (N) (نیوٹن) [p. 72]: The force that produces an acceleration of 1 m/s² in a mass of 1 kg.
• Newton’s third law (نیوٹن کا تیسرا قانون) [p. 72]: Whenever one object exerts a force on another, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.
• Mass (کمیت) [p. 74]: The quantity of matter in a body; a measure of its inertia.
• Weight (وزن) [p. 74]: The force with which a planet’s gravity pulls a body towards its centre (W = mg).
• Gravitational field (ثقلی میدان) [p. 77]: The region around a massive object in which its gravitational force acts.
• Gravitational field strength (ثقلی میدان کی شدت) [p. 77]: Gravitational force per unit mass at a point (g = F/m), unit N/kg.
• Momentum (مومینٹم / معیارِ حرکت) [p. 78]: The product of mass and velocity of a body (p = mv); a vector.
• Impulse (امپلس / ضرب) [p. 80]: The product of a force and the time for which it acts; equal to the change in momentum.
• Isolated system (علیحدہ نظام) [p. 81]: A system on which the net external force is zero.
• Law of conservation of momentum (مومینٹم کی بقا کا قانون) [p. 81]: If no external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Force (قوت): Push or pull
• Inertia (جمود): Resistance to change in motion
• Mass (کمیت): Quantity of matter
• Weight (وزن): Pull of gravity
• Momentum (معیارِ حرکت): Mass × velocity
• Impulse (ضربہ): Force × time
• Recoil (پسپائی): Backward motion of gun
• Friction (رگڑ): Force opposing sliding
• Tension (تناؤ): Pull in a rope
• Normal force (عمودی قوت): Support force
• Field strength (میدان کی شدت): Force per unit mass
• Isolated system (علیحدہ نظام): No external force
• Action (عمل): First force
• Reaction (ردِعمل): Equal opposite force
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Newton’s second law: F = ma (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²)
• Weight: W = mg (g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth)
• Gravitational field strength: g = F/m = W/m (N/kg)
• Momentum: p = mv (kg m/s = N s)
• Force and momentum: F = Δp/Δt = (mvf − mvᵢ)/t
• Impulse: J = FΔt = Δp (N s)
• Conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
• Recoil velocity: V = −m v/M (gun mass M, bullet m)
• Lifting with acceleration: F = m(g + a) (Upward acceleration)
• Third law: F_AB = −F_BA

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• a ∝ F and a ∝ 1/m  →  a ∝ F/m  →  F = ma (with k = 1 in SI) — Derivation of Newton’s second law.
• F = Δp/Δt = (mvf − mvᵢ)/t = m(vf − vᵢ)/t = ma — Second law in terms of momentum.
• F = 0  →  a = 0  →  v = constant — First law deduced from the second.
• FΔt = mvf − mvᵢ — Impulse–momentum relation.
• 0 = m v + M V  →  V = −mv/M — Recoil of gun.
• N s = (kg m s⁻²) s = kg m s⁻¹ — Units of momentum are equal.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does a heavier truck need stronger brakes than a car moving at the same speed?
   Answer: It has more momentum (and inertia); a larger force is needed to change it in the same time.
2. Is a force needed to keep a body moving at constant velocity in space?
   Answer: No – by the first law no net force is needed.
3. Why does a gun recoil less than the bullet moves forward?
   Answer: Equal momenta; the gun’s mass is much larger, so its velocity is much smaller.
4. Why are action and reaction never balanced?
   Answer: They act on different bodies.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why do car makers fit crumple zones and air bags?
   Answer: They increase the collision time, reducing the force on passengers (F = Δp/Δt).
2. Why do long jumpers land in a sand pit?
   Answer: Sand increases the stopping time, reducing the force on the legs.
3. How do you tighten a loose hammer head by striking the handle on the ground?
   Answer: The handle stops suddenly; the head continues moving down (inertia) and fits tightly.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. An engine applies 3000 N. What acceleration does it give a 12 000 kg bus and a 1200 kg car? (Example 3.1)
   Given: F = 3000 N; m_bus = 12 000 kg; m_car = 1200 kg
   Required: a_bus, a_car
   Formula: a = F/m
   Substitution: 3000/12 000; 3000/1200
   Calculation: 0.25; 2.5
   Final Answer: Bus 0.25 m/s², car 2.5 m/s²

2. A school bag has mass 8 kg. Find its weight on Earth (g = 9.8) and on the Moon (g = 1.625 m/s²). (Example 3.2)
   Given: m = 8 kg; g_E = 9.8, g_M = 1.625 m/s²
   Required: W_E, W_M
   Formula: W = mg
   Substitution: 8 × 9.8; 8 × 1.625
   Calculation: 78.4; 13
   Final Answer: 78.4 N on Earth; 13 N on the Moon

3. A box weighs 400 N on Earth and 150 N on an unknown planet. Find g there. (Example 3.3)
   Given: W_E = 400 N, W_P = 150 N, g_E = 9.8 N/kg
   Required: g_P
   Formula: m = W_E/g_E; g_P = W_P/m
   Substitution: m = 400/9.8 = 40.8 kg; g_P = 150/40.8
   Calculation: g_P = 3.675
   Final Answer: 3.68 N/kg (Mars)

4. A golfer hits a 45 g ball which leaves at 80 m/s. What momentum is given to it? (Example 3.4)
   Given: m = 45 g = 0.045 kg, v = 80 m/s
   Required: p
   Formula: p = mv
   Substitution: 0.045 × 80
   Calculation: 3.6
   Final Answer: 3.6 kg m/s

5. A car (1200 kg) and a truck (10 000 kg) both move at 8 m/s and must stop in 5 s. Find the force needed for each. (Example 3.5)
   Given: vᵢ = 8 m/s, vf = 0, t = 5 s
   Required: F_car, F_truck
   Formula: F = (mvf − mvᵢ)/t
   Substitution: 1200(0 − 8)/5; 10 000(0 − 8)/5
   Calculation: −1920 N; −16 000 N
   Final Answer: Car −1920 N, truck −16 000 N (negative = opposite to motion); the truck is harder to stop

6. A 20 g bullet leaves a 5 kg rifle at 300 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the rifle.
   Given: m = 0.02 kg, v = 300 m/s, M = 5 kg, initial momentum 0
   Required: V
   Formula: 0 = mv + MV → V = −mv/M
   Substitution: V = −(0.02 × 300)/5
   Calculation: V = −1.2
   Final Answer: 1.2 m/s backward


══ ADDITIONAL SLO NUMERICAL PRACTICE ══

1. A 1000 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s. Find the net force.
   Given: m = 1000 kg, vᵢ = 0, vf = 20 m/s, t = 10 s
   Required: F
   Formula: F = m(vf − vᵢ)/t
   Substitution: 1000 × 20/10
   Calculation: 2000
   Final Answer: 2000 N

2. A 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is caught and stopped in 0.1 s. Find the force on the hands. What if the time is increased to 0.3 s?
   Given: m = 0.15 kg, Δv = 30 m/s
   Required: F for t = 0.1 s and 0.3 s
   Formula: F = mΔv/t
   Substitution: 4.5/0.1; 4.5/0.3
   Calculation: 45 N; 15 N
   Final Answer: 45 N; 15 N – moving the hands back reduces the force

3. Two trolleys of 2 kg each: one moving at 6 m/s hits the other at rest and they stick together. Find their common velocity.
   Given: m₁ = m₂ = 2 kg, u₁ = 6 m/s, u₂ = 0
   Required: v
   Formula: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v
   Substitution: 2 × 6 + 0 = 4v
   Calculation: v = 3
   Final Answer: 3 m/s

NBF Chapter 3 Exercises (83–86):

— Exercise MCQs —
1. Inertia of a body is related to which of the following quantities? → A (mass) | Mass measures inertia.
2. A force of 5 N is applied to a body weighing 10 N. Its acceleration in m/s² is: → C (5) | m = 10/10 = 1 kg (g = 10), a = 5/1 = 5 m/s² (4.9 with g = 9.8).
3. SI unit of linear momentum is: → D (kg m s⁻¹) | p = mv.
4. The rate of change of momentum of a freely falling body is equal to its: → C (weight) | Δp/Δt = net force = weight.
5. Change in momentum of a body is equal to: → B ((force)(time)) | Impulse.
6. A book of mass 5 kg is placed on a table. The magnitude of net force acting on the book is: → 
7. Thrust force is a consequence of which law of motion? → C (Third) | Action–reaction.
8. A force acts on a body for 2 s and produces a change in momentum of 50 kg m/s. The force is: → C (25 N) | 50/2.
9. At the fairground, the force that balances your weight is: → D (frictional force) | In a rotor ride the wall’s friction holds you up.
10. When a hanging carpet is beaten by a stick, dust flies off. It is mainly due to: → C (inertia of dust) | Dust stays at rest.
12. A bucket of water is revolved in a vertical circle. Water does not spill even upside down, due to: → C (inertia of water) | The water’s tendency to move straight (inertia) presses it into the bucket; the bucket supplies the centripetal force.
13. The force which moves the car is: → B (force of friction between road and tyre) | Tyres push the road back; friction pushes the car forward.
14. N kg⁻¹ is equivalent to: → B (m s⁻²) | (kg m s⁻²)/kg.
15. An object of mass 1 kg at the Earth’s surface experiences a force of: → B (9.8 N) | W = mg.
16. Net force on a body falling in air with uniform velocity is equal to: → D (zero) | Uniform velocity → a = 0 (terminal velocity).

— Q II. Short-response questions —
1 When a motorcyclist hits a stationary car, he may fly off the motorcycle and the driver in the car may get a neck injury. Explain.
   Answer: Inertia. The motorcycle stops suddenly but the rider’s body tends to keep moving forward, so he is thrown off. The car is pushed forward suddenly; the driver’s body moves with the seat but his head tends to stay at rest, so it jerks backward – causing a neck injury.
2 In autumn, when you shake a branch, the leaves are detached. Why?
   Answer: The branch is suddenly moved, but the leaves (with weak stalks) tend to remain at rest due to inertia; they break off.
3 Why is it not safe to apply brakes only on the front wheel of a bicycle?
   Answer: The front wheel stops but the rider and the rest of the bicycle tend to keep moving forward (inertia); the bicycle can tip over the front wheel and the rider is thrown forward.
4 Deduce Newton’s first law of motion from Newton’s second law.
   Answer: F = ma. If the net force F = 0, then a = 0, so the velocity does not change: a body at rest stays at rest and a moving body keeps moving uniformly in a straight line – the first law.
5 Action and reaction are equal but opposite. They always act in pairs. Do they balance each other? Can bodies move under an action–reaction pair?
   Answer: They do not balance because they act on different bodies. Yes, bodies can move: each body accelerates due to the force acting on it (e.g. a rocket and its exhaust gases, a person walking).
6 A man slips on an oily floor; he is alone and throws his bag to move out of the slippery area. Why is it so?
   Answer: With no friction, he can only move by conservation of momentum / third law: throwing the bag forward gives the bag momentum in one direction and him equal momentum in the opposite direction, so he slides away.
7 How would you use Newton’s third law and the law of conservation of momentum to explain the motion of a rocket?
   Answer: The rocket pushes hot gases out backward at high speed (action); the gases push the rocket forward (reaction). Total momentum stays zero/constant: the momentum of the gases backward equals the momentum gained by the rocket forward. It works in space because it does not need air to push against.
8 Why are cricket batter gloves padded with foam?
   Answer: The foam increases the time Δt over which the ball’s momentum changes; since F = Δp/Δt, the force on the hands is reduced, preventing injury.
9 Where will your weight be greater – near the Earth or near the Moon? What about mass?
   Answer: Weight is greater near the Earth (g = 9.8 vs 1.6 N/kg, about 6 times). Mass is the same everywhere.
10 When Ronaldo kicks the ball, at the highest point both Earth and ball attract each other with the same force. Why does the ball move towards the Earth and not the Earth towards the ball?
   Answer: Forces are equal (third law) but a = F/m. The ball’s mass is tiny, so its acceleration is large and visible; the Earth’s mass is enormous, so its acceleration is negligibly small.
10b What are gravitational field and gravitational field strength? Explain.
   Answer: Gravitational field: region around a mass where its gravitational force acts. Field strength g = force per unit mass = W/m, unit N/kg, vector towards the centre; 9.8 N/kg on Earth; decreases with height.
11 Justify and illustrate the use of electronic balances to measure mass.
   Answer: An electronic balance has a load cell (strain gauge) that converts the force of the object into an electrical signal; the circuit divides by g and shows mass in g/kg digitally – quick and precise (0.01 g). Place on a level surface, away from draughts, tare (zero) before use, place the object gently in the centre.
12 State and prove Newton’s second law of motion in terms of momentum.
   Answer: The rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net force on it: F = Δp/Δt. Proof: F = ma = m(vf − vᵢ)/t = (mvf − mvᵢ)/t = Δp/Δt.
13 Define isolated system. State the law of conservation of linear momentum. Explain with an example.
   Answer: Isolated system: no net external force acts on it. Law: total momentum of an isolated system remains constant. Example: gun and bullet – before firing total momentum 0; after, bullet forward and gun backward with equal and opposite momenta (m v = −M V).

— Q III. Extended-response questions —
1 State Newton’s first law of motion. Explain with examples. Why is it called the law of inertia?
   Answer: Statement and examples as in topic 3.4 (bus starting/stopping, carpet dust, coin and card, ball rolling until friction stops it, probes in space). It is called the law of inertia because it describes inertia – the natural tendency of bodies to keep their state of rest or uniform motion.
2 Define inertia. Why is knowledge of inertia important in daily life? Elaborate with examples.
   Answer: Inertia: resistance of a body to change in its state of rest or motion; depends on mass. Importance: wearing seat belts and having air bags/headrests; not jumping from a moving bus; braking gradually; securing loads on trucks; leaving gaps between vehicles; athletes running on after the finish line; shaking a tree to drop fruit; beating dust from a carpet.
3 State and prove Newton’s second law of motion. Deduce Newton’s second law from the first law.
   Answer: Statement: a ∝ F and a ∝ 1/m → F = ma. From the first law, a change in velocity needs a net force; experiments show a doubles when F doubles and halves when m doubles, giving a ∝ F/m; with SI units k = 1 → F = ma. In momentum form: F = Δp/Δt = ma.
4 State Newton’s third law of motion. Explain with daily-life examples.
   Answer: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction acting on a different body. Examples: walking, swimming, rowing, jumping, rocket propulsion, gun recoil, punching a wall, a book pressing on a table and the table pushing up, Earth–ball attraction.
5 State the limitations of Newton’s laws of motion.
   Answer: They fail for atomic/sub-atomic particles (quantum mechanics needed) and for speeds close to the speed of light (relativity needed); they hold only in non-accelerating (inertial) frames. Otherwise they are excellent approximations for everyday objects.
6 Differentiate with examples between contact and non-contact forces. Also explain the fundamental forces and the role of Dr Abdus Salam in unifying two of them.
   Answer: Contact: normal force, friction, tension, air resistance; non-contact: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic. Fundamental forces: strong nuclear (strongest, short range, nucleus), electromagnetic (charges, infinite range, photon), weak nuclear (radioactive decay, W/Z bosons), gravitational (weakest, infinite range). Dr Abdus Salam, with Weinberg and Glashow, developed the electroweak theory (late 1960s) showing electromagnetic and weak forces are one force; Nobel Prize 1979.
7 Represent the forces acting on a body using free-body diagrams.
   Answer: Draw the body as a box/dot and arrows from its centre: book on table (weight down, normal up); box pushed on floor (applied forward, friction backward, weight, normal); hanging lamp (tension up, weight down); falling parachutist (weight down, air resistance up). See the diagram in Tables & Diagrams.
8 Define momentum. What are its formula and unit? Is it scalar or vector? Show that the units of momentum N s and kg m/s are equal.
   Answer: Momentum = mass × velocity, p = mv; vector in the direction of velocity; unit kg m/s. N s = (kg m s⁻²) × s = kg m s⁻¹.
9 Differentiate between mass and weight of a body.
   Answer: See the table in topic 3.7: mass – quantity of matter, scalar, kg, constant, beam balance; weight – gravitational force, vector, N, varies with g, spring balance; W = mg.

chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B)] How can changes in force and mass affect the acceleration of an object? Explain in the light of Newton’s second law.
   Answer: a = F/m: for a fixed mass, a larger force gives a proportionally larger acceleration; for a fixed force, a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration (inverse proportion).

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B); old scheme] Under what conditions do Newton’s laws not remain applicable? (Give two conditions.)
   Answer: (1) For atomic and sub-atomic particles (quantum mechanics). (2) For speeds close to the speed of light (relativity).

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B)] A 2 kg ball changes its velocity from 4 m/s to 10 m/s. Calculate the impulse applied to the ball.
   Answer: J = m(vf − vᵢ) = 2 × (10 − 4) = 12 N s.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] Name any three fundamental forces of nature. Briefly describe each in one sentence.
   Answer: Strong nuclear – strongest, holds the nucleus together; electromagnetic – between charges, causes friction/normal forces; gravitational – weakest, attraction between all masses (weak nuclear – causes radioactive decay).

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] State Newton’s third law of motion. Give at least three daily-life examples.
   Answer: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction on a different body. Examples: walking (foot pushes ground back), rocket (gases down, rocket up), gun recoil, swimming, jumping.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] A 2 kg object changes its velocity from 3 m/s to 7 m/s in a short time. Calculate the impulse.
   Answer: J = 2 × (7 − 3) = 8 N s.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] A truck of mass 1500 kg moves at 10 m/s, while a motorcycle of mass 150 kg moves at 20 m/s. (a) Calculate the momentum of each. (b) Which has greater momentum and why?
   Answer: (a) Truck 1500 × 10 = 15 000 kg m/s; motorcycle 150 × 20 = 3000 kg m/s. (b) The truck – its much larger mass outweighs the motorcycle’s higher speed.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme); Annual 2025 (D)] A rifle of mass 5 kg fires a bullet of mass 20 g at 300 m/s. What is the recoil velocity of the rifle?
   Answer: V = −(0.02 × 300)/5 = −1.2 m/s (backward).

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] Enlist the fundamental forces of nature in descending order of strength.
   Answer: Strong nuclear > electromagnetic > weak nuclear > gravitational.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] A passenger standing in a bus falls backward when the bus suddenly moves forward. Why?
   Answer: Inertia: his feet move with the bus but his upper body tends to remain at rest, so he falls backward.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] An object weighs 200 N on Earth while 50 N on an unknown planet. Find the gravitational field strength on that planet.
   Answer: m = 200/10 = 20 kg (g = 10); gₚ = 50/20 = 2.5 N/kg (2.45 N/kg with g = 9.8).

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] Differentiate between contact and non-contact forces.
   Answer: Contact forces need touching (friction, normal force, tension); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, electrostatic, magnetic).

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] Briefly explain the system of gun and bullet using the law of conservation of momentum.
   Answer: Before firing total momentum = 0. After firing the bullet gains momentum mv forward; to keep the total zero the gun gains equal momentum backward: MV = −mv, so V = −mv/M, small because M is large.

14. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B, D)] What is impulse? How is it related to force? Give the equation.
   Answer: Impulse = force × time it acts = change in momentum: J = FΔt = mvf − mvᵢ. A given change in momentum over a longer time needs a smaller force.

15. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] State Newton’s second law of motion in terms of acceleration. Write its mathematical forms.
   Answer: Acceleration ∝ net force and ∝ 1/mass, in the direction of the force: a = F/m, F = ma, m = F/a.

16. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] An object weighs 300 N on Earth and 100 N on an unknown planet. Find the gravitational field there.
   Answer: m = 300/10 = 30 kg; g = 100/30 = 3.33 N/kg (≈ 3.27 with g = 9.8).

17. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What is meant by force? State its SI unit.
   Answer: A push or pull that changes or tends to change the state of rest/motion, speed, direction or shape of a body; SI unit newton (N).

18. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] State and briefly explain Newton’s first law of motion.
   Answer: A body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced external force acts on it; it describes inertia (e.g. passengers lurching when a bus starts or stops).

19. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Differentiate between mass and weight (any three points).
   Answer: Mass: quantity of matter, scalar, kg, constant everywhere. Weight: gravitational force, vector, N, changes with g.

20. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Explain the motion of a rocket using the law of conservation of momentum.
   Answer: Initially total momentum = 0. Burning fuel ejects gases backward with high momentum; the rocket gains equal momentum forward, so it accelerates upward; it works in vacuum.

21. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Two identical balls roll on a smooth floor; ball A has twice the momentum of ball B. Both are stopped by the same force. Which takes more time? Give mathematical reasoning.
   Answer: t = Δp/F. With the same F, t ∝ Δp; A has twice the momentum, so A takes twice as long to stop.

22. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Define impulse. Write its formula and SI unit.
   Answer: Impulse = force × time for which it acts = change in momentum; J = FΔt = Δp; unit N s (= kg m/s).

23. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Differentiate between the strong nuclear force and the electromagnetic force.
   Answer: Strong: strongest, acts only between nucleons, range ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m, always attractive, holds nucleus together. Electromagnetic: weaker, acts between charged particles, infinite range, attractive or repulsive, carried by photons.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M) Q4] (a) State Newton’s second law. (b) A 15 kg cart moving at 25 m/s is stopped by a 75 N force. How long does it take to stop?
   Answer: (a) a = F/m (F = ma). (b) a = 75/15 = 5 m/s² (deceleration); t = (25 − 0)/5 = 5 s.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme) Q4] (a) State Newton’s second law in words (b) mathematical form (c) what happens to acceleration when (i) force increases with mass constant (ii) mass increases with force constant?
   Answer: (a) Acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass, in the direction of the force. (b) F = ma. (c)(i) acceleration increases in proportion; (ii) acceleration decreases (inversely).

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D) Q4] (a) What is friction? (b) How does friction in machine parts lead to energy dissipation as heat? (c) Explain two methods to reduce friction.
   Answer: See Chapter 4 (friction): (a) force opposing relative motion between surfaces; (b) rubbing surfaces do work against friction, converting kinetic energy into heat (wasted energy, wear); (c) lubrication with oil/grease, ball bearings, smoothing/polishing surfaces, streamlining.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B) Q4] Explain the limitations of Newton’s laws of motion.
   Answer: Fail at atomic scale (quantum mechanics), at speeds near c (relativity), and in accelerating frames; they are approximations valid for macroscopic objects at ordinary speeds – still used in engineering.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025 Q5] Which is more difficult to stop in 5 s and why: (a) a 2500 kg car at 10 m/s (b) a 5000 kg van at 4 m/s?
   Answer: p_car = 25 000 kg m/s; p_van = 20 000 kg m/s. F = Δp/t: car 5000 N, van 4000 N. The car is harder to stop because it has more momentum.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF) Q4] State and prove Newton’s second law of motion.
   Answer: Statement as above. Proof via a ∝ F, a ∝ 1/m → F = kma, k = 1 by definition of the newton; or via momentum F = Δp/Δt = m(vf − vᵢ)/t = ma.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 3 in one page
- Force: push/pull changing state of motion, speed, direction or shape; vector; N. Contact: normal, friction, tension, air resistance. Non-contact: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic.
- Fundamental forces: strong (strongest, nucleus, 10⁻¹⁵ m) > electromagnetic (photon, infinite) > weak (radioactive decay, W/Z) > gravitational (weakest, infinite). Abdus Salam: electroweak theory, Nobel 1979.
- FBD: object + all force arrows. Like forces add, unlike subtract; balanced → no acceleration.
- 1st law (inertia): rest/uniform motion continues unless net force acts. Mass measures inertia. Bus start/stop, carpet dust, coin on card, seat belts.
- 2nd law: F = ma; 1 N = 1 kg m/s². Also F = Δp/Δt. Lifting with acceleration: F = m(g + a).
- 3rd law: F_AB = −F_BA; act on different bodies, never cancel. Rocket, recoil, walking, swimming.
- Limitations: atomic scale (quantum), speeds near c (relativity).
- Mass vs weight: kg vs N; W = mg; Moon ≈ 1/6. Spring balance → weight; electronic balance → mass.
- Field strength: g = F/m, N/kg, 9.8 on Earth, decreases with height.
- Momentum p = mv (kg m/s = N s). Impulse J = FΔt = Δp; padding/air bags increase Δt to cut force.
- Conservation: isolated system → total momentum constant; recoil V = −mv/M.

قوت دھکا یا کھنچاؤ ہے۔ چار بنیادی قوتیں (مضبوط، برقی مقناطیسی، کمزور، ثقلی)۔ نیوٹن کا پہلا قانون جمود، دوسرا F = ma، تیسرا عمل اور ردعمل۔ وزن W = mg، کمیت ہر جگہ یکساں۔ مومینٹم p = mv، امپلس FΔt = Δp، اور بیرونی قوت نہ ہو تو مومینٹم محفوظ رہتا ہے (بندوق کا پیچھے ہٹنا، راکٹ)۔

chapters.title: Dynamics – II
chapters.introduction:
Dynamics II deals with the turning effect of forces and circular motion. It covers like and unlike parallel forces, moment of force (torque) and the principle of moments, centre of mass and centre of gravity (plumb-line method), equilibrium – its two conditions, static/dynamic, and stable, unstable and neutral states – stability and how to improve it, friction (sliding, rolling, fluid drag), methods to reduce it, terminal velocity, centripetal force, and orbital speed of satellites with planetary data.

19 summative SLOs. Favourites: torque τ = Fd (spanner/door numericals), principle of moments (seesaw/metre-rod balance), CG vs CM, three states of equilibrium with examples, improving stability (lower CG, wider base), sliding vs rolling friction, methods to reduce friction, terminal velocity, centripetal force F = mv²/r and its sources (Moon, car on a curve), average orbital speed v = 2πr/T (satellite/planet numericals).
