chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B)] State the relationship between force and extension for a spring according to Hooke’s law.
   Answer: Within the limit of proportionality, extension is directly proportional to the force: F = kx.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] A spring has k = 8000 N/m. If 500 N is applied, what is the displacement? Give the answer in correct significant figures.
   Answer: x = 500/8000 = 0.0625 m → 0.063 m (6.3 cm) to 2 significant figures.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] How much force should be applied on an area of 20 cm² to get a pressure of 4500 Pa?
   Answer: F = PA = 4500 × 0.002 = 9 N.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] How does a rapid rise or fall in the liquid column of a barometer help predict weather changes?
   Answer: A rapid fall shows falling pressure → approaching low-pressure system: clouds, rain or storm. A rise shows increasing pressure → clear, fair weather.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] How does the rise of liquid in a drinking straw or dropper justify that the atmosphere exerts pressure?
   Answer: Sucking or squeezing lowers the pressure inside; the higher atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface pushes the liquid up – this would not happen without atmospheric pressure (e.g. on the Moon).

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D); AF Model Paper] What is pressure? Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt knife?
   Answer: Pressure = force per unit area. A sharp edge has a tiny area, so the same force gives a much larger pressure, which cuts easily.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] Why do areas with high pressure generally have clear skies, while areas with low pressure often have cloudy or rainy weather?
   Answer: In high pressure, air sinks and warms, so clouds evaporate – clear skies. In low pressure, air rises and cools, water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] How does atmospheric pressure vary with altitude? What special measures do mountain climbers take?
   Answer: It decreases with height because there is less air above. Climbers carry oxygen cylinders, acclimatise slowly, and use pressure cookers for cooking.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] How is Pascal’s law used in a hydraulic press to multiply force?
   Answer: Pressure F₁/A₁ on the small piston is transmitted unchanged to the large piston, so F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁ – larger by the area ratio.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] Describe that atmospheric pressure decreases with increase in height above the Earth’s surface.
   Answer: The weight of air above decreases as we go higher and the air becomes thinner, so pressure falls – from ≈ 101 kPa at sea level to ≈ 33 kPa on Everest; a barometer reading falls as you climb.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] A person sinks when standing on soft sand but not when lying down. Use P = F/A to explain.
   Answer: His weight (F) is the same, but lying down spreads it over a much larger area A, so P = F/A is much smaller and the sand can support him.

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme); AF Model Paper] State Pascal’s law. Enlist two of its applications.
   Answer: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Applications: hydraulic lift/jack, hydraulic brakes (also hydraulic press).

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] Justify that the atmosphere exerts pressure.
   Answer: Collapsing can when air is removed, suction cup, Magdeburg hemispheres, drinking straw, syringe.

14. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme); Annual 2025 (B)] How does pressure vary with depth in a liquid? Explain with the formula.
   Answer: P = ρgh: pressure increases in direct proportion to depth (for a given liquid).

15. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] Enlist any three applications of Hooke’s law.
   Answer: Spring balance, mechanical watch balance wheel, car suspension (galvanometer, mattress, trampoline).

16. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B, D)] How are hydraulic lifts capable of lifting heavy loads? Show mathematically.
   Answer: P = F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ → F₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁); with A₂ ≫ A₁, F₂ ≫ F₁.

17. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] Briefly describe any three applications of a liquid barometer.
   Answer: Weather forecasting, altitude measurement (altimeters), measuring pressure in industry/laboratories (calibration).

18. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] How much pressure does a 15 N suitcase exert on a table if its base is 0.8 m long and 0.5 m wide?
   Answer: A = 0.4 m²; P = 15/0.4 = 37.5 Pa.

19. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Differentiate between manometer and barometer.
   Answer: Manometer measures gas/fluid pressure (often relative to atmosphere), one end open, many forms. Barometer measures atmospheric pressure, closed tube with vacuum (or aneroid).

20. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Describe the working of a hydraulic car brake system.
   Answer: Pedal pushes master-cylinder piston → pressure in brake fluid → transmitted equally through brake lines (Pascal’s law) → wheel cylinders/calipers push brake pads against discs/drums → friction stops wheels.

21. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Derive the formula for liquid pressure.
   Answer: m = ρAh, F = ρAhg, P = F/A = ρgh.

22. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Can we drink water with a straw on the Moon? Justify.
   Answer: No – there is no atmosphere to push the water up.

23. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] A submarine is moving in the Pacific Ocean at a depth of 6 km. How much pressure is exerted on it if water density is 1000 kg/m³?
   Answer: P = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 6000 = 6 × 10⁷ Pa (5.88 × 10⁷ Pa with g = 9.8), plus atmospheric pressure.

24. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF, 50%)] Which will have a greater spring constant: a steel spring or a rubber spring?
   Answer: The steel spring – it needs a much larger force for the same extension because steel is stiffer (stronger interatomic forces).

25. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] With an example from everyday life, show how pressure exerts a force perpendicular to a surface.
   Answer: Water in a tank pushes out at right angles to the walls – holes in the side make water jet out perpendicular to the wall; an inflated balloon is pushed outward normal to its surface.

26. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] How is a manometer used to measure gas pressure?
   Answer: Connect one arm of a liquid-filled U-tube to the gas, leave the other open. Measure the difference in levels h: P_gas = P_atm + ρgh.

27. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Prove that the pressure of a liquid of density ρ at depth h is P = ρgh.
   Answer: As in topic 5.7.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B) Q3] On what principle do hydraulic brakes in vehicles work? How does the system multiply force to stop the vehicle effectively? Make a neat sketch.
   Answer: Pascal’s law. Pedal → master cylinder (small area) → pressure in fluid transmitted equally → wheel cylinders (larger area) give larger force on pads → friction on discs/drums. Force is multiplied by the area ratio; all wheels brake equally. Sketch: pedal, master cylinder, brake lines, wheel cylinders, pads, disc.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D) Q5] State Pascal’s law. How does it apply to a hydraulic car lift? Explain and show mathematically. Make a sketch.
   Answer: Statement; F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂; F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁; diagram of two pistons connected by oil.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M) Q4] Explain the principle on which a manometer works. Describe its construction and working.
   Answer: Principle: pressure difference supports a liquid column of height h (ΔP = ρgh). Construction: U-tube with liquid; one arm to gas, one open. Working: level difference h gives P_gas = P_atm ± ρgh.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme) Q6] How is Pascal’s law applied in hydraulic brakes in vehicles? Draw a labelled sketch.
   Answer: See above.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B) Q3] What is a manometer? Make its diagram and list its four applications.
   Answer: U-tube liquid device measuring gas pressure. Applications: gas pressure in pipes, blood pressure, vacuum measurement, leak testing, tank liquid level, flow measurement.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B) Q5] A hydraulic lift has a narrow cylinder of 0.003 m² and a wide cylinder of 0.9 m². What force on the narrow cylinder lifts a 1600 kg car?
   Answer: F₂ = 16 000 N (g = 10); F₁ = 16 000 × 0.003/0.9 = 53.3 N (52.3 N with g = 9.8).

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D) Q3] State Pascal’s principle. How is it applied in a hydraulic brake system? Explain with a diagram.
   Answer: As above.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D) Q5] Calculate the force required to lift a 2000 kg car with a hydraulic jack whose small piston area is 4 cm² and large piston area 80 cm².
   Answer: F₂ = 20 000 N (g = 10); F₁ = 20 000 × 4/80 = 1000 N.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025 Q4] Calculate the force required to lift a 2500 kg car with a hydraulic jack whose small piston is 6 cm² and large piston 90 cm².
   Answer: F₂ = 25 000 N; F₁ = 25 000 × 6/90 = 1666.7 N (g = 10).

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF) Q5] A hydraulic press lifts 500 kg when 10 N is applied on the small piston of radius 15 cm. Find the radius of the large piston.
   Answer: F₂ = 5000 N (g = 10); (r₂/r₁)² = 5000/10 = 500 → r₂ = 15 × √500 ≈ 15 × 22.4 = 335 cm (3.35 m).
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 5 in one page
- Elasticity: regains shape (steel, rubber); inelastic: plasticine, clay. Elastic limit → permanent deformation beyond it.
- Hooke’s law F = kx up to the limit of proportionality; k = F/x (N/m); steel spring k > rubber; half spring → 2k. Load–extension graph: straight through origin (gradient k), then curves. Stress–strain: proportional limit, elastic limit, ultimate stress, breaking point.
- Applications: spring balance, watch balance wheel, galvanometer, suspension, mattresses, trampolines.
- Pressure P = F/A (Pa = N/m²); small area → high pressure (knife, needle, heels); large area → low (snowshoes, camel, lying on sand). Fluid force ⟂ surface.
- Atmospheric pressure: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 760 mmHg = 1013 mbar. Evidence: suction cup, collapsing can, Magdeburg hemispheres, straw, syringe. Falls with height (Everest 33 kPa). High pressure → clear; low → cloudy/rain; rapid fall → storm. Isobars.
- Mercury barometer: inverted tube, 76 cm column, vacuum above; denser liquid → shorter column; weather and altitude.
- Liquid pressure P = ρgh (derive: m = ρAh, F = ρAhg, P = F/A); independent of shape; dams thicker at bottom.
- Manometer: U-tube, P_gas = P_atm + ρgh.
- Pascal’s law: pressure transmitted equally; F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂; hydraulic lift, press, jack, brakes.

لچک اور ہُک کا قانون F = kx۔ دباؤ P = F/A (پاسکل)؛ کم رقبہ زیادہ دباؤ۔ کرۂ ہوائی کا دباؤ 760 mmHg، اونچائی پر کم۔ بیرومیٹر موسم بتاتا ہے۔ مائع کا دباؤ P = ρgh۔ مینو میٹر گیس کا دباؤ ناپتا ہے۔ پاسکل کا قانون: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ (ہائیڈرولک لفٹ اور بریک)۔

chapters.title: Work and Energy
chapters.introduction:
This unit explains work (W = Fd), energy and its forms, kinetic energy (Eₖ = ½mv², proved from the force–displacement graph), gravitational potential energy (Eₚ = mgh) and other stored energies, energy transfer and conversion, the law of conservation of energy (and why perpetual motion machines cannot work), renewable and non-renewable energy resources with their advantages and disadvantages, power (watt, horsepower, kWh) and efficiency with energy-flow diagrams.

Note: Some textbook items are inconsistent: MCQ 3 has no correct option (50 N × 5 m = 250 J); numerical Q IV 6 gives an output (100 kg raised 10 m = 9800 J) larger than the input (2238 J); numerical Q IV 7 works out to about 11 hp, not 95 hp. These are flagged with the worked values.

══ 6.1 Work (pp. 138–140) ══
In physics, work is done when a force moves a body in the direction of the force:
W = F × d (force × displacement in the direction of the force). Work is a scalar; SI unit joule (J).
1 joule: the work done when a force of 1 N moves a body 1 m in its own direction (1 J = 1 N m).
Conditions: work needs (1) a force and (2) a displacement in the direction of the force.
- No work if there is no displacement (pushing a wall or a stationary truck; holding a book on your head while standing still) or if the force is perpendicular to the motion (carrying a bag horizontally at constant height; centripetal force on an orbiting satellite does no work, so its speed stays the same).
- Work is maximum when the force is along the displacement (θ = 0°); if the force is at an angle θ, only its component F cos θ does work: W = Fd cos θ; negative work when the force opposes motion (friction, braking).
- A car moving at constant speed on a straight road: the engine does positive work and friction/air resistance do equal negative work – net work = 0, so its kinetic energy does not change.
- The work done in raising a box to a height does not depend on how fast it is raised or the path taken – only on its weight and the vertical height: W = mgh.
Example: pushing a box with 100 N through 200 m → W = 20 000 J = 20 kJ.
فزکس میں کام تب ہوتا ہے جب قوت جسم کو اپنی سمت میں ہٹائے: W = F × d، اکائی جول، اسکیلر۔ ہٹاؤ نہ ہو (دیوار دھکیلنا) یا قوت حرکت پر عمودی ہو (مدار میں سیٹلائٹ پر مرکز مائل قوت) تو کام صفر ہے۔ کسی ڈبے کو اوپر لے جانے کا کام صرف اونچائی اور وزن پر منحصر ہے، رفتار یا راستے پر نہیں۔

══ 6.2 Energy and its forms (pp. 140–141) ══
Energy is the ability (capacity) of a body to do work. Unit joule; scalar. When work is done, energy is transferred (a boy pushing a toy car transfers energy to it).
Forms of energy: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic (strain) potential, chemical (food, fuels, batteries), electrical, thermal/internal (heat), light/electromagnetic (radiant) (energy from the Sun), sound (sonic), nuclear (from changes in atomic nuclei – nuclear power stations).
All forms can be grouped as kinetic (due to motion of objects or particles) or potential (stored).
Stored energy (potential):
- Gravitational potential energy – book on a high shelf, water behind a dam.
- Elastic (strain) energy – stretched catapult, compressed spring, wound-up clock or toy, bow.
- Chemical energy – food, petrol, coal, cells/batteries.
- Nuclear energy – in uranium nuclei.
- Electrostatic energy – between the plates of a charged capacitor.
- Internal (thermal) energy – a hot object.
[Table: Table 6.1 – Forms of energy]
Form | Description | Example
• Kinetic | Energy of motion | Moving car, flowing water
• Gravitational potential | Stored due to height | Water behind a dam
• Elastic potential | Stored in stretched/compressed objects | Catapult, spring
• Chemical | Stored in chemical bonds | Food, petrol, battery
• Electrical | Energy of moving charges | Current in a circuit
• Radiant (light) | Carried by electromagnetic waves | Sunlight
• Thermal (internal) | Kinetic + potential energy of particles | Hot water
• Sound | Carried by vibrations | Loudspeaker, drum
• Nuclear | Stored in atomic nuclei | Uranium in a reactor
توانائی کام کرنے کی صلاحیت ہے (جول)۔ اقسام: حرکی، ثقلی مخفی، لچکدار، کیمیائی (خوراک، ایندھن)، برقی، روشنی، حرارتی، صوتی اور نیوکلیائی۔ ذخیرہ شدہ توانائی کی مثالیں: ڈیم کا پانی، کھنچی غلیل، بیٹری، یورینیم۔

══ 6.3 Kinetic energy: Eₖ = ½mv² (pp. 141–143) ══
Kinetic energy (Eₖ): the energy a body possesses due to its motion. It depends on mass and speed: a football is harder to stop than a tennis ball at the same speed; a faster ball is harder to stop than a slower one.
Proof (work–energy, graphical method): a constant force F accelerates a mass m from rest to speed v over displacement d on a frictionless surface.
1. Work done = F × d = area under the force–displacement graph (a rectangle) = gain in kinetic energy.
2. F = ma, and a = (v − 0)/t = v/t.
3. d = average speed × t = (0 + v)/2 × t = ½vt.
4. Eₖ = F × d = m(v/t) × ½vt = ½mv².
Work–energy theorem: the work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy (W = ΔEₖ).
- Doubling the speed makes Eₖ four times (Eₖ ∝ v²); doubling the mass doubles Eₖ.
- For the same momentum, the lighter body has more KE (Eₖ = p²/2m).
- For the same KE, the lightest body (a cricket ball rather than a car or elephant) has the greatest speed.
Example: a 100 g ball at 2 m/s has Eₖ = 0.2 J; Babar Azam gives a 120 g ball 50 J → v = √(2 × 50/0.12) = 28.9 m/s.
حرکت کی وجہ سے جسم کی توانائی حرکی توانائی ہے: Eₖ = ½mv²۔ ثبوت: کام = Fd = ma × ½vt = m(v/t) × ½vt = ½mv²۔ رفتار دگنی کرنے سے حرکی توانائی چار گنا ہو جاتی ہے۔

══ 6.4 Gravitational potential energy: Eₚ = mgh (pp. 143–145) ══
Potential energy: energy stored in a body because of its position (in a force field) or its state/configuration.
Gravitational potential energy (Eₚ): energy stored in a body when it is raised to a height against gravity. Lifting a book to a shelf stores the work done in it; when it falls, Eₚ turns into Eₖ.
Proof: to lift a mass m through height h at constant speed, the force needed equals its weight: F = mg. Work done = F × d = mg × h. This work is stored as Eₚ = mgh.
- Eₚ depends on mass, g and height (measured from a chosen reference level, usually the ground).
Examples: a 5 kg stone raised 20 m stores 5 × 9.8 × 20 = 980 J; Kamil (60 kg) high-jumps 1.5 m: Eₚ = 60 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 882 J, which came from the kinetic energy of his push-off (from chemical energy in his muscles).
جسم کی جگہ یا حالت کی وجہ سے ذخیرہ توانائی مخفی توانائی ہے۔ جسم کو اونچائی h تک اٹھانے میں قوت mg اور کام mgh ہوتا ہے جو ثقلی مخفی توانائی Eₚ = mgh کی صورت میں ذخیرہ ہو جاتا ہے۔

══ 6.5 Energy conversion, conservation and perpetual motion (pp. 145–148) ══
Energy conversion (transformation): changing energy from one form to another.
- Hydroelectric power: gravitational PE of stored water → KE of falling water → KE of turbine → electrical energy.
- Cyclist going up a hill: chemical energy (food) → KE → gravitational PE at the top (+ heat); going down: PE → KE.
- Electric bulb: electrical → light + heat. Car: chemical (petrol) → KE + heat + sound. Battery torch: chemical → electrical → light. Fan: electrical → KE (+ heat, sound). Bullet into sand: KE → heat, sound and work deforming the sand.
Dissipated (wasted) energy: energy that ends up in non-useful forms, mostly heat to the surroundings (by friction, air resistance, electrical resistance, sound). Only ~17–21% of petrol’s energy moves a car; electric cars are much more efficient.
Law (principle) of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another, and the total energy remains constant. E_initial = E_final.
Falling ball (no air resistance): at the top E = mgh (all PE); halfway E = ½mgh + ½mv²; at the bottom E = ½mv² (all KE). Mechanical energy (PE + KE) stays constant: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh).
With friction: Eₚ (initial) = Eₖ (final) + work done against friction.
Example: a 450 g football kicked up at 22 m/s: h_max = v²/2g = 24.7 m (g = 9.8); if it reaches only 20 m, work against air resistance = mg(24.7 − 20) ≈ 20.7 J.
Perpetual motion machines – imagined machines that would run forever, or give out more energy than put in, without an energy supply – cannot work: (1) energy cannot be created, so output cannot exceed input; (2) some energy is always dissipated as heat by friction and resistance, so the machine gradually runs down. Efficiency can never be 1 (100%).
توانائی کی بقا کا قانون: توانائی نہ پیدا کی جا سکتی ہے نہ ختم کی جا سکتی ہے؛ صرف ایک صورت سے دوسری میں بدلتی ہے اور کل مقدار مستقل رہتی ہے۔ گرتی گیند میں مخفی توانائی حرکی توانائی میں بدلتی ہے۔ رگڑ ہو تو کچھ توانائی حرارت میں ضائع ہوتی ہے۔ دائمی حرکت والی مشین ممکن نہیں کیونکہ توانائی پیدا نہیں ہو سکتی اور کچھ ہمیشہ حرارت میں ضائع ہوتی ہے۔

══ 6.6 Energy resources: non-renewable and renewable (pp. 148–155) ══
Society needs a sustainable energy supply – one that does not run out or harm the environment.
Non-renewable resources: limited; cannot be replaced in a short time – fossil fuels (coal, oil/petroleum, natural gas) and nuclear fuel (uranium).
Renewable resources: replaced naturally and continuously – solar, wind, hydroelectric (flowing water), tides, waves, geothermal, biomass.
How useful energy is obtained (energy chains):
- Fossil fuel power station: chemical energy of fuel → (burning in a boiler) heat → water turns to high-pressure steam → steam turns a turbine (KE) → turbine drives a generator → electrical energy → transformers and transmission lines. Block diagram: fuel → boiler → steam → turbine → generator → grid.
- Nuclear power: fission of uranium nuclei releases heat → steam → turbine → generator.
- Hydroelectric: water stored in a dam (PE) flows down (KE), turns turbines → generator (e.g. Tarbela, Mangla).
- Solar: solar cells (photovoltaic) convert light directly into electricity; solar panels/heaters heat water.
- Wind: KE of wind turns the blades of a wind turbine → generator (e.g. Jhimpir wind farms, Sindh).
- Geothermal: heat from hot rocks/heated groundwater inside the Earth makes steam → turbine.
- Tidal: rise and fall of tides drives turbines in barrages; wave energy from ocean waves.
- Biomass: wood, crop waste, animal dung burned or converted to biogas (chemical energy).
[Table: Advantages and disadvantages of energy sources]
Source | Advantages | Disadvantages
• Fossil fuels | Reliable, high energy, available any time, existing technology | Non-renewable; CO₂ (global warming), SO₂ (acid rain), air pollution
• Nuclear | Huge energy from small fuel; no CO₂; reliable | Radioactive waste; risk of accidents; expensive; non-renewable
• Hydroelectric | Renewable, no pollution, quick start, stores water | Expensive dams; floods land/displaces people; needs rivers
• Solar | Renewable, free, clean, good for remote areas | Not at night/cloudy; panels costly; large area
• Wind | Renewable, clean, free | Wind not constant; noisy; spoils landscape; harms birds
• Geothermal | Renewable, reliable, little pollution | Only in a few places; drilling cost
• Tidal/waves | Renewable, predictable (tides) | Few suitable sites; high cost; affects marine life
• Biomass/biogas | Renewable, uses waste, cheap fuel for villages | Releases CO₂/smoke; needs land; low energy density
[Table: Renewable vs non-renewable]
Renewable | Non-renewable
• Replaced naturally; will not run out | Limited; will run out
• Sunlight, wind, water, tides, geothermal, biomass | Coal, oil, natural gas, uranium
• Mostly clean (little CO₂) | Pollution and greenhouse gases
• Often intermittent; high initial cost | Reliable supply; cheaper existing plants
ناقابلِ تجدید وسائل محدود ہیں (کوئلہ، تیل، قدرتی گیس، یورینیم)؛ قابلِ تجدید قدرتی طور پر بحال ہوتے ہیں (شمسی، ہوا، پانی، مد و جزر، جیو تھرمل، بایوماس)۔ بجلی گھر میں ایندھن جلا کر بھاپ بنائی جاتی ہے جو ٹربائن اور جنریٹر چلاتی ہے۔ قابلِ تجدید وسائل ماحول کے لیے بہتر ہیں مگر ہمیشہ دستیاب نہیں اور مہنگے ہیں۔

══ 6.7 Power (pp. 156–157) ══
Power is the rate of doing work or the rate of transfer/conversion of energy:
P = W/t = E/t. Scalar; SI unit watt (W) = 1 J/s (after James Watt).
- 1 watt: 1 joule of work done in 1 second.
- 1 kW = 1000 W; 1 MW = 10⁶ W.
- 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W (550 ft·lb/s).
- A 100 W bulb converts 100 J of electrical energy every second.
Kilowatt-hour (kWh) – a unit of energy: the energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour = 1000 × 3600 = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Electricity bills: 1 unit = 1 kWh.
- More powerful machine → does the same work in less time (but uses energy faster); increasing power at the same efficiency increases energy consumption per second.
Example: an engine does 3 × 10⁷ J in 1 minute: P = 3 × 10⁷/60 = 5 × 10⁵ W = 500 kW ≈ 670 hp.
طاقت کام کرنے کی شرح ہے: P = W/t، اکائی واٹ (1 J/s)۔ 1 ہارس پاور = 746 W۔ 1 کلو واٹ آور = 3.6 × 10⁶ جول؛ بجلی کا 1 یونٹ = 1 kWh۔

══ 6.8 Efficiency and energy-flow diagrams (pp. 157–160) ══
Efficiency (η): the ratio of useful energy (or work) output to total energy (or work) input:
η = useful output/total input;  % efficiency = (useful output/input) × 100%. Also η = P_out/P_in. No unit.
- A petrol engine taking 400 J and doing 120 J of useful work: η = 120/400 = 30%.
- A bulb using 60 J to give 9 J of light: η = 9/60 = 15%.
No machine can be 100% efficient: some input energy is always wasted – mostly as heat due to friction, air resistance and electrical resistance (also sound, vibration). So useful output < input and η < 1. (An LED with 80% efficiency does not violate conservation of energy: the other 20% becomes heat.)
Why high efficiency matters: less fuel/electricity for the same job → lower cost, fewer resources used, less pollution and heating; longer battery life.
Energy flow (Sankey) diagrams show input splitting into useful and wasted outputs (arrow widths ∝ energy):
- Filament lamp: 100 J electrical → 5 J light (useful) + 95 J heat (wasted) – 5% efficient (fluorescent ≈ 20%, LED ≈ 80%).
- Power station: chemical energy of fuel → ≈ 40% electrical + ≈ 60% heat lost in cooling towers and gases.
- Car at constant speed on a level road: chemical energy of fuel → work against friction and air resistance + heat in engine + sound; KE stays constant (≈ 25% useful).
[Table: Table 6.3 – Typical efficiencies]
Device | Efficiency (%)
• Electric generator | 98
• Hydroelectric power plant | 95
• Large electric motor | 95
• Home gas furnace | 85
• Wind generator | 55
• Fossil-fuel power plant | 40
• Automobile engine | 25
• Fluorescent light | 20
• Incandescent light | 5
استعداد = مفید حاصل ÷ کل دی گئی توانائی (× 100%)۔ کوئی مشین 100% مستعد نہیں ہو سکتی کیونکہ رگڑ وغیرہ سے کچھ توانائی ہمیشہ حرارت میں ضائع ہوتی ہے۔ زیادہ استعداد سے ایندھن، خرچ اور آلودگی کم ہوتی ہے۔ عام بلب صرف 5% اور LED تقریباً 80% مستعد ہے۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Energy flow (Sankey) diagram of a filament lamp: Of 100 J electrical energy, only 5 J becomes light; 95 J is wasted as heat (5% efficient).
2. Fossil-fuel power station (block diagram): Chemical energy → heat → steam → turbine (kinetic) → generator → electrical energy.

chapters.definitions:
• Work (کام) [p. 138]: Work is done when a force moves a body in the direction of the force; W = Fd.
• Joule (جول) [p. 138]: Work done when a force of 1 N moves a body through 1 m in its direction.
• Energy (توانائی) [p. 140]: The ability (capacity) of a body to do work.
• Kinetic energy (حرکی توانائی) [p. 141]: Energy possessed by a body due to its motion; Eₖ = ½mv².
• Potential energy (مخفی توانائی) [p. 143]: Energy possessed by a body due to its position or state.
• Gravitational potential energy (ثقلی مخفی توانائی) [p. 144]: Energy stored in a body raised against gravity; Eₚ = mgh.
• Elastic potential energy (لچکدار مخفی توانائی) [p. 144]: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object.
• Energy conversion (توانائی کی تبدیلی) [p. 145]: Changing energy from one form into another.
• Law of conservation of energy (بقائے توانائی کا قانون) [p. 146]: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it changes form, and total energy stays constant.
• Dissipated energy (ضائع شدہ توانائی) [p. 146]: Energy transferred to non-useful forms, usually heat to the surroundings.
• Perpetual motion machine (دائمی حرکت والی مشین) [p. 148]: A hypothetical machine that would work forever without an energy input; impossible.
• Non-renewable resource (ناقابلِ تجدید وسیلہ) [p. 149]: An energy resource that is limited and cannot be replaced in a short time.
• Renewable resource (قابلِ تجدید وسیلہ) [p. 149]: An energy resource that is replaced naturally and continuously.
• Fossil fuels (رکازی ایندھن) [p. 150]: Coal, oil and natural gas formed from remains of plants and animals over millions of years.
• Geothermal energy (ارضی حرارتی توانائی) [p. 153]: Energy from heat inside the Earth, e.g. heated groundwater.
• Power (طاقت) [p. 156]: The rate of doing work or of converting energy; P = W/t.
• Watt (واٹ) [p. 156]: Power when 1 J of work is done in 1 s.
• Horsepower (ہارس پاور) [p. 156]: A unit of power equal to 746 W.
• Kilowatt-hour (کلو واٹ آور) [p. 157]: Energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; one electricity unit.
• Efficiency (استعداد) [p. 158]: Ratio of useful energy (work) output to total energy (work) input.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Work (کام): Force × distance
• Energy (توانائی): Ability to do work
• Kinetic (حرکی): Due to motion
• Potential (مخفی): Stored
• Conservation (بقا): Remaining constant
• Dissipation (ضیاع): Loss as heat
• Renewable (قابلِ تجدید): Naturally replaced
• Fossil fuel (رکازی ایندھن): Coal, oil, gas
• Turbine (ٹربائن): Rotating machine
• Generator (جنریٹر): Makes electricity
• Power (طاقت): Rate of work
• Efficiency (استعداد / کارکردگی): Useful ÷ input
• Geothermal (ارضی حرارت): Earth’s heat
• Perpetual (دائمی): Everlasting
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Work: W = Fd (W = Fd cos θ) (J)
• Kinetic energy: Eₖ = ½mv²
• Gravitational PE: Eₚ = mgh
• Work–energy theorem: W = ΔEₖ
• Free fall energy: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh) (No friction)
• With friction: mgh = ½mv² + Wf
• Power: P = W/t = E/t (W = J/s)
• Horsepower: 1 hp = 746 W
• Kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (1 unit)
• Efficiency: η = E_out/E_in × 100% (η = P_out/P_in)
• KE and momentum: Eₖ = p²/2m

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• W = Fd;  F = ma = m(v/t);  d = ½vt;  Eₖ = m(v/t)(½vt) = ½mv² — Proof of kinetic energy.
• F = mg;  W = F × h = mgh = Eₚ — Proof of gravitational potential energy.
• Eₖ(2v) = ½m(2v)² = 4(½mv²) — Doubling speed quadruples KE.
• P = W/t = mgh/t — Power when lifting.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. A coolie carries a load on his head and walks on level ground. Does he do work against gravity?
   Answer: No – the force (upward) is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement.
2. Which has more KE: a 1 kg ball at 4 m/s or a 4 kg ball at 1 m/s?
   Answer: 1 kg ball: 8 J vs 2 J.
3. Why is an LED lamp better than a filament lamp?
   Answer: Much higher efficiency (≈ 80% vs 5%) – less waste heat, lower bills.
4. Why does a ball bounce to a lower height each time?
   Answer: Some energy is converted to heat and sound at each impact and against air resistance.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why are speed limits lower in towns than on motorways?
   Answer: KE ∝ v²; even a small increase in speed greatly increases the energy (damage) in a collision and the stopping distance.
2. Why is Pakistan building wind farms at Jhimpir and solar parks like Quaid-e-Azam Solar Park?
   Answer: To use free renewable energy, reduce costly oil imports and cut pollution.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Muhammad Tuaha pushes a box with 100 N through 200 m on a frictionless surface. How much work does he do? (Example 6.1)
   Given: F = 100 N, d = 200 m
   Required: W
   Formula: W = Fd
   Substitution: 100 × 200
   Calculation: 20 000
   Final Answer: 20 000 J = 20 kJ

2. Babar Azam gives a 120 g ball 50 J of kinetic energy. Find its speed. (Example 6.2)
   Given: Eₖ = 50 J, m = 0.12 kg
   Required: v
   Formula: v = √(2Eₖ/m)
   Substitution: √(2 × 50/0.12)
   Calculation: √833.3 = 28.9
   Final Answer: ≈ 28.9 m/s

3. Kamil (60 kg) high-jumps 1.5 m. Find his gravitational PE at the top. Where does it come from? (Example 6.3)
   Given: m = 60 kg, h = 1.5 m, g = 9.8 m/s²
   Required: Eₚ
   Formula: Eₚ = mgh
   Substitution: 60 × 9.8 × 1.5
   Calculation: 882
   Final Answer: 882 J – from the kinetic energy of his take-off, supplied by chemical energy in his muscles

4. A 450 g football is kicked vertically up at 22 m/s. (a) Height reached with no air resistance (b) if it rises only 20 m, the work done against air resistance. (Example 6.4)
   Given: m = 0.45 kg, v = 22 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s², h_actual = 20 m
   Required: h_max, Wf
   Formula: ½mv² = mgh;  Wf = ½mv² − mgh_actual
   Substitution: h = 22²/(2 × 9.8); Wf = 0.45 × 9.8 × (24.7 − 20)
   Calculation: h = 24.7 m; Wf ≈ 20.7 J
   Final Answer: (a) 24.7 m (b) ≈ 20.7 J lost to air resistance

5. A car engine does 3 × 10⁷ J of work in 1 minute. Find its power in kW and hp. (Example 6.5)
   Given: W = 3 × 10⁷ J, t = 60 s
   Required: P
   Formula: P = W/t; hp = W/746
   Substitution: 3 × 10⁷/60
   Calculation: 5 × 10⁵ W = 500 kW; ÷ 746 ≈ 670 hp
   Final Answer: 500 kW ≈ 670 hp

6. A petrol engine takes in 400 J of fuel energy and does 120 J of useful work. How efficient is it? (Example 6.6)
   Given: E_in = 400 J, E_out = 120 J
   Required: η
   Formula: η = E_out/E_in × 100%
   Substitution: 120/400 × 100%
   Calculation: 0.3 × 100%
   Final Answer: 30%


══ ADDITIONAL SLO NUMERICAL PRACTICE ══

1. A 1200 kg car moves at 20 m/s. Find its KE and the braking work needed to stop it.
   Given: m = 1200 kg, v = 20 m/s
   Required: Eₖ, W
   Formula: Eₖ = ½mv²; W = −Eₖ
   Substitution: ½ × 1200 × 400
   Calculation: 240 000
   Final Answer: 2.4 × 10⁵ J; −2.4 × 10⁵ J by the brakes

2. A 60 W bulb runs 5 h a day for 30 days. How many units (kWh) does it use?
   Given: P = 0.06 kW, t = 150 h
   Required: Energy in kWh
   Formula: E = Pt
   Substitution: 0.06 × 150
   Calculation: 9
   Final Answer: 9 kWh (9 units)

3. A motor of input power 2 kW lifts 500 kg through 6 m in 20 s. Find its efficiency.
   Given: P_in = 2000 W, t = 20 s, m = 500 kg, h = 6 m
   Required: η
   Formula: η = mgh/(P_in t) × 100%
   Substitution: 500 × 9.8 × 6/(2000 × 20)
   Calculation: 29 400/40 000 = 0.735
   Final Answer: 73.5%

— Exercise MCQs —
1. The unit of work or energy, joule (J), is equal to: → C (watt second) | J = W × s.
2. A car, an elephant and a cricket ball have the same kinetic energy. Which has the greatest speed? → C (Cricket ball) | v = √(2E/m): smallest mass.
3. A ball weighing 50 N is lifted to a height of 5 m. The potential energy stored in it is: → 
4. The power used when 100 J of work is done in 5 s is: → B (20 W) | 100/5.
5. The SI unit of power is: → B (watt) | J/s.
6. A 4 kg body is thrown up from the ground at 5 m/s. Neglecting friction, its KE just before hitting the ground is: → B (50 J) | Energy conserved: ½ × 4 × 25 = 50 J.
7. A ball is thrown downward with an initial velocity. Its: → A (Eₖ increases and Eₚ decreases) | PE → KE.
8. The energy derived from heated groundwater is: → B (geothermal energy) | Earth’s internal heat.
9. A weightlifter of power 1960 W lifts a load of mass M through 2 m in 3 s. M is: → C (300 kg) | M = Pt/(gh) = 1960 × 3/(9.8 × 2) = 300 kg.
10. Which one is a renewable source of energy? → C (Sunlight) | Replenished naturally.
11. One horsepower is equivalent to: → D (746 W) | Standard value.
12. A practical engine cannot have an efficiency equal to or greater than: → D (1) | Losses always occur.
13. A heavy and a lighter object have the same momentum. The object with greater kinetic energy is: → A (lighter) | Eₖ = p²/2m.
14. A force acts on a body but causes no displacement. The work done is: → C (zero) | d = 0.
15. A box is taken to the second floor of a building. The work done is converted to: → B (potential energy) | mgh.

— Q II. Short-response questions —
1 A car moves with constant speed along a straight road. Is any work done on the car?
   Answer: The engine force does positive work and friction/air resistance do equal negative work; the net work is zero, so the car’s kinetic energy stays constant (the engine’s energy is dissipated as heat).
2 Does the work done in raising a box up a building depend on how fast it is raised? On the path? On the height?
   Answer: It does not depend on speed or path (stairs, lift or ramp) – only on the weight and the vertical height: W = mgh. Speed affects only the power needed.
3 Work done on a body speeds it up or slows it down. How much work is done by the centripetal force on an orbiting satellite?
   Answer: Zero – the centripetal force is perpendicular to the satellite’s motion at every instant, so there is no displacement along the force; the satellite’s speed (KE) stays constant.
4 A car has kinetic energy Eₖ. By what factor does it change if its velocity is doubled?
   Answer: Eₖ ∝ v², so it becomes 4 times (½m(2v)² = 4 × ½mv²).
5 A bullet fired into a sand wall stops. Where does its kinetic energy go?
   Answer: Into work done against friction pushing the sand aside (deforming the wall), and finally into heat (internal energy of the bullet and sand) and some sound.
6 An LED bulb has an efficiency of 80%. Does it violate the conservation of energy?
   Answer: No – 80% of the input becomes light and the remaining 20% becomes heat; total output = input, so energy is conserved; only the useful part is 80%.
7 How does using renewable energy reduce environmental impact compared with non-renewable sources?
   Answer: Renewables (solar, wind, hydro) produce little or no CO₂, SO₂ or smoke, so they reduce global warming, acid rain and air pollution, and they do not run out or need mining/drilling.
8 Will we eventually rely entirely on renewable energy sources? Why or why not?
   Answer: Possibly in the long term, because fossil fuels will run out and cause pollution; but at present renewables are intermittent (night, still days), need large areas, storage (batteries) and high initial cost, so a mix of sources is still needed while technology improves.
9 How can increasing the power of a machine impact its energy consumption?
   Answer: Power is energy per second; a more powerful machine uses more energy each second (P = E/t). It finishes a job faster, but unless its efficiency is higher, the total energy for the job is the same or more, and running it longer consumes much more.
10 A perpetual engine has an efficiency equal to 1. Why will it not work?
   Answer: An efficiency of 1 means no energy loss, but friction and resistance always convert some energy to heat; also energy cannot be created, so a machine cannot keep running forever without an energy supply.

— Q III. Extended-response questions —
1 Define work and its unit. Describe the conditions for maximum and minimum work.
   Answer: W = Fd, joule. Maximum work when the force is in the same direction as the displacement (θ = 0°, W = Fd); zero (minimum) work when the force is perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°) or when there is no displacement; negative when the force opposes motion.
2 What is kinetic energy? Derive its expression using graphical analysis.
   Answer: Energy due to motion. Force–displacement graph: area = Fd = work = gain in KE. With F = mv/t and d = ½vt: Eₖ = ½mv².
3 What is potential energy? What are its types? Show that gravitational PE = mgh.
   Answer: Stored energy due to position/state. Types: gravitational, elastic, chemical, electrostatic, nuclear. Proof: F = mg, W = mgh stored as Eₚ.
4 What is meant by energy conversion and energy conservation?
   Answer: Conversion: change of energy from one form to another (examples). Conservation: total energy stays constant – it is never created or destroyed; e.g. falling ball PE → KE; with friction, some becomes heat.
5 Describe how useful energy may be obtained from natural resources.
   Answer: Fossil fuels burned → steam → turbine → generator; nuclear fission → heat → steam; hydro: water PE → turbine; solar cells; wind turbines; geothermal steam; tides and waves; biomass/biogas.
6 Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable energy sources with examples. Write advantages and disadvantages of each regarding availability and environmental impact.
   Answer: See tables in topic 6.6.
7 Describe the processes by which energy is converted from one form to another with reference to fossil fuel, hydroelectric, solar, nuclear, geothermal, wind and biomass energy.
   Answer: Fossil fuel: chemical → heat → KE (steam/turbine) → electrical. Hydro: PE → KE → electrical. Solar: light → electrical (cells) or heat. Nuclear: nuclear → heat → KE → electrical. Geothermal: internal heat → steam KE → electrical. Wind: KE of air → KE of blades → electrical. Biomass: chemical → heat/biogas → electrical/heat.
8 Describe the process of electricity generation with a block diagram from fossil-fuel input to electricity output.
   Answer: Fuel → boiler (burning: chemical → heat) → water → high-pressure steam → turbine (heat → kinetic) → generator (kinetic → electrical) → step-up transformer → transmission lines; spent steam is condensed and reused; ≈ 40% efficient.
9 Define power. What is the relation of its SI unit with horsepower?
   Answer: Rate of doing work, P = W/t, unit watt; 1 hp = 746 W.
10 What is efficiency? Why is it important for cars or electronic devices to have high efficiency? Why can the efficiency of a machine never be 100%?
   Answer: Useful output/input. High efficiency saves fuel/electricity and money, reduces pollution and heating, and extends battery life. Never 100% because friction, air resistance and electrical resistance always waste some energy as heat and sound.
11 Explain with energy-flow diagrams: filament lamp, power station, vehicle travelling at constant speed on a level road.
   Answer: Lamp: 100% electrical → 5% light + 95% heat. Power station: 100% chemical → ~40% electrical + ~60% heat. Car at steady speed: 100% chemical → ~25% work against friction/air resistance + ~75% heat and sound (KE constant).

══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D)] What is efficiency? Write the formula for percentage efficiency.
   Answer: Ratio of useful output to total input; % η = (useful output/input) × 100%.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] Discuss the energy conversions when a cyclist goes up to the top of a hill.
   Answer: Chemical energy in muscles (from food) → kinetic energy of cyclist and bicycle → gravitational PE gained at the top, plus heat (body, friction) and sound; going down, PE → KE.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M)] What is meant by efficiency? Can any machine be 100% efficient? Justify.
   Answer: Useful output ÷ input. No – friction, air resistance and electrical resistance always waste some energy as heat/sound, so output < input.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme)] Determine the efficiency of a light bulb that uses 60 J of electrical energy to produce 9 J of light.
   Answer: η = 9/60 × 100% = 15%.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] A car’s kinetic energy is Eₖ. If its velocity is doubled, by what factor will its kinetic energy change? Show with the equation.
   Answer: Eₖ′ = ½m(2v)² = 4 × ½mv² = 4Eₖ.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (B)] How powerful is a car’s engine if it does 3 × 10⁷ J of work in 1 minute?
   Answer: P = 3 × 10⁷/60 = 5 × 10⁵ W = 500 kW (≈ 670 hp).

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] Show that Eₚ(grav) = mgh with a neat sketch.
   Answer: Lift mass m at constant speed through height h; force = mg; work = mgh, stored as Eₚ.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025 (D)] A box is dragged across the floor for 10 m with a 50 N force in the direction of movement. Calculate the work done.
   Answer: W = 50 × 10 = 500 J.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] A bullet fired from a gun penetrates into sand and stops. Where is its kinetic energy used?
   Answer: In doing work against the resistance of the sand (pushing it aside) and finally as heat in the bullet and sand, plus sound.

10. State the principle of conservation of energy and apply it to a falling ball.
   Answer: Energy is not created or destroyed. At the top PE = mgh, KE = 0; at the bottom PE = 0, KE = ½mv² = mgh (no air resistance); total stays constant.

11. Why do perpetual motion machines not work?
   Answer: Energy cannot be created, and friction always dissipates some energy as heat, so a machine cannot run forever or give out more than it receives.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B); old scheme; AF Model Paper] Prove that K.E = ½mv².
   Answer: W = Fd; F = ma = mv/t; d = (0 + v)/2 × t = ½vt; W = (mv/t)(½vt) = ½mv² = Eₖ. (Graphically: area under F–d graph.)

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B) Q4] A 500 kg roller-coaster car starts from rest at the top of a 20 m hill. (a) Its PE at the top (b) its KE at the bottom with no friction (c) how friction and air resistance affect KE in real situations.
   Answer: (a) Eₚ = mgh = 500 × 10 × 20 = 100 000 J (g = 10). (b) All PE → KE = 100 000 J. (c) Some energy is converted into heat and sound by friction and air resistance, so the KE at the bottom is less than 100 kJ (lower speed).

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (B) Q5] Describe the long-term advantages of using renewable sources. Also give the limitations of non-renewable sources (three points each).
   Answer: Renewable: never run out; little/no pollution or CO₂; free fuel and lower running cost; energy security (local supply). Non-renewable limitations: will run out; cause air pollution, acid rain and global warming; price rises and dependence on imports; mining/drilling damages land; nuclear waste.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (D) Q3] A player kicks a 450 g football vertically upward at 22 m/s. (a) Neglecting air resistance, how high would it reach? (b) If due to air friction it rises only 20 m, what is the work done against resistance?
   Answer: (a) h = v²/2g = 484/20 = 24.2 m (g = 10). (b) Wf = mg(24.2 − 20) = 0.45 × 10 × 4.2 = 18.9 J (with g = 9.8: 24.7 m and 20.7 J).

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (M) Q3] (a) Describe power as the rate of doing work and write its formula. (b) State the SI units of power and work. (c) A person does 300 J of work in 10 s. Calculate the power.
   Answer: (a) P = W/t. (b) Power – watt; work – joule. (c) P = 300/10 = 30 W.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (old scheme) Q5] What is meant by kinetic energy? Prove that K.E = ½mv².
   Answer: As above.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025 Q3] What is meant by kinetic energy? Derive its expression using the graphical method.
   Answer: Area under force–displacement graph = Fd = ½mv².

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%) Q8] State two real-life situations in which energy is converted from one form to another. Describe the mechanism in each. Why is some energy transferred to the surroundings as heat?
   Answer: (1) Hydroelectric plant: PE of water → KE → turbine → generator → electrical. (2) Car engine: chemical energy of petrol burns → hot gases push pistons → KE. Heat is lost because of friction between moving parts, air resistance and the high temperature of exhaust gases – unavoidable losses.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF) Q4] Define kinetic energy and derive its formula.
   Answer: As above.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 6 in one page
- Work W = Fd (in the direction of force), joule; zero if no displacement or force ⟂ motion (satellite); raising a box: W = mgh, independent of path/speed.
- Energy = ability to do work. Forms: kinetic, gravitational/elastic potential, chemical, electrical, light, heat, sound, nuclear.
- KE Eₖ = ½mv² (proof: Fd = (mv/t)(½vt)); doubling v → 4×KE; same KE → lightest is fastest; same p → lighter has more KE.
- GPE Eₚ = mgh (proof: F = mg, W = mgh).
- Conversion: hydro PE → KE → electrical; cyclist chemical → KE → PE; bulb electrical → light + heat. Conservation: total energy constant; mgh = ½mv² (no friction); with friction mgh = ½mv² + Wf. Perpetual motion impossible.
- Resources: non-renewable (coal, oil, gas, uranium) vs renewable (solar, wind, hydro, tides, waves, geothermal, biomass). Power station: fuel → boiler → steam → turbine → generator. Know advantages/disadvantages.
- Power P = W/t (W = J/s); 1 hp = 746 W; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 1 unit.
- Efficiency η = useful output/input × 100% (bulb 5%, car 25%, power station 40%, generator 98%); never 100% (friction → heat). Energy-flow (Sankey) diagrams.

chapters.title: Density and Temperature
chapters.introduction:
This unit links the particle model with density and temperature. It covers density (ρ = m/V) and how to measure it for liquids, regular solids and irregular solids (by displacement); the particle structure of solids, liquids and gases; plasma as the fourth state of matter; how temperature relates to the motion (kinetic energy) of particles and absolute zero; internal energy; thermometric properties; fixed points (ice point and steam point); the sensitivity, range and linearity of thermometers; and the liquid-in-glass and thermocouple thermometers.

11 summative SLOs (C-01 to C-11). Frequently asked: density definition, formula and units with numericals (cylinder, cube, stone by displacement), five comparisons of solids/liquids/gases and particle diagrams, plasma as the fourth state (stars, neon lights, lightning), temperature and internal energy, why mercury is used, fixed points, sensitivity/range/linearity, increasing sensitivity and range, construction and working of liquid-in-glass and thermocouple thermometers.

══ 7.1 Density (pp. 166–167) ══
Density (ρ): the mass per unit volume of a substance: ρ = m/V.
- SI unit kg/m³; smaller units g/cm³ and (for liquids) g/mL. 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (petrol 0.9 g/cm³ = 900 kg/m³). Density is a scalar.
- Density depends on how closely the particles are packed: solids > liquids > gases in general. Osmium is the densest metal (≈ 22.59 g/cm³).
- A small piece of a material has the same density as a big block of it (density is a property of the material, not the size).
- Density changes with temperature: on heating most substances expand (V increases, m stays the same), so their density decreases.
- Floating: a liquid or object of lower density floats on one of higher density (oil on water; of two liquids of 1 g/mL and 1.2 g/mL, the 1 g/mL liquid is on top).
Typical densities (kg/m³): air 1.3, wood ≈ 500–700, ice 920, water 1000, aluminium 2700, iron 7870, copper 8900, mercury 13 600, gold 19 300.
Example: a cube of side 5 cm and mass 500 g: V = 125 cm³; ρ = 500/125 = 4 g/cm³ = 4000 kg/m³.
کثافت فی اکائی حجم کمیت ہے: ρ = m/V، اکائی kg/m³ (1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³)۔ ٹھوس عموماً مائع سے اور مائع گیس سے زیادہ کثیف ہیں۔ کم کثافت والی چیز زیادہ کثافت والے مائع پر تیرتی ہے۔ گرم کرنے پر عام طور پر کثافت کم ہو جاتی ہے۔

══ 7.2 Measuring density (pp. 167–171) ══
(a) Density of a liquid:
1. Find the mass of an empty measuring cylinder on a balance (m₁).
2. Pour in the liquid; read its volume V from the cylinder (eye level with the bottom of the meniscus).
3. Find the mass of cylinder + liquid (m₂). Mass of liquid = m₂ − m₁.
4. ρ = (m₂ − m₁)/V.
Example: empty cylinder 145 g; with 60 mL liquid 205 g → m = 60 g; ρ = 60/60 = 1 g/mL (water).
(b) Regular-shaped solid (cube, cuboid, cylinder, sphere):
1. Find its mass on a balance.
2. Measure its dimensions (ruler/vernier callipers) and calculate the volume: cuboid = l × w × h; cube = side³; cylinder = πr²h; sphere = 4/3 πr³.
3. ρ = m/V.
Example: brick 3.30 kg, 21.6 cm × 10.2 cm × 6.35 cm: V = 0.216 × 0.102 × 0.0635 = 1.40 × 10⁻³ m³; ρ = 3.30/0.00140 ≈ 2360 kg/m³.
(c) Irregular solid that sinks (displacement method):
1. Find the mass of the object (e.g. a stone).
2. Pour water into a measuring cylinder; note the initial volume V₁.
3. Tie the stone to a thread and lower it gently until fully immersed; note the final volume V₂.
4. Volume of stone = V₂ − V₁; ρ = m/(V₂ − V₁).
(For large objects use a displacement (eureka) can and collect the overflow in a cylinder.)
Example: rock 80.52 g; water rises from 18 mL to 46 mL → V = 28 cm³; ρ = 80.52/28 ≈ 2.88 g/cm³.
Human body: volume found by full immersion in a tank of water (overflow measured), mass from a scale; ρ ≈ 1000 kg/m³ (close to water – we nearly float).
مائع کی کثافت: خالی سلنڈر کی کمیت، پھر مائع سمیت کمیت، فرق ÷ حجم۔ باقاعدہ ٹھوس: کمیت ÷ (لمبائی × چوڑائی × اونچائی)۔ بے قاعدہ ٹھوس: سلنڈر میں پانی کا ابتدائی حجم V₁، پتھر ڈالنے کے بعد V₂؛ پتھر کا حجم V₂ − V₁ اور کثافت = کمیت ÷ حجم۔

══ 7.3 Particle structure of solids, liquids and gases (pp. 172–174) ══
Matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules, ions) with attractive forces between them. The strength of these forces and the spacing decide the state.
Solids: particles closely packed in a regular pattern (lattice); strong forces; particles only vibrate about fixed positions; fixed shape and volume; not compressible; highest density; lowest particle energy.
Liquids: particles close together but randomly arranged; forces weaker than in solids; particles move around and slide (glide) past each other; fixed volume but no fixed shape (take the shape of the container); almost incompressible; flow.
Gases: particles far apart (gaps much larger than particle size), random arrangement; negligible forces; particles move quickly in all directions in constant random motion, colliding with each other and the walls (causing pressure); no fixed shape or volume (fill the container); highly compressible; lowest density.
Liquids and gases can flow, so together they are called fluids.
Heating a solid into a liquid: particles gain energy, vibrate more, overcome some of the attractive forces and move farther apart, sliding past each other.
[Table: Table 7.2 – Comparison of states of matter]
Property | Solid | Liquid | Gas
• Arrangement | Regular, closely packed | Random, close together | Random, far apart
• Forces between particles | Strong | Moderate (weaker) | Negligible
• Movement | Vibrate about fixed positions | Move around / slide past each other | Move quickly in all directions
• Energy of particles | Low | Greater | Highest
• Shape / volume | Fixed / fixed | Not fixed / fixed | Not fixed / not fixed
• Compressibility | Not compressible | Almost incompressible | Highly compressible
• Density | High | Intermediate | Low
ٹھوس: ذرات قریب قریب باقاعدہ ترتیب میں، مضبوط قوتیں، صرف اپنی جگہ ارتعاش؛ شکل اور حجم مقرر۔ مائع: ذرات قریب مگر بے ترتیب، ایک دوسرے پر پھسلتے ہیں؛ حجم مقرر، شکل برتن کی۔ گیس: ذرات دور دور، کمزور قوتیں، ہر سمت تیز حرکت؛ نہ شکل مقرر نہ حجم۔ مائع اور گیس کو سیال کہتے ہیں۔

══ 7.4 Plasma – the fourth state of matter (pp. 174–175) ══
Plasma is an ionised gas: a mixture of positive ions, free electrons and some neutral atoms, in which a significant part of the material is made of ions and electrons.
How it forms: when a gas is heated to a very high temperature (or a strong electric/magnetic field is applied), its particles move so fast that violent collisions knock electrons out of atoms – the atoms become positive ions and the electrons are free.
Why it is a separate (fourth) state – how it differs from a gas:
- It contains free charged particles (ions and electrons), while an ordinary gas is mostly neutral atoms/molecules.
- It is a very good conductor of electricity and is strongly affected by electric and magnetic fields.
- It is usually very hot and glows (emits light).
Examples: the Sun and stars (stars glow because of plasma), lightning, neon signs and fluorescent tubes, plasma lamps and TVs, welding arcs, auroras (northern/southern lights caused by charged particles from the Sun hitting the upper atmosphere) and nebulae (huge clouds of dust and ionised gas). About 99% of the visible universe is plasma.
پلازما آئنائزڈ گیس ہے جس میں مثبت آئن اور آزاد الیکٹران ہوتے ہیں۔ بہت زیادہ درجۂ حرارت یا طاقتور برقی میدان سے ایٹموں کے الیکٹران نکل جاتے ہیں۔ یہ بجلی کا اچھا موصل ہے، مقناطیسی میدان سے متاثر ہوتا ہے اور چمکتا ہے، اس لیے اسے مادے کی چوتھی حالت کہتے ہیں۔ مثالیں: سورج اور ستارے، آسمانی بجلی، نیون لائٹ، ارورا۔

══ 7.5 Temperature, particle motion and absolute zero (pp. 175–176) ══
Temperature is the measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body; it is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy of its particles.
- Heating a substance makes its particles move (vibrate/translate) faster → greater average KE → higher temperature. (Sometimes the heat instead breaks bonds – during melting and boiling – and then the temperature stays constant.)
- Cooling slows the particles → lower average KE → lower temperature.
- Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder one because of a temperature difference.
Absolute zero: the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles have the least kinetic energy (they can no longer exert pressure, P = 0). It is 0 K = −273.15 °C (≈ −273 °C). It cannot actually be reached – we can only get very close.
Temperature scales: Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F), Kelvin (K). T(K) = θ(°C) + 273; F = 9/5 C + 32.
Why temperature stays constant at the melting and boiling points: the heat supplied is used to weaken/break the attractive forces (increase the gaps) and change the state, not to increase the KE of the particles, so the temperature does not rise.
درجۂ حرارت جسم کی گرمی یا سردی کا پیمانہ ہے اور ذرات کی اوسط حرکی توانائی کے راست متناسب ہے۔ گرم کرنے سے ذرات تیز ہوتے ہیں اور درجۂ حرارت بڑھتا ہے۔ مطلق صفر (0 K = −273 °C) سب سے کم ممکن درجۂ حرارت ہے جس پر ذرات کی حرکی توانائی کم ترین ہوتی ہے۔

══ 7.6 Internal energy (pp. 177) ══
Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles of a substance = total kinetic energy (translational, rotational, vibrational) + total potential energy (due to the attractive forces between particles). For an ideal gas it is only the kinetic energy of the particles.
- Increasing the temperature of an object increases its internal energy, because its particles move faster (more KE).
- Water in two beakers: the beaker at 60 °C has more internal energy than the same mass at 30 °C.
- Internal energy can also be increased without heating: by doing work on it – rubbing hands, hammering a nail, compressing a gas in a bicycle pump.
- It can increase without a rise in temperature: during melting or boiling, energy goes into potential energy (separating the particles).
- Internal energy also depends on mass: a bathtub of warm water has more internal energy than a cup of boiling water.
- An ideal gas expanded at constant temperature keeps the same internal energy.
اندرونی توانائی کسی شے کے تمام ذرات کی کل حرکی اور مخفی توانائی ہے۔ درجۂ حرارت بڑھنے سے ذرات تیز ہوتے ہیں اس لیے اندرونی توانائی بڑھتی ہے۔ کام کرنے (ہاتھ رگڑنا، گیس دبانا) سے بھی یہ بڑھ سکتی ہے؛ پگھلنے اور ابلنے کے دوران درجۂ حرارت بدلے بغیر بڑھتی ہے۔

══ 7.7 Thermometric properties and thermometers (pp. 177–179) ══
A thermometer measures temperature. It uses a thermometric property – a physical property that changes regularly (predictably) with temperature.
[Table: Table 7.3 – Thermometric properties]
Thermometric property | Thermometer
• Volume expansion of a liquid | Liquid-in-glass (laboratory, clinical) thermometer
• Volume of a gas at constant pressure | Constant-pressure gas thermometer
• Pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume | Constant-volume gas thermometer
• Expansion of a solid (two metals) | Bimetallic-strip thermometer
• Electrical resistance | Resistance thermometer / thermistor
• Voltage (e.m.f.) at the junction of two metals | Thermocouple
• Colour change of liquid crystals | Liquid-crystal strip thermometer
تھرمامیٹر وہ خاصیت استعمال کرتا ہے جو درجۂ حرارت کے ساتھ باقاعدگی سے بدلے: مائع کا پھیلاؤ، گیس کا حجم یا دباؤ، برقی مزاحمت، دو دھاتوں کے جوڑ پر وولٹیج، یا مائع کرسٹل کا رنگ۔

══ 7.8 Fixed points and calibration (pp. 179–180) ══
To put a scale on a thermometer (calibrate it), we need two fixed points – standard, easily obtainable and reproducible temperatures.
- Lower fixed point (ice point): the temperature of pure melting ice at standard pressure: 0 °C = 32 °F = 273 K.
- Upper fixed point (steam point): the temperature of steam above pure boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm): 100 °C = 212 °F = 373 K.
- The gap between the fixed points (the fundamental interval) is divided into equal parts: 100 divisions on Celsius and Kelvin, 180 on Fahrenheit.
Why fixed points are needed: without them each thermometer would have its own arbitrary marks; fixed points let all thermometers be calibrated to the same standard so readings agree everywhere.
Difficulties: the ice and water must be pure (impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point), the pressure must be standard (boiling point changes with pressure/altitude), the thermometer must reach thermal equilibrium, and the liquid’s expansion may not be perfectly uniform between the points.
Example: a thermometer reads 2 cm at the ice point and 6 cm at the steam point: 4 cm for 100 °C → 0.04 cm per °C.
تھرمامیٹر پر پیمانہ بنانے کے لیے دو مقررہ نقاط چاہئیں: برف کے پگھلنے کا نقطہ (0 °C) اور خالص پانی کی بھاپ کا نقطہ (100 °C) معیاری دباؤ پر۔ ان کے درمیان سیلسیس میں 100 اور فارن ہائیٹ میں 180 برابر حصے ہوتے ہیں۔ پانی خالص اور دباؤ معیاری ہونا ضروری ہے۔

══ 7.9 Sensitivity, range and linearity (pp. 180–181) ══
Sensitivity: the ability of a thermometer to detect (show) a small change in temperature – the smallest temperature change it can measure, or how far the thread moves per degree. A thermometer that shows 0.1 °C changes is more sensitive than one that shows only 1 °C (like the least count of an instrument).
Range: the span between the lowest and highest temperatures a thermometer can measure. Clinical thermometer: 35 °C to 42 °C (94 °F to 108 °F); laboratory mercury thermometer: −10 °C to 110 °C; digital thermometers have a wide range.
Linearity: the ability of a thermometer to show equal changes in reading (equal spacing of divisions) for equal changes in temperature over its whole range – e.g. a rise from 0 to 50 °C gives the same length change as 50 to 100 °C. A linear thermometer has an evenly spaced scale. Mercury and bimetallic thermometers are fairly linear.
حساسیت: درجۂ حرارت کی معمولی تبدیلی ظاہر کرنے کی صلاحیت۔ رینج: کم سے کم اور زیادہ سے زیادہ درجۂ حرارت جو ناپا جا سکے (کلینیکل 35–42 °C)۔ خطیت: درجۂ حرارت کی برابر تبدیلی پر ریڈنگ میں برابر تبدیلی، یعنی یکساں پیمانہ۔

══ 7.10 Liquid-in-glass and thermocouple thermometers (pp. 181–183) ══
Liquid-in-glass thermometer – structure: a thin-walled glass bulb containing the liquid (mercury or coloured alcohol); a fine, uniform capillary tube inside a thick glass stem (which acts as a magnifying lens); a scale; a vacuum (or nitrogen) above the thread; an expansion chamber at the top. A clinical thermometer also has a constriction (kink) near the bulb so the mercury does not fall back before it is read.
Working: when the bulb is heated, the liquid expands and rises up the capillary; when cooled, it contracts. The length of the thread is read against the calibrated scale.
Why mercury? It expands uniformly (linear); does not wet (stick to) glass; is opaque and shiny (easy to see); is a good conductor of heat (quick response); has a wide liquid range (freezes at −39 °C, boils at 357 °C). Alcohol freezes at −115 °C (good for very cold places) and expands more (more sensitive) but boils at 78 °C. Water is not used: it expands irregularly (anomalously near 4 °C), wets glass, is transparent, has a small range (0–100 °C) and expands little.
Thermocouple thermometer – structure: two wires of different metals (e.g. copper and iron, or copper and constantan) joined to form a hot junction (placed at the object) and a cold (reference) junction, connected to a sensitive voltmeter/galvanometer.
Working: a temperature difference between the junctions produces a small voltage (e.m.f.) that increases with the temperature difference; the meter is calibrated in °C.
Advantages: very wide range (≈ −200 °C to 1500 °C or more), small junction → responds very quickly to rapidly changing temperatures, can measure at a point and remotely, robust, gives an electrical output for computers. Used for furnaces, kilns, engines, ovens, industry. A liquid-in-glass thermometer cannot do this because the glass would melt/the liquid would boil and it responds slowly.
[Table: Liquid-in-glass vs thermocouple thermometer]
Liquid-in-glass | Thermocouple
• Uses expansion of a liquid | Uses voltage produced at a junction of two different metals
• Glass bulb, capillary tube, scale | Two different metal wires, hot and cold junctions, voltmeter
• Limited range (≈ −39 °C to 357 °C for mercury) | Very wide range (up to ≈ 1500 °C)
• Slower response | Very fast response (small junction)
• Read directly by eye | Needs a meter; can record remotely/digitally
• Homes, schools, clinics | Furnaces, engines, kilns, industry
مائع والا شیشے کا تھرمامیٹر: بلب، باریک کیپلری نلی، پیمانہ؛ گرمی سے پارہ پھیلتا اور اوپر چڑھتا ہے۔ پارہ یکساں پھیلتا ہے، شیشے سے نہیں چپکتا، چمکدار ہے اور اس کی رینج وسیع ہے۔ تھرموکپل: دو مختلف دھاتوں کے جوڑ؛ گرم اور ٹھنڈے جوڑ کے درجۂ حرارت کے فرق سے وولٹیج پیدا ہوتا ہے۔ یہ بہت زیادہ درجۂ حرارت اور تیزی سے بدلتے درجۂ حرارت ناپ سکتا ہے (بھٹیاں، انجن)۔

══ 7.11 How structure affects sensitivity, range and linearity (pp. 182–183) ══
Sensitivity can be increased by:
- a narrower (finer) capillary tube – the same expansion makes a longer thread move;
- a larger bulb (more liquid → more expansion per degree) – but a big bulb responds more slowly;
- a thin-walled bulb (heat reaches the liquid quickly);
- a liquid that expands more per degree (alcohol expands more than mercury).
Range depends on:
- the liquid’s freezing and boiling points – mercury (−39 °C to 357 °C) has a wide range; alcohol for very low temperatures;
- the length of the capillary/stem and the bulb size: a larger bulb or narrower tube (more sensitive) gives a smaller range for the same tube length. To increase sensitivity without reducing range, use a narrower tube and a longer stem.
Linearity depends on:
- a liquid that expands uniformly (mercury);
- a capillary of uniform bore (same diameter throughout);
- the type of glass – borosilicate glass expands more uniformly than soda-lime glass.
Verifying a “more sensitive” thermometer: place it and a standard thermometer in the same water bath; change the temperature by a small amount (e.g. 0.5 °C); the more sensitive one shows a larger movement of the thread / detects the smaller change.
حساسیت بڑھانے کے لیے باریک کیپلری، بڑا اور پتلی دیوار والا بلب، اور زیادہ پھیلنے والا مائع استعمال کریں۔ رینج مائع کے نقطۂ انجماد اور نقطۂ جوش اور نلی کی لمبائی پر منحصر ہے۔ خطیت کے لیے یکساں پھیلنے والا مائع، یکساں قطر کی نلی اور بوروسلیکیٹ شیشہ ضروری ہے۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Particle arrangement in solid, liquid and gas: Solid: regular and close; liquid: close but random; gas: far apart and random.
2. Liquid-in-glass (clinical) thermometer: Bulb, constriction, capillary tube, stem with scale, expansion chamber.
3. Thermocouple thermometer: Two different metals; the voltage between hot and cold junctions depends on the temperature difference.

chapters.definitions:
• Density (کثافت) [p. 166]: Mass per unit volume of a substance; ρ = m/V (kg/m³).
• Displacement method (ہٹاؤ کا طریقہ) [p. 170]: Finding the volume of an irregular solid from the rise in water level when it is immersed.
• Fluids (سیال) [p. 173]: Liquids and gases, which can flow.
• Plasma (پلازما) [p. 174]: An ionised gas of positive ions and free electrons; the fourth state of matter.
• Aurora (قطبی روشنی) [p. 175]: Coloured lights in the polar sky caused by charged particles from the Sun striking the upper atmosphere.
• Temperature (درجۂ حرارت) [p. 175]: The degree of hotness or coldness of a body; proportional to the average KE of its particles.
• Heat (حرارت) [p. 183]: Energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference.
• Absolute zero (مطلق صفر) [p. 176]: The lowest possible temperature (0 K = −273.15 °C), where particles have the least KE.
• Internal energy (اندرونی توانائی) [p. 177]: The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles of a substance.
• Thermometric property (حرارت پیما خاصیت) [p. 177]: A physical property that changes regularly with temperature and is used to measure it.
• Thermometry (حرارت پیمائی) [p. 183]: The branch of physics dealing with measurement of temperature.
• Fixed point (مقررہ نقطہ) [p. 179]: A standard, reproducible temperature used to calibrate a thermometer (ice point, steam point).
• Sensitivity (حساسیت) [p. 180]: The ability of a thermometer to detect a small change in temperature.
• Range (رینج / حد) [p. 180]: The span between the lowest and highest temperatures a thermometer can measure.
• Linearity (خطیت) [p. 181]: Equal changes in reading for equal changes in temperature throughout the range.
• Thermocouple (تھرموکپل) [p. 182]: A thermometer of two different metals whose junction voltage depends on temperature difference.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Density (کثافت): Mass per volume
• Volume (حجم): Space occupied
• Displacement (ہٹاؤ): Water pushed aside
• Particle (ذرہ): Tiny piece of matter
• Fluid (سیال): Flows
• Plasma (پلازما): Ionised gas
• Ion (آئن): Charged atom
• Temperature (درجۂ حرارت): Hotness
• Absolute zero (مطلق صفر): Lowest temperature
• Internal energy (اندرونی توانائی): Energy of particles
• Thermometer (تھرمامیٹر / حرارت پیما): Measures temperature
• Sensitivity (حساسیت): Detects small change
• Range (حد): Span of readings
• Capillary (شعری نلی): Very fine tube
• Junction (جوڑ): Meeting point of wires
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Density: ρ = m/V (kg/m³)
• Unit conversion: 1 g/cm³ = 1 g/mL = 1000 kg/m³
• Volume by displacement: V = V₂ − V₁ (1 mL = 1 cm³)
• Volumes: cuboid lwh; cube a³; cylinder πr²h; sphere 4/3 πr³
• Kelvin: T(K) = θ(°C) + 273
• Fahrenheit: °F = 9/5 °C + 32
• Calibration: θ = (l_θ − l₀)/(l₁₀₀ − l₀) × 100 (°C)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• m_liquid = m(cylinder + liquid) − m(empty cylinder);  ρ = m_liquid/V — Density of a liquid.
• ρ = m/(V₂ − V₁) — Irregular solid by displacement.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does ice float on water?
   Answer: Ice (920 kg/m³) is less dense than water (1000 kg/m³).
2. Why can gases be compressed easily but solids cannot?
   Answer: Gas particles have large gaps between them; solid particles are tightly packed.
3. Why does a clinical thermometer have a constriction?
   Answer: It stops mercury flowing back so the maximum temperature can be read after removing it.
4. Why is alcohol used in thermometers in very cold regions?
   Answer: It freezes at −115 °C, whereas mercury freezes at −39 °C.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why do engineers use thermocouples in car engines and furnaces?
   Answer: Wide high-temperature range, fast response, robust, and an electrical output for gauges/computers.
2. Why do hot-air balloons rise?
   Answer: Heated air expands and becomes less dense than the cooler air around it.
